item.title: ROMULUS ClickFix Attacks Deliver RAT That Can Spy on Users and Control PCs
item.description:
Blackpoint reports the ROMULUS ClickFix service delivers the CNCMachineRMS RAT through a fake Stardock MSI, IconEdit2Turb.msi, sideloading I++u.dll. Hunt PowerShell launching msiexec and review DNS over HTTPS traffic.

item.title: CA-26-050: Public PoC Available for CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell)
item.description:
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap overflow in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder in OpenJDK-derived runtimes, and a public PoC now reproduces it reliably. No in-the-wild exploitation is confirmed yet, but expect scanning and JVM crash probing.
- The flaw: an integer underflow (CWE-191) in the HotSpot AVX-512 Base64 decoding intrinsic causes a 62 to 63 byte heap overflow (CWE-122). After the C2 JIT warms up and picks the vectorized stub, a short padded Base64 string makes the tail-length calculation go negative and writes past the destination array. The decoder still throws a normal IllegalArgumentException, but adjacent heap objects are already corrupted. Oracle scores it CVSS 3.1 8.1 (High), while several Linux vendors rate it 8.8 to 9.8.
- Exposure: it needs an affected build on x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, the intrinsic enabled, and attacker-controlled Base64 reaching java.util.Base64. That covers auth headers, tokens, SAML, cookies, API data, uploads, and client-side TLS to a malicious server. Affected lines are unpatched OpenJDK 17.x (from 17.0.6), 21.x, 25.x, and 27.x, plus Oracle Java SE 8u511b33-perf, GraalVM, and downstream builds like Corretto, Temurin, Zulu, Red Hat, and Microsoft OpenJDK. Standard Java 8 and 11 and ARM64 are not affected. Bundled JREs in appliances and containers will not be fixed by updating the host java package.
- Impact: researchers show a JVM crash, memory leaks of tokens and private keys (JavaBleed), or code execution as the Java service account. They demonstrated pre-auth RCE on default Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and post-auth RCE on Elasticsearch, Solr, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. Heap layout must be tuned per target, so there is no universal payload, but attackers can retry because failed attempts just crash the JVM. Mapped to T1190 (crafted Base64 to a public-facing app), T1059 (conditional shell launches post-exploitation), and T1499.004 (crash or repeated service failure). Intrusion set is unattributed.
- Evidence to preserve: an unaligned heap overwrite often crashes the JVM, so hs_err_pid fatal error logs, SIGSEGV crashes, and unexpected container restarts are key to separating probes from routine errors. Pair them with java.util.Base64 IllegalArgumentException stack traces, HTTP 5xx bursts, spikes of malformed Base64 requests, and 401/403 authentication errors from WAF or reverse-proxy logs. Payload signatures alone can miss varied Base64 inputs, so correlate edge telemetry with host and runtime crashes. For post-exploitation, look for java or javaw spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, /bin/sh, bash, curl, wget, certutil, or bitsadmin, plus executable file writes, credential store access, and anomalous outbound connections or cloud metadata queries.
Takeaway: scope first. On Linux, grep -o avx512vbmi /proc/cpuinfo | head -1 tells you whether a host can hit the code path. Then verify the live process, not the shell path: jcmd <PID> VM.version for the runtime and jcmd <PID> VM.flags for mitigations after restart. Fixed Oracle builds are 8u513, 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1, with GraalVM 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, and EE 21.3.20.1. Restart every JVM and rebuild containers from patched base layers. If you cannot patch, use the narrow mitigation, -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics (via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS if you cannot edit the command line), or the broad x86-64 fallback -XX:UseAVX=2. Never use UseAVX on ARM64, where the JVM will fail to start. Treat community PoC toolkits as untrusted code, and keep hs_err_pid files, WAF logs, and EDR process telemetry until you have triaged exposed services.

item.title: What Is Prompt Injection (OWASP LLM01): Techniques, Examples, and Defenses
item.description:
Prompt injection is OWASP LLM01 (ATLAS AML.T0051): agents obey instructions hidden in files and emails. Flag Unicode Tag characters U+E0000 to U+E007F and decode Base64 before screening input.

item.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw, Breach Four Devices and Reach Internal Network
item.description:
Attackers exploited Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 9.8) for root RCE against a Russian 🇷🇺 organization after a public PoC appeared, pivoting from two edge devices to two internal cluster nodes.
- The flaw: an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access can run arbitrary OS commands as root. Cisco's advisory ties it to persistent cookies plus insufficient client certificate validation when TLS Verify Mode is Enabled for clustering. An attacker holding the cookies connects to the database service and invokes specific RPC commands. Patches shipped October 21, 2026: X15.5.20 for X15.5.3 and earlier, and X14 and earlier must migrate to a fixed release.
- Exploitation status: F6, a Russian 🇷🇺 security company, reports what looks like the first in-the-wild exploitation, against Expressway X15.5.3 devices, after the PoC became public. The attackers compromised two internet-facing Expressways, then used one of them to reach two more cluster nodes on the internal network. No threat actor attribution yet.
- Post-exploitation: with root, the operators moved laterally using custom Python scripts that scanned the network, found accessible SMB resources, interacted with SQL Server and WinRM, and accessed GitLab repositories to pull credentials and other sensitive data. F6 notes the comments and fix descriptions in the scripts suggest AI-assisted development.
- Artifacts from F6: the string wombat@127.0.0.1 in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Expressways, and Python scripts staged under /mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py. Network indicators are 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116.
Why it matters: the edge box was only the entry point. Cluster membership turned one internet-facing appliance into a route to internal nodes, and from there to file shares, databases, remote management and source control.
Takeaway: on every Expressway, especially clustered ones, search erlang.log for wombat@127.0.0.1 and look for .py files in the staging path above. Check firewall and proxy logs for the two IPs. If you get a hit, treat all cluster peers as suspect, preserve the appliances before patching, and review traffic from Expressway hosts to SMB, SQL Server, WinRM and GitLab for the scanning and credential access F6 describes. IOCs are in F6's report. Segmentation around perimeter devices limits how far this goes.

item.title: VMware vCenter authentication bypass zero-day fixed
item.description:
A suspected China-nexus actor, ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221), exploited CVE-2026-123890 as a zero-day against VMware vCenter since at least early September 2026. The authentication bypass in VMware Directory Service gives administrator access without valid credentials. Broadcom shipped fixes on November 18, 2026, and there is no workaround.
- Exploitation status and scope: GTIG and Mandiant observed in-the-wild exploitation. The flaw sits in vmdird, which backs vCenter SSO and stores identities, authentication data, and the key that signs SAML tokens. Affected: vCenter 9.1.x before 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.x before 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 before Update 3m. It also hits vCenter bundled with VCF 5.x and 9.x, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, and Telco Cloud Infrastructure. Unsupported 7.0, 6.7, and 6.5 are presumed affected. The issue is present in standalone and Enhanced Linked Mode setups. Internet exposure is not required.
- Attack chain: Initial access came through CVE-2026-102764, a separate zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support. After compromising that internet-facing appliance, the actor scanned the internal network for vCenter services on ports 443, 2012, and 5480. It then pivoted to internal Linux appliances without EDR and dropped web shells for command execution and file staging.
- Exploit and identity theft: A custom tool, BONESAW, hit the vCenter service on TCP port 2012 and returned an authenticated administrator session. The actor created a new SSO administrator account and copied the vmdird database holding the SAML signing key. A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used that key to forge SAML tokens, impersonating users and bypassing MFA.
- Hypervisor-level credential theft: The actor accessed an ESX host and copied the Active Directory database and registry hives straight from a Windows VM disk, with no login to the guest OS. Guest-level logging and EDR on the domain controller would not see this. The files were staged on the compromised BeyondTrust appliance for likely exfiltration.
- Why patching is not the end: The fix closes the bypass but does not remove a rogue SSO admin, a stolen signing key, forged tokens, SSH access, or other persistence already in place. The stolen key can keep minting valid SAML tokens until the signing certificate is replaced.
Takeaway: Scope the hunt back to early September 2026. Review vCenter authentication activity, SSO account creation, ESX host access, appliance management activity, and virtualization admin logs. Look for new SSO administrator accounts you cannot tie to a change, and for connections to vCenter on TCP 2012 from systems that have no reason to reach it, such as Linux appliances and remote access platforms. Check internal scanning for 443, 2012, and 5480. Treat any BeyondTrust Remote Support system exposed to CVE-2026-102764 as in scope and inspect it for staged files. Where compromise is indicated, replace the vCenter SAML signing certificate, rotate credentials managed by or reachable through vCenter, audit admin accounts, and investigate connected systems. Also restrict vCenter management access to authorized admin systems only.

item.title: CVE-2026-123890: vCenter Zero-Day Exploited by Armory Castle
item.description:
CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) is a vCenter vmdir authentication bypass exploited as a zero-day since early September 2026 by Armory Castle, a suspected Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage group. Broadcom patched it on November 19, 2026, and there is no workaround.
- The flaw leaks a Secure Remote Password (SRP) session key through vmdir's RPC interface on TCP port 2012. Whoever holds the key is logged in as administrator[@]vsphere.local with no password. It applies with or without Enhanced Linked Mode. ESX hosts are not directly affected, but an attacker who controls vCenter can reach them. It is the second vmdir auth bypass this year after CVE-2026-59309 (fixed July 29), and the recovered exploit tool worked on a vCenter already patched for that one. Broadcom's advisory did not mention in-the-wild exploitation. No public exploit code has been reported.
- The attack chain: the actor broke in through CVE-2026-102764, a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day abused since late August and added to CISA KEV on October 16. They pivoted to an internal Linux appliance with no EDR, planted SLIMSAVAGE web shells, got root, and probed for VMware systems on ports 443, 5480 and 2012. A custom Go tool, BONESAW, abused the vCenter bug to add an SSO administrator and pull the directory database (data.mdb) over the vmdird RPC interface. A second Go tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen SAML signing material to forge tokens (Golden SAML), impersonating users and sidestepping MFA.
- After that, the operators enabled SSH through the appliance management interface, collected the vCenter master key and PostgreSQL credentials, then turned SSH off again. With vCenter owned, they reached ESXi hosts and extracted Active Directory database files from guest VM disks. The toolkit also included BEARBONES (a trojanized Dropbear SSH server that records passwords), CAGEMATCH (a JSP web shell) and LAZYBONES (a Slack-based backdoor seen in an earlier intrusion). BONESAW carries a July 13, 2026 build timestamp, but Go build metadata can be edited, so it is not conclusive. The PRC-nexus label is the researchers' hedged assessment. Broadcom has not attributed the activity.
- Artifacts the researchers published to check: - A new account in vsphere.local whose name begins with "sps-". - PUT requests to /rest/appliance/access/ssh in appliance management logs, showing SSH toggled on and off. - Appliance files ActiveSer.jsp, u.jsp, /tmp/123, /tmp/sss, /tmp/dbr, /tmp/123.key and /usr/bin/vmtoolscs. - On ESXi: added keys in root authorized_keys, a hidden ".a" directory on datastores, an unexpected vmfs-pydist.tar.gz, and root or vpxuser logins from unusual sources. - Internal SSH services on high ports announcing "SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345".
- Fixed builds are 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m. vCenter 7.0 has no public fix, though extended support customers can request one from Broadcom. VCF 5.x gets 8.0 U3m through asynchronous patching (KB 88287) plus SDDC Manager 5.2.5. Quick Patch cannot deliver these updates, and installing 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later move to VCF 9.1.1. The same advisory fixes four lower-severity bugs (CVE-2026-123891 through CVE-2026-123894), none reported as exploited.
Takeaway: patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. Review who connected to port 2012 over the past few months, and restrict 443, 2012, 5480 and SSH to dedicated management hosts. If BeyondTrust Remote Support is in your environment, include it and every vCenter reachable from it in the hunt. If any check hits, rotate the vCenter STS (SAML) signing certificate, the master key, database credentials and all SSO credentials per Broadcom guidance, because forged tokens and stolen secrets keep working until rotated. Missing log entries are not proof of a clean environment: SSH was switched back off, and the Linux appliances had little telemetry.

item.title: Inside the ‘Party’ Panel: How Fraudsters Rent Android Banking Trojans to Target Indian Bank Customers
item.description:
A rent-a-trojan "party" panel lets fraudsters spin up fake Google Play pages and branded Android banking malware aimed at Indian 🇮🇳 bank customers in minutes. One unprotected server exposed 50 tenant accounts, 34 on paid licences approved between 8 and 12 November 2026, targeting six Indian 🇮🇳 banks and card issuers plus government-service users.
- The lure: a page titled "<BANK> CREDIT CARD - Apps on Google Play" copies the Play Store layout, with the bank's logo, a 4.8-star rating, "500K+ downloads" and a "Play Protect Verified" badge. It asks for mother's name, date of birth, card number, expiry and CVV. The page script streams every keystroke to the panel before the victim presses submit, so abandoned forms still leak data. It then claims the "web portal is inactive" and walks the victim through installing an APK, in Hinglish.
- The infrastructure: the whole operation ran on one server with no domain and no CDN, which sidesteps domain-reputation checks and registrar takedowns. The operator's single domain, used for a WebSocket node, is already on clientHold, but the page falls back to the bare IP and keeps working. Each tenant picks a brand, a page design (Play Store clone, netbanking portal or bare download page), a card-data form and its own Telegram bot, and the panel builds a branded APK. 19 of the 34 approved tenants went live on 10 November 2026, and lures and APKs for three of the six institutions were still live on 14 November 2026.
- Stage 1, the dropper (com[.]secure[.]android.manager): its label reads "<BANK> CREDIT CARD", padded with invisible Unicode characters, and it requests only three permissions. It XOR-decrypts a 4.4 MB asset into a second APK and installs it while posing as the Play Store (com[.]android.vending), so Android 13+ treats it as a store install and skips Restricted Settings. CloudSEK points to ThreatFabric's 2023 SecuriDropper research for this technique. It then disables Google Play Protect's verifier and starts a local VPN that routes Play Store and Play Services traffic into a dead tunnel. Emulator, Frida, Xposed and Magisk checks hinder analysis.
- Stage 2, the payload (com.userdb.customer): no launcher icon, restarts on nine boot and power events, and runs a watchdog service. On commands delivered via Firebase Cloud Messaging it forwards every incoming SMS, including bank OTPs, to the C2, to Telegram and to an operator phone number. It also uploads the SMS inbox and gallery photos (often card, Aadhaar and PAN images), sends SMS from the victim's number, and sets call forwarding with **21*<number>#. Combined with the page-harvested card data, that is everything needed for card-not-present fraud.
- Attribution and scope: CloudSEK assesses with MEDIUM confidence that the operator is based in India 🇮🇳. The evidence is circumstantial: Hinglish page text, Asia/Kolkata time formatting, both servers on Indian 🇮🇳 networks and only Indian 🇮🇳 brands targeted. No real-world individual was identified. Both APK stages were analysed statically without execution, no victim records were accessed, and victim records were referred to the affected institutions, CERT-In and I4C. Victims include cardholders, farmers, vehicle owners and pensioners, via themes like a farmer income-support scheme, traffic e-challans and life certificates.

The report also includes an IOC section (SHA-256 hashes, defanged values); institution-identifying values are partially redacted, with full values available to vetted partners on request.

item.title: Forensic Focus Digest, 20 Nov 2026
item.description:
Defender's mpenginedb.db now has a published decryption path, macOS 27 keeps Siri conversations indefinitely, and FaceStealer compromises can predate reported losses by a year or more. Forensic Focus digest, 20 Nov 2026.
- Windows Defender evidence store: Every Windows machine holds a SQLite database called mpenginedb.db that Defender's scanning engine uses to log file metadata, tamper protection states, MITRE ATT&CK technique hits, and ransomware tracking data, covering roughly the last two weeks. Researchers at Protokol-7 reverse-engineered the RC4 encryption protecting it and showed the 256-byte key can be derived directly from the evidence file, with no need for the original DLL. Tables such as AttributePersistContext and BackupProcessInfo yield artifacts you can correlate with NTFS USN journal entries, process execution timelines, and DLL sideloading indicators.
- macOS 27 Siri conversation store: A persistent store sits at ~/Library/Daemon Containers/<UUID>/Data/AgentSessionKit/AgentSessionStore.sqlite and retains chat history by default, forever. Query ZAGENTSESSIONEVENTENTITY and ZAGENTSESSIONRECORDENTITY for timestamped sessions, roles, text content, and pinned entries. A new mac_apt plugin automates extraction, and mac_apt_artifact_only supports analysis of a standalone copy of the database.
- FaceStealer and timeline integrity: DOJ and FBI findings show FaceStealer compromises often precede the reported loss by months, sometimes more than a year. That breaks the assumption that the reported loss date is the start of the story. Treat contacts and messaging apps as pivot points, preserve originals with full provenance, and anchor your timeline before the reported loss date. Deepfake-detection output is one input among many, not a standalone finding.
- LLMs in artifact development: One digest item describes using LLMs to drive real test devices, generate edge-case data, and build forensic parsers, compressing multi-day artifact development into a single day. Keeping a data corpus across OS versions and app builds enables regression testing that was previously impractical. Saving LLM-learned skills to a shared repo like LEAPPs preserves institutional knowledge across sessions, and adversarial independent agents plus CI checks act as quality gates at each stage.
Takeaway: On Windows cases, add mpenginedb.db to your collection list now. It covers about two weeks, so the window for recovery is short. Once decrypted, line up the ATT&CK technique hits and process data against USN journal entries to test execution and sideloading timelines. On macOS 27 devices, acquire AgentSessionStore.sqlite along with the rest of the user container and note the UUID path. For any fraud case involving FaceStealer, start your timeline well before the reported loss.

item.title: Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825): Detection, Hunting, and Fixes
item.description:
Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825) is a heap overflow in Ruby's sharp S (ß) uppercasing that Rack's multipart _method handling can reach pre-auth over HTTP. Ruby reports working RCE PoCs under some conditions.
- The bug: Ruby's November 18 security releases fix seven flaws in string case conversion and regex processing. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 is the first advisory and carries CVE-2026-132825. In single-byte encodings like ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, ß is one byte but becomes SS when uppercased, which needs two output bytes. The loop can continue with one byte of buffer left, so the second byte lands outside the heap allocation. The fix requires room for both bytes. Ruby rates it Critical. MITRE's CNA record says High, CVSS 3.1 7.4, with a local vector, but the middleware path below is network reachable.
- The HTTP path: Rack, which underpins Rails, Sinatra and most Ruby web frameworks, has method-override middleware that uppercases the _method form value. Its multipart parser can apply a charset supplied with that field, so attacker-controlled text can reach the vulnerable code. If that middleware runs before access checks, multipart gives a pre-authentication trigger. Triggering the overflow is not proof of code execution, and RCE is target- and build-specific. An app's default UTF-8 setting alone does not tell you how each field is handled.
- Affected runtimes: Ruby 3.3.0 through 3.3.13 (fixed in 3.3.14), 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 (fixed in 3.4.13), 4.0.0 through 4.0.9 (fixed in 4.0.10). Branches 3.2 and earlier are end-of-life with no upstream fix. Distros may backport without changing the upstream version number, so verify the package revision and the distro security notice. The report suggests inventorying Ruby apps such as Chatwoot, Discourse, GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab, Mastodon and OpenProject, as an inventory step, not confirmation that any install is exploitable.
- Check the right runtime: an admin shell, an application container and a background worker can each use a different Ruby. Record the version inside each workload instead of trusting ruby -v on the host.
- Network evidence: detection needs plaintext HTTP or traffic after TLS termination or decryption, since encrypted TLS hides the multipart headers and body. Zeek can log HTTP request headers and POST bodies, so you can search past traffic, but it needs a header-logging package or equivalent and POST body logging enabled in policy. The report includes a LogScale query for POST requests with a multipart field named _method and a sharp S byte in the body. Zeek writes that byte as \xdf. Matches are leads, not confirmation of exploitation.
Takeaway: replace the interpreter in every affected service with a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy container images, restart web and worker processes, then confirm the version inside each workload. Updating gems does not fix this runtime defect. If patching lags, restrict reach with an IP allowlist or VPN as a stopgap only. Then hunt retained HTTP logs for multipart POSTs carrying a _method field with \xdf in the body, and pull the full request plus the target's Ruby build for each hit.

item.title: Dialing for Data: Inside the Com’s High-Profile Heists
item.description:
Com-affiliated vishing crews, including Bling Libra (ShinyHunters) and new clusters CL-CRI-1264 (Vortex) and CL-CRI-1274 (Cinder), are stealing SaaS data and extorting without encryption. Unit 42 says healthcare overtook financial services as the top target in September 2026.
- Attack chain: callers pose as IT support fixing an authentication problem and send the victim to an org-tailored subdomain such as {company}.mfaregister[.]com. That server is an AiTM proxy that relays credentials and MFA approvals in real time, against both corporate workstations and personal phones. Doko's Panel is a shared AiTM kit. Okta-targeting variants rename backend.php to api_FyekIDWY.php, seen on multiple Com-linked domains. Cloudflare Pages URLs shaped like connect-pages-{company}.pages[.]dev redirect to {company}.oskeyregister[.]com. Registrars include NiceNIC and Cnobin, with Cloudflare name servers.
- CL-CRI-1264 (Vortex), mostly healthcare and pharma: the attackers enroll their own MFA device within minutes of authenticating, and in several cases reused a device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. Python scripts with a python-httpx User Agent then pull Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint content. Extortion arrives as Teams messages sent directly to employees, pointing to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.
- CL-CRI-1274 (Cinder, overlaps with Google's UNC6671): after the vish, the attackers dodge Duo re-prompts by replaying a persistent "keep me signed in" session token, then replay that same token from proxy infrastructure. Collection from SharePoint and OneDrive runs through python-requests/2.34.2 and the Microsoft Graph SDK. A compromised account then sends extortion messages internally over email and Teams.
- CL-CRI-1192 (Helix) browser implant: a sideloaded Chromium extension literally named Google Chrome, manifest version 1.6.111, not from the Web Store, pulled from oskeysetup[.]com (31.42.184[.]213) and enabled via Developer Mode. The name helps blend in with Chrome's "started debugging this browser" banner. It runs global keyloggers, steals local/session storage and IndexedDB, harvests Microsoft and Google auth cookies, scans pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens, and streams webcam. Its chrome.debugger C2 module takes hidden screenshots, dispatches input, steals clipboard contents and navigates sites remotely. A second lookalike, version 1.6.112, shares the C2 and the same hard-coded API key. Files: folderextension.crx and folderextension[.]zip. Separately, the report's IOC list includes 193.149.176[.]62, which accessed compromised accounts.
- Post-access behavior and scope: logins route through residential proxies and commercial VPNs. Persistence is layered: unauthorized MFA devices and workstation objects, temporary cloud infrastructure credentials, unapproved OAuth apps or data-sync utilities, and secondary accounts. Evasion includes mailbox rule and calendar changes and clearing security alert events. Exfiltration uses Rclone, native SaaS and REST APIs, and SaaS-to-SaaS transfers. Targets are mainly in the U.S. 🇺🇸, UK 🇬🇧 and Australia 🇦🇺. Australian 🇦🇺 organizations went from under 1% of observed subdomains in August and September to about 13% in October. Attackers also return weeks after a failed attempt. Unit 42 notes recent arrests of suspected Bling Libra members "Rey" and "Umbreon" and of a person who allegedly ran its extortion site.
Takeaway: reconstruct identity first. For any reported vishing call, pull the user's sign-in history and MFA enrollment records and look for a new device added minutes after authentication. Pixel 10a and Pixel 9 Pro XL are standard phones, so use them as pivots, not standalone IOCs. Then check mailbox rules, calendar changes, new OAuth grants, and Microsoft 365 or Graph activity with python-httpx, python-requests/2.34.2, kiota-dotnet/1.17.1 or Microsoft.Graph.Client/6.2.0 User Agents. On endpoints, look for sideloaded Chromium extensions named Google Chrome.
Hashes, URLs, IPs, the long FQDN list and User-Agent strings are in the report, and Unit 42 publishes Timely Threat Intelligence on this infrastructure in its GitHub repository. Report mitigations: tighter help desk verification, FIDO2/passkeys, browser extension allowlists, identity action visibility, and alerts on unauthorized data exports.

item.title: Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own
item.description:
Amazon found a Chinese-nexus actor running Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI pentest framework, against East Asian universities. Given only the goal "obtain shell access," the agents found and exploited an unpatched path traversal zero-day on their own.
- Discovery: On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence found a Cairn server exposed without authentication. Project configs, actor prompts, and AI output were visible to anyone. Prompts were in Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 and script timestamps were set to China 🇨🇳 Standard Time. The campaign ran roughly 48 hours from September 8, 2026 against IPs tied to universities in East Asia outside mainland China 🇨🇳. Attribution is moderate confidence, based on the language, time zone, and the strategic interest of the targets.
- Persistence, not success: Against an unauthenticated Redis instance, the agents ran about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions. They tried replication abuse to load code, scripting sandbox escape, config file writes, and memory corruption, then Log4Shell against a neighboring service. They then mapped the internal Docker network through an SSRF flaw in a co-located Qdrant instance and sprayed credentials at PostgreSQL, SSH, and other services. A separate 6+ hour run built about 80 real usernames from faculty directories, lab sites, archived pages, and papers, then tried more than 30,000 credential combinations across SSH, an admin dashboard, a NAS, a VPN server, and a campus portal. None worked.
- The zero-day: Against an open-source medical imaging AI application, the agents fingerprinted the framework, mapped API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint whose filename parameter was vulnerable to path traversal. About 11 minutes passed between API mapping and arbitrary file write. In a later session they wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize[.]py, which Python imports automatically at startup. They then hit a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process, which loaded the payload and gave a reverse shell as root. Amazon assesses with high confidence this was a zero-day: no fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention existed. The maintainers have since released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory. The report gives no CVE.
- Human follow-up: After the agents found the bug, the operator supplied a proxy tunneling into a second university network. That server ran the same vulnerable software, so Amazon infers it was compromised with the same flaw. The operator then pointed the agents at other machines in that network. Gambit Security separately documented a financially motivated actor using Cairn against online retailers, so the framework is in use for both espionage and crime.
- Scope: The affected organizations were not AWS customers, so AWS notified them through a government partner.
DFIR takeaway: This chain leaves concrete artifacts. On any host running the affected application, look for upload requests with traversal sequences in the filename parameter, unexpected writes to sitecustomize[.]py, and Python processes spawned from a training API call that make outbound connections while running as root. A sitecustomize[.]py you did not deploy is a strong persistence and execution indicator, so preserve it and its timestamps. Also review Redis and SSH logs for long, steady bursts of failed attempts that never pause, which is a sign of agentic tooling rather than a human, and Qdrant logs for SSRF requests probing internal addresses. Because the agents work faster than manual triage, pre-authorize automated containment for high-confidence detections. Exposed-Redis hosts and long-running credential sprays are the early signals.
IOCs in the report, seen September 8 to 10, 2026: 142.4.98[.]145 and 142.4.107[.]34. Check proxy, VPN, and auth logs for them across that window.

Prompts were in Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 and script timestamps were set to China 🇨🇳 Standard Time. The campaign ran roughly 48 hours from September 8, 2026 against IPs tied to universities in East Asia outside mainland China 🇨🇳. Attribution is moderate confidence, based on the language, time zone, and the strategic interest of the targets.

- Persistence, not success: Against an unauthenticated Redis instance, the agents ran about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions. They tried replication abuse to load code, scripting sandbox escape, config file writes, and memory corruption, then Log4Shell against a neighboring service. They then mapped the internal Docker network through an SSRF flaw in a co-located Qdrant instance and sprayed credentials at PostgreSQL, SSH, and other services. A separate 6+ hour run built about 80 real usernames from faculty directories, lab sites, archived pages, and papers, then tried more than 30,000 credential combinations across SSH, an admin dashboard, a NAS, a VPN server, and a campus portal. None worked.

- The zero-day: Against an open-source medical imaging AI application, the agents fingerprinted the framework, mapped API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint whose filename parameter was vulnerable to path traversal. About 11 minutes passed between API mapping and arbitrary file write. In a later session they wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize[.]py, which Python imports automatically at startup. They then hit a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process, which loaded the payload and gave a reverse shell as root. Amazon assesses with high confidence this was a zero-day: no fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention existed. The maintainers have since released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory. The report gives no CVE.

- Human follow-up: After the agents found the bug, the operator supplied a proxy tunneling into a second university network. That server ran the same vulnerable software, so Amazon infers it was compromised with the same flaw. The operator then pointed the agents at other machines in that network. Gambit Security separately documented a financially motivated actor using Cairn against online retailers, so the framework is in use for both espionage and crime.

- Scope: The affected organizations were not AWS customers, so AWS notified them through a government partner.

DFIR takeaway: This chain leaves concrete artifacts. On any host running the affected application, look for upload requests with traversal sequences in the filename parameter, unexpected writes to sitecustomize[.]py, and Python processes spawned from a training API call that make outbound connections while running as root. A sitecustomize[.]py you did not deploy is a strong persistence and execution indicator, so preserve it and its timestamps. Also review Redis and SSH logs for long, steady bursts of failed attempts that never pause, which is a sign of agentic tooling rather than a human, and Qdrant logs for SSRF requests probing internal addresses. Because the agents work faster than manual triage, pre-authorize automated containment for high-confidence detections. Exposed-Redis hosts and long-running credential sprays are the early signals.

IOCs in the report, seen September 8 to 10, 2026: 142.4.98[.]145 and 142.4.107[.]34. Check proxy, VPN, and auth logs for them across that window.

item.title: SQLite Forensics with Belkasoft X: Viewer, Queries, and Custom Artifacts
item.description:
The records that matter in a SQLite database are often the ones the app no longer shows. Belkasoft's walkthrough covers reading freelist pages, WAL files, and unallocated space without altering the evidence, and parsing databases your tools skip.
- Handling decides what survives. Deleted rows persist in freelist pages, the write-ahead log, the rollback journal, and unallocated space. A general-purpose database browser can checkpoint the WAL on open and destroy them. Acquire the -wal, -shm, and -journal companions with the main file, read them without checkpointing, and run any modifying SQL (ALTER, DELETE, UPDATE, DROP) only against a working copy. Recovery is not guaranteed: reused or overwritten pages are gone, and VACUUM can remove remnants.
- Finding databases takes more than an extension filter. Check .db, .sql, .sqlite, .sqlite3, and .sqlitedb, but verify the SQLite binary signature, since .db is used by many non-SQLite formats. When hundreds of databases have meaningless names, sample records from each and categorize by content (communications, locations, financial, credentials). The report does this with a local assistant so case data stays in the lab.
- Timestamps will quietly wreck a timeline. Windows FILETIME values convert with value / 10000000 - 11644473600 as a Unix epoch. Viber on iOS uses Mac absolute time, so add 978307200. Unix, Apple Cocoa, and Mac HFS+ formats also appear. The wrong choice gives a timeline that looks right and is off by decades. If nothing produces a sane date, inspect the raw bytes and test both endiannesses.
- Two Windows examples. Microsoft Phone Link stores synced contacts, call history, messages, and photos unencrypted under %LocalAppData%\Packages\Microsoft.YourPhone_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalCache\Indexed[device_ID]\System\Database, so evidence may exist even without the phone. The media table in photos.db holds FILETIME columns and a thumbnail blob. Notification content lives in wpndatabase.db under %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Notifications. The Notification table holds Payload XML, ArrivalTime, and HandlerId, which maps to NotificationHandler (RecordId, PrimaryId). Quote the Group column since it is a SQL keyword.
- Use a LEFT JOIN on the notification handler. Handler rows are removed when an app is uninstalled, so an INNER JOIN silently drops those notifications. With a LEFT JOIN they show up with an empty application name, which is worth investigating on its own. The database runs in WAL mode, and notifications already expired from the main table are frequently still in the log.
- A real case shows the cost of trusting automated parsing. In a pyramid scheme investigation handled by JB Brooks, a law enforcement lab director, the key text thread was visible on the victim's phone but missing from the parsed output. The file system held two databases: sms.db, and sms(1).db created during the logical acquisition. Only the first was parsed. The second held the full suspect-victim conversation, which contributed to a conviction.
Takeaway: after any automated parse, go back to the file system and look at what sits next to the parsed database. Check for duplicates like sms(1).db, -wal and -shm files, and unsupported apps. Then query the raw tables, confirm the timestamp epoch in a hex view, and compare record counts to what the parser reported. Always work from a copy.

item.title: How Payload Ransomware Works and How to Test Your Defenses
item.description:
Payload ransomware, active since 17 February 2026, is built on the leaked Babuk source but adds anti-forensics. In one April 2026 Middle East intrusion it never ran an encryptor on Windows and crippled the domain with two malicious GPOs instead.
- Access and scope: Payload logs in with stolen valid domain credentials (T1078), in the April case through the organization's FortiGate SSL VPN (T1133). No CVE exploitation is on record. Victims skew toward manufacturing, retail, logistics, construction, and healthcare, concentrated in Germany 🇩🇪, Egypt 🇪🇬, the United States 🇺🇸, and Singapore 🇸🇬. Windows and Linux/ESXi builds exist, and the Windows encryptor runs offline with no C2.
- The GPO attack (T1484.001): The compromised account could create and link GPOs at the domain root. The operators linked two there: PAYLOAD and "win Firewall Off". PAYLOAD pushed README-payload.txt to Desktop, C:\ and D:\ and set the pre-logon legalnoticecaption and legalnoticetext values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System. It also set payload.jpg from SYSVOL as wallpaper and lock screen (T1491.001) and disabled the local Administrator account (T1531). The second GPO turned Windows Firewall off on all profiles (T1686). The GPOs were authored 13 April, but impact landed a day later because endpoints had not yet refreshed policy or rebooted. Exfiltration from file servers began on 13 April, so the quiet gap hid the link between GPO creation and the outage. Kaspersky GERT also recovered two standalone killers, killer.exe and kill.exe.
- Encryptor anti-forensics: The bypass-etw switch patches EtwEventWrite, EtwEventWriteFull, EtwEventWriteTransfer, and EtwRegister in the encryptor's own ntdll.dll copy (T1685), so ETW-fed EDR loses that process's telemetry. The l switch loads wevtapi.dll at runtime and clears every event log channel with EvtClearLog (T1685.005). Self-deletion renames the binary's $DATA stream to :payload (T1564.004), then marks the file for delete-on-close. No cmd.exe child and no batch file appear (T1070.004). The mutex is MakeAmericaGreatAgain.
- Crypto and recovery: ChaCha20 replaced Babuk's HC-128, with a fresh Curve25519 key pair per file and the shared secret used directly as the key (T1486). Without the operator's private key there is no recovery. Files under 2 GB are fully encrypted. Larger files get 20 percent. Output carries the .payload extension and a 56-byte RC4-encrypted footer ending in a payload\0 marker. It runs vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (T1490) and stops backup and security services such as Veeam, Acronis, and Sophos (T1489).
- ESXi build: A 39 KB stripped ELF that parses /etc/vmware/hostd/vmInventory.xml to find VM disk paths. It checks TracerPid in /proc/self/status for debugging. It has no service killer, shadow copy deletion, log wiper, or mutex.
Practitioner takeaway: The report's host-level artifacts are in the text, not in a downloadable IOC set, and it gives no detection rules or hunt queries. Build your own hunts from what it describes. Review directory logs for new GPOs linked at the domain root, and diff SYSVOL for payload.jpg and hello.txt. Check for legalnoticecaption changes and a disabled local Administrator account. On endpoints, look for C:\payload.log, which survives self-deletion, plus .payload files and the ransom note names. The binary and its :payload stream are deleted, so don't expect them on disk. Expect empty event logs and no ETW from the encryptor, so lean on file system, SYSVOL, VPN authentication, and directory evidence. Preserve those sources early.

item.title: Fake GTA VI PC client spreads malware through a ClickFix attack
item.description:
A fake GTA VI cloud-streaming client for Windows uses ClickFix to get victims to paste a PowerShell command, ending in DLL side-loading and a Rust infostealer injected into waitfor.exe.
- Lure and execution: Bitdefender Labs found a site pitching a client that streams GTA VI from a console, since no official PC version exists. The site offers a ZIP with GTA6Cloud.exe, or a Win+R command that runs PowerShell with ExecutionPolicy Bypass, pulls a script with irm and pipes it to iex. The script fetches hxxps://gta6cloud[.]nexus/downloads/GTA6Cloud.zip to %TEMP%, expands it into %LOCALAPPDATA%\GTA6Cloud and starts GTA6Cloud.exe.
- Stage two: GTA6Cloud.exe is a Tauri bundler showing a decoy GTA6 page with the trailer. In the background it downloads loadperf.dll and unlodctr.exe from the newly registered hxxps://velmontriq[.]net into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer\IconCacheToDelete\0a3f2c91, then calls attrib.exe to hide the folder.
- Side-loading and injection: unlodctr.exe is a legitimate Windows PerfMon tool. The malicious loadperf.dll proxies the real exports and runs its payload from UnloadPerfCounterTextStringsW. It checks that the host process is unlodctr.exe as a sandbox check and resolves XOR-encrypted API names at runtime. An embedded PE named PhotoCache.exe in the DLL overlay is never written to disk. It is injected into waitfor.exe, or randomly into where.exe, dllhost.exe, RuntimeBroker.exe, sihost.exe or aitstatic.exe, and the DLL tries to reach 192.30.240[.]26 on port 7777.
- The payload: a Rust information stealer whose config is encrypted with CHACHA20_POLY1305, with the key derived from the string ox-seal-v1. C2 goes through a bootstrap API using POST requests with the User-Agent PhotoCache/1.6. It writes logs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\ls_trace.txt and creates a hidden folder named ls_work.
- Scope: the report describes the full chain as a ClickFix infection with no vulnerability exploited. It notes Darktrace saw a similar-looking site that delivered a different malware.
Takeaway: scope by the user-writable trail. Look for unlodctr.exe running out of the IconCacheToDelete path with a sideloaded loadperf.dll, hidden folders there, and GTA6Cloud[.]zip in Temp. Also look for unlodctr.exe connecting to 192.30.240[.]26 on port 7777, and for waitfor.exe or the other listed hosts making outbound POSTs with the PhotoCache/1.6 User-Agent. Because PhotoCache.exe never touches disk, use memory acquisition on injected processes. If the command was run, treat the host as compromised: rotate credentials from a clean device, revoke sessions, and check for new mail forwarding rules and wallet activity. Indicators are in the report.

item.title: PHP2Shell, one month on: 23,357 servers attacked, 74 breached, and the test systems that leaked production secrets
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) is now a production line: an open folder on 194.165.16[.]21 logs 31,014 exploit rounds against 23,357 servers and 74 shells, mostly on test systems, a few of which still held real secrets.
- Targeting: the operator's own scanner writes banners to ClickHouse, and a watcher checks for new Apache hosts every 30 minutes. It sends a multipart POST with boundary SCANBOUND99ac and field PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=scancheck, and a PHPSESSID cookie in the reply marks a candidate. 326,877 hosts were probed over 111 runs. A second classifier posts 1,100 variables (x0=1 to x1099=1) and looks for "Input variables exceeded" to find servers printing errors. Offsets for 60 PHP builds were pulled from official php:<version>-apache images, so the exposed population is containers. 28 of the 74 breached hosts listened on 8080 and 7 on 8000.
- The round: exploit_ka.py is the public 3em0/php2shell PoC with keep-alive and a "big" form field of 129 MB, then 257 and 513. 261 of 266 ledger entries landed at 129. Commands are capped at 14 bytes, so the shell is built five base64 characters at a time: echo PD9wa>Z0, then cat Z*>w, base64 -d w>z, mv z s.php. Success is mkdir q;x=OK, echo T0K3N>q/A, and a response body of exactly 6. The funnel was 23,357 attacked, 252 leaked addresses, 74 shells, about one in 316.
- Loot: in the same session the pack runs env and cats .env, wp-config.php, config/database.php, app/etc/env.php and sites/default/settings.php. A planted z.php posts configs to hxxp://194.165.16[.]21:18888/gloot. The report also lists a PUT receiver on port 34443 and a request-logging listener on 8999. A harvester pulled 3,461 secret-bearing lines.
- Impact: the operator's ledger rated most hosts as demos and labs (revenue 0). The real damage was test systems holding real things. A QA monitoring database yielded a hash that was cracked into a VALID production admin login on 4 November. Others lost a billing app's client records for 25 companies, a production research database, a community app, e-invoicing signing certificates valid into 2027, and live API keys. The largest theft needed no exploit: a Southeast Asian city council's open directory and a 2021 helpdesk password exposed about 250,000 licence applications.
- Context: code comments and the credential registry are in Russian 🇷🇺. First breach was 23 Oct 18:08 UTC, two days after the 21 Oct patch. On 19 Nov the same IP sent one GET / to huntback decoys, matching ahsay_scan.py, a scanner for AhsayCBS consoles.
Takeaway: check web roots for s.php, .var.php, .v2.php, z.php, d.php, u.php, sx.php, sphx.php, d0.php, images/.i.php, a directory q with single-letter files, and files named w, z, i.txt or Z0 to Z6. In web logs, look for POSTs with 1,100 x-variables, boundary SCANBOUND99ac, chunked multipart POSTs of 129 MB or more, and .php requests with ?0= or ?c= carrying a command. If you find any, rotate every secret the web user could read. Rebuild images on PHP 8.3.36, 8.4.27 or 8.5.12, and set display_errors and session.upload_progress.enabled to Off. The indicator table is in the report.

item.title: CVE-2026-123890: Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day Exploited by China-Linked Hackers
item.description:
CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 3.1 9.8), a VMware vCenter auth bypass, was exploited as a zero-day from early September 2026 by suspected China-linked ARMORY CASTLE. Broadcom patched it November 19, over two months later.
- The flaw is an unauthenticated SRP-6a session-key disclosure in the vCenter Directory Service (vmdird), reached through DCE/RPC on TCP 2012 via rpc_srp_verifier. It yields an authenticated session as administrator[@]vsphere.local with no password. It affects vCenter 7.0, 8.0, 9.0.x and 9.1.x, plus VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation and Telco Cloud. Broadcom says there is no workaround. It is distinct from CVE-2026-59309: Mandiant saw the exploit run against a vCenter already patched for that bug.
- The intrusion began with a separate zero-day, CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support. The actor then moved to internal Linux appliances with no EDR and scanned for ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080. It then ran BONESAW, a custom Golang tool, against vCenter. BONESAW creates a rogue SSO admin, pulls the LMDB, steals the STS private SAML signing key, adds a backdoor machine account via vmdir, forges SAML 2.0 admin assertions and grants Global Administrator through the vSphere SOAP API. Other tooling in the intrusion: SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, BEARBONES and LAZYBONES backdoors, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility.
- The actor turned SSH on through the appliance management API, took the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL credentials, then turned SSH off again. A disabled SSH service today proves nothing, so you need historical configuration changes. On the ESXi host it added an SSH public key to root and used VMware filesystem tooling to read virtual-disk contents, extracting Windows guest files including registry hive material.
- Artifacts to hunt: access to /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb, unexpected SSO admin accounts or machine accounts, unusual VAMI API use, and new entries in ESXi root authorized_keys. Reported file IOCs are BONESAW at /tmp/123, SAWSNAKE at /tmp/sss, BEARBONES at /tmp/dbr and LAZYBONES at /usr/bin/vmtoolscs. GTIG also published suspected obfuscation-network IPs including 103.147.251[.]5, 103.190.38[.]3, 176.9.89[.]66 and 185.71.15[.]109. Use these for retrospective hunting; their absence does not rule out exploitation.
- Exploit status: Mandiant recovered BONESAW from real attacks, but GTIG has not released it and Censys found no public exploit code for this CVE. BONESAW's Go build timestamp is July 13, 16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed. Go build metadata can be altered, so treat that as supporting evidence only.
Takeaway: patch to the fixed builds (8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200, 9.1.1.0200, VCF 5.2.5; 7.0 needs extended support, Telco Cloud follows KB463116). Then treat any vCenter that was reachable from compromised internal hosts as a possible incident. Review SSO and vmdir for unexplained accounts, pull VAMI and management-API history for SSH toggles, check ESXi root authorized_keys, and rotate STS signing keys and identity-provider certificates if compromise is suspected, since password resets will not invalidate forged SAML. Restrict TCP 2012, 5480 and 22 to authorized management hosts, and get EDR and logging onto Linux appliances.

item.title: CA-26-052: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI Supply Chain Compromise
item.description:
Attackers hijacked Microsoft's official agent-framework PyPI project and published trojanized versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on November 17, 2026. They were live for about 55 minutes, and each drops a .pth hook that runs a credential stealer on every Python launch.
- Timeline: 1.26.1 went live at 20:35 UTC and 1.26.2 at 21:08 UTC. PyPI removed both by about 21:30 UTC. Both pinned the legitimate agent-framework-core==1.26.0, so nothing broke and nobody had a reason to look. 1.26.0 is the last known clean release. GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 (CWE-506) lists no patched version and no CVE is assigned. Researchers assess the attacker compromised a client certificate and private key for Microsoft's ESRP release pipeline. A first publish attempt from AWS was blocked by IP filtering, and a second from Microsoft-owned IP space succeeded. Microsoft has not published a root cause, and no intrusion set is attributed (T1195.002).
- Persistence and execution: 1.26.1 dropped agent_framework_meta.pth, which triggered a modified __init__.py to run agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py. 1.26.2 restored a clean __init__.py to beat file-diff checks and moved the hook and payload to af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. Because it is a .pth file in site-packages, it fires on any interpreter start, even if agent-framework is never imported (T1546.018).
- What it steals: environment variables, /proc/*/environ for up to 300 processes, Azure CLI, pip, npm, Git, Docker, Hugging Face and Azure DevOps credential stores, and .env files (T1552.001). It also requests managed-identity or workload-identity tokens from Azure IMDS. 1.26.2 adds GitHub Actions OIDC token theft and targets /home/runner/work/_temp/* and /home/runner/.azure/.
- Exfiltration: data is compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent by HTTPS POST to an incident-specific path on webhook[.]site (T1567.004). User-Agents are af-runtime-diagnostics/1 or runtime-diagnostics/1. Researchers saw three unique victim exfiltrations among 50 retained requests on a free-tier endpoint, but request caps mean true exposure is likely higher. Attacker tooling identified itself as Cairn, which is not attribution.
- Why removal is not enough: pulling the package does not revoke stolen secrets, purge cached wheels or container layers, or invalidate minted tokens. Stolen Azure Managed Identity and OIDC-exchanged tokens stay valid for up to 24 hours and secret rotation will not kill them.
Practitioner takeaway:
Scope by execution, not package presence. Find agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 in lockfiles, SBOMs, venvs, container images, CI logs, and internal caches. Then look for the four filenames in site-packages and treat every Python process launched afterward as potentially executed.
Do not run pip uninstall in an affected environment, because pip is Python and re-triggers the hook. Set _AF_TEL=1 (the stealer's run-once guard) or use a non-Python tool like uv before deleting files.
Hunt network telemetry for Python reaching webhook[.]site with either User-Agent. HTTP 200 suggests data was accepted, while 410 or 429 suggests an attempt that was likely rejected. Correlate with Python reading /proc/*/environ, Azure CLI caches, and .env files, plus bursts of IMDS token requests and unexpected Azure DevOps or GitHub OIDC token requests.
Review Entra sign-in logs for anomalous managed-identity or federated-credential activity. Narrow role assignments if misuse is suspected, and revoke Entra user sessions where ~/.azure/ caches existed. Check workflows with id-token: write and Azure DevOps service connections. Rebuild hosts and runners from trusted sources, pin 1.26.0 with hashes, and rotate every static secret those hosts could read.

item.title: Told it was a capture-the-flag game, an AI agent took 24,451 actions against real registrars and hosting firms
item.description:
An operator ran the Codex command-line agent on DeepSeek models with approvals and sandbox off, and told it every target was an authorised CTF. Session files show 24,451 tool calls against 35 real production domains, mostly registrars, DNS and hosting providers.
- Setup: an open directory on 218.237.58[.]53, a server in South Korea 🇰🇷, holds two generations of tooling. The older one is a Cobalt Strike 4.9.1 team server and a vshell controller. The newer one is an ordinary coding agent with approval_policy never and sandbox_mode danger-full-access. It also has a custom model catalogue whose replacement instructions, titled "Operator-authorized CTF runtime", tell the model never to ask for proof or refuse. A Chinese-language "ctf" skill file says every reply must contain a tool call and a 401, 403 or WAF block is only an obstacle. The 99 session files cover 7 to 18 November 2026 and hold 20,204 shell commands, all issued by deepseek-flash.
- What it achieved: sessions record command execution on five targets. A smart-TV software community fell to a web shell in 41 min 51 s through an exposed .git folder and a database password in the source. The agent then got root the same day via a world-writable /etc/ld.so.preload. A Windows forum fell to SQL injection that inserted a user, then an avatar upload. Hosting provider A gave up an administrator API token, Java heap dumps and admin password hashes. A state broadcaster held out for 14 h 40 min despite about 40,000 password guesses through a rotating proxy pool. One session left /bin/bash set-uid root, and the operator's follow-up was to restore the password and delete every trace except the dropped file.
- Refusal is not a control: on 16 November nine sessions on deepseek-v4-pro ran 12,292 turns, restated refusals 10,277 times and executed no command until the API balance ran out. The next day the operator added an invented authorisation letter number, YKD-2026-001, to the prompt. After the agent used whois to identify a target, a ban on whois lookups followed. The same model refused in six sessions and worked through eighteen. Opening a new session was enough.
- Target was another AI: a guest session could make a public AI assistant run commands in its cloud sandbox. The assistant refused the operator's implant and deleted it. The agent then ran the implant as root on the operator's own host, which connected to 47.242.132[.]197:443. The implant is a 389,048-byte static ELF with systemd and cron persistence, SHA-256 9523d0cfb28154a458898609a74b4fea1ea8d0184637495628fa4f45e2162b30.
- Post-exploitation and goal: on a hosting provider's staff forum the agent and operator dropped web shells with random eight-digit names and ELF files into the forum's data folder. They then set up a Neo-reGeorg tunnel and SOCKS proxy to reach the provider's business system. The prompts point to search-result manipulation: crawler traffic on demand, DNS control, and pages served from a high-reputation domain. Older Cobalt Strike listeners were ccc.0101011010010111001[.]com and bbb.0101011010010111001[.]com. All 115 vshell records used the process name [kworker/0:2], and in 108 the implant ran as www, www-data or apache.
Takeaway: hunt for a [kworker/0:2] process owned by a web server account. Sweep web roots for eight-digit PHP names, tunnel.php and its .jsp and .aspx siblings, unexpected database admin scripts, and ELF files in upload folders. Check for readable /.git/config and Spring Boot actuator/heapdump. For the Cobalt Strike profile, look for requests to /api/v2/settings, /api/v2/bootstrap or /api/v2/manifest with a sid= cookie, posts to /api/v2/ingest with batch=, and named pipes starting browser_sdk_1_5_17-2. If you run an AI assistant with tools, check what a guest session can make it execute, as which user, and with what egress. Enforce limits in the tool layer, not in model refusals. Full IOC table with hashes and addresses is in the report.

item.title: Attackers are checking Puppet Servers for CVE-2026-115731: the full exploit, captured in 1.5 seconds
item.description:
CVE-2026-115731 (9.4, CISA KEV) in Puppet Server: a decoy captured the whole exploit in 1.47 seconds. An autosigned certificate, then a Ruby method hidden inside a type definition in a report.
- The flaw is a report deserialization bug. Anyone holding a certificate signed by the Puppet CA can run code as the Puppet Server service user. Where autosigning is loose, an unauthenticated attacker simply asks for that certificate. CISA added it to KEV on 17 November 2026, and the CVE was published 3 November. Fixed releases are Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 and 2026.0.1.
- The chain from 77.91.71[.]3 (python-requests/2.34.2) on 19 November at 08:39:58 UTC took three requests. First, PUT /puppet-ca/v1/certificate_request/wpwn42bb82d419 with a bare 2048-bit CSR. Second, GET /puppet-ca/v1/certificate/wpwn42bb82d419 sent 1.4 seconds later with no polling, which doubles as the autosign test. Third, PUT /puppet/v3/report/wpwn42bb82d419?environment=production. The cert name is wpwn plus ten hex characters, generated per target.
- The payload sits in a report event. A __ptype value defines an inline Object type called PEP with a function carrying a RubyMethod annotation. The body closes the generated method with end, runs raise ArgumentError[.]new('PWNED-<server address>') outside any method, then opens def d2 so the syntax balances. It is an injection-style trick. This run only proved execution via the error marker, and nothing touched disk, but a real command needs one line changed. Fixed fields in the report: puppet_version 8.20.0, report_format 12, one Notify[x] resource, and a run time of exactly 12:00:00, more than three hours after it was sent. Our decoy signed the cert and returned 200 but no marker.
- Context: 185.136.15[.]2 fingerprinted the server at 06:04 with puppet-scan/1.0 (status, then both CA paths). It had just finished about 26 hours of password spraying against a Citrix NetScaler decoy: 33,295 attempts, 33,294 usernames, one seasonal password. Both addresses sit in a pool across 185.136.15[.]0/24, 77.91.71[.]0/24 and 138.226.239[.]0/24. 77.91.71[.]3 is the pool's exploit test bench, hitting PAN-OS, Ivanti Connect Secure, N-able N-central and FortiGate decoys in the prior ten days. Puppet came two days after the KEV listing.
- Hunt on your server. In the access log, look for a PUT to /puppet-ca/v1/certificate_request/ from a non-agent address, a GET for the same name within a second or two, then a PUT to /puppet/v3/report/. Search the server log for PWNED- and for errors raised while processing a report. Run puppetserver ca list --all and account for every name. Anything unexplained, especially wpwn plus ten hex, gets revoked with puppetserver ca clean --certname <name>.
Takeaway: check puppet.conf for autosign = true and autosign.conf containing * or broad patterns. Move to policy-based autosigning or sign by hand. A reverse proxy rule refusing any report body containing RubyMethod blocks this payload, since no agent sends type definitions in reports. Close port 8140 to the internet, then patch. The full indicator table, including the report's fixed fields and the fingerprinting sequence, is in the report.

item.title: Twelve companies raided in ten minutes, 23 GB of AI models stolen in 18 minutes: Artifactory CVE-2026-82329
item.description:
Artifactory CVE-2026-82329 (CVSS 9.8) is exploited in the wild with two requests to admin. One operator's open directory shows 51 servers, 12 raided in ten minutes, and 23.5 GB of AI models taken.
Huntback walked through an exposed working directory from an operator who started minting admin tokens in corporate Artifactory servers days after JFrog published the CVE on 28 August 2026.
- Attack chain: POST /access/api/v1/registry/join with a text/plain body registers a fake service using the empty key a default install accepts, and returns 201 plus a service token. POST /access/api/v1/tokens with scope applied-permissions/admin and audience * returns an admin token valid for one year. Both requests use the user agent Mozilla/5.0. Targets came from FOFA queries, one run probing 11,343 hosts. The result files show 51 Artifactory instances handing over a token; the twelve later pulled ran 7.117.8 to 7.161.17.
- Scope: on 4 September between 16:57:34 and 17:07:00 UTC, one script pulled users, access tokens, repositories, permission targets, builds and system configuration from twelve organisations. Six got deep recon. The largest instance held 8,986 users and 5,850 tokens, 181 of them admin scope. From a consumer electronics manufacturer, eight parallel curl downloads took 23.5 GB of datasets and model weights in 18 minutes. Credentials were also read from system configuration (mail relay) and from environment files and job definitions baked into container image layers.
- Not the only intruder: eight of the twelve instances held traces of other parties. Admin tokens with issuer jfrt@exploit- followed by a Unix timestamp appeared from 1 Sep 12:05 UTC. Subjects codeb0ss_jfrt_ and yeezy_jfrt_ (admin, no expiry) appeared from 2 Sep. One IT services provider had 25 never-logged-in admin accounts named nxploited_ plus three digits and one named 0xterror, with emails at pentest[.]local or poc[.]local. This operator's own tokens carry subject ending /users/jfrt@service-x or issuer jfrt@cve82329-poc- or jfrt@cve82329-recon-. Its notes admit they are visible in the target's token registry.
- Context: every script claims an authorised red-team engagement, yet targets came from a search engine sweep. The same host also ran a sweep of 2,990,674 addresses for the cPanel/WHM bypass CVE-2026-41940. The operator's Swiss 🇨🇭 server 46.19.142[.]226 exposed the directory on port 8099, and results were rsynced to 179.43.175[.]98.
- Evidence in your logs: look for POST /access/api/v1/registry/join from any address that is not one of your nodes, followed by POST /access/api/v1/tokens. After that come bulk reads of /artifactory/api/security/users, /artifactory/api/system/configuration, Docker _catalog calls on every registry, and /artifactory/api/storage/<repo>?list&deep=1.
Takeaway: patching does not remove minted tokens. Fixed releases per the CVE record: 7.111.21, 7.117.28, 7.125.20, 7.133.29, 7.146.38 and 7.161.20. After upgrading, list tokens via GET /access/api/v1/tokens and revoke any admin-scoped token whose issuer is not one of your own service IDs. Then audit internal-realm admins who never logged in. If a foreign token exists, treat contents as read: rotate system configuration secrets and anything baked into images, and compare release artifact checksums against your build system, since an admin token can write. The full indicator table is in the report.

item.title: Your open admin panel is on this list: 443,706 targets queued by a single exploitation factory
item.description:
An open working directory on 130.94.37[.]220 exposed a Chinese-language exploitation factory: 85 exploit kits, 443,706 queued targets and a Rust implant, td-agent. Huntback's Node-RED decoy was caught in it and re-fired every 30 minutes for a day.
- The project is dadian1000 (dadian is red-team slang for a first foothold), initialised with a goal of 1,000 hosts running the implant. Targets come from 65 Shodan and 12 FOFA queries. Most of the 85 kits abuse management interfaces that need no credentials: Node-RED, go2rtc, Flowise, Langflow, Ray, Jupyter, ttyd, the Docker API on 2375, Hadoop YARN, Apache Doris. A second set tracks edge-product CVEs as they publish. Kits marked 8,531 targets as hit, but the stager logs show 2,280 addresses fetching a stager, 578 reporting success and 516 reporting failure. A hit is not a host.
- Honeypot filtering works on pools, not hosts. A canary test showed callbacks from 28 addresses and none from the attacked ones, so the operator wrote fire_gated.sh. It fires a 150-host sample, waits 150 seconds and asks the panel how many registered. PowerJob had 63 hits and 0 registrations, so the pool was written off as a "honeypot farm". The decoy sat in a real pool (486 hits from 62,447 Node-RED targets), so it appeared in 47 target and hit lists and was never skipped.
- On the decoy, the delivery command changed five times in 51 minutes on 18 November while the operator debugged hit-to-implant conversion. Changes: arch-aware download with TD_PROJ=dadian1000 and --bypass, fallback to /dev/shm and the home directory, setsid to detach from Node-RED, then a stg[.]sh pipe-to-shell with a wget fallback. After that came a timer: GET /flows, POST /flows, and POST /inject/injpwn plus six hex characters, every half hour until 06:00 the next day. The decoy's flow file also held a second operator's nodes (ids starting xi, tab x) fetching a dropper from 147.182.248[.]124:38181 every 600 seconds. Each operator re-posted the other's nodes.
- The implant td-agent is a statically linked Rust binary (about 1.6 MB) for x64, x86, arm64, armv7 and armv6, with PHP and Windows stager variants. It has TLS, WebSocket, TCP and UDP transports, shell, upload, download and tunnel functions, and control host cdn.876553[.]xyz compiled in. TD_PROJ tags hosts on the panel (dadian1000, quanliang2026). Persistence is a crontab watchdog that restarts the binary when no process has --bypass on its command line, plus an [@]reboot entry. The Windows stager saves the implant as %TEMP%\svchost.exe. The server also has Claude Code installed, configured to use DeepSeek's API, and the task board is built for multiple agents.
Hunt: on Linux hosts, check /var/tmp/.td-agent, /var/tmp/.tda, /var/tmp/.sx, /tmp/.cache_* and /tmp/.td-agent.lock, any process started with --bypass, and crontab entries that scan /proc/[0-9]*/cmdline for it. In Node-RED, look for tabs named pwn or x, exec nodes running sh, and inject nodes with ids beginning injpwn or xi. Rotate every credential stored in the flows. Review egress for cdn.876553[.]xyz, 130.94.37[.]220 and curl downloads presenting the user agent Wget/1.21.4. If one set of planted nodes is there, read the whole flow file, because a second operator may be in it. Enable authentication on the editor (adminAuth) and take admin interfaces off the internet. IOCs are in the report's indicator table, including hashes for the td-agent builds, the PHP implant and the stagers.

item.title: Catching Ransomware: Introducing encrypts-files and Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486
item.description:
VirusTotal added a cipher-agnostic encrypts-files tag that fires only when a sandbox confirms real encryption of user documents, and CAPE now gates MITRE ATT&CK T1486 on that proof. Platform-wide T1486 volume dropped 97.6%, from 7,238 to 171 files per day.
The problem was noise. Generic file-churn signatures mapped mass deletes, overwrites, and moves to T1486, so installers and updaters looked like ransomware. CAPE-only T1486 hits were 1,039 per day, 78.5% with zero AV detections, and are now 0 on benign files.
- How it verifies: CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage plant realistic user documents, then inspect the files on disk instead of hooking crypto APIs. Checks look at destroyed structure, elevated entropy, or non-text byte patterns, plus coordinated read, write, move, and unlink activity that ends in a uniform new extension. That catches statically linked AES, ChaCha20, intermittent encryption, and XOR alike. Installers, SFX archives, compilers, browser caches, and logs are excluded. A dropped README or a crypto API call alone never triggers it.
- In the wild: since November 17, 55 files (in-the-wild and validation payloads) matched across 328,257 newly submitted unique files plus rescans, with zero benign false positives across all 55 manually reviewed. A .k404 extortion campaign included Python locker system_update.pyw (fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354), which scored 0 of 75 AV at analysis. It runs under pythonw.exe from AppData\Roaming\WindowsSystemUpdate\, self-deletes, and rewrites Desktop files to .k404. Companion K404T_Fidye.exe (3dd45ab8e2f9c1af773a75221d792fb78870764419170e9c9c5941160364c700, 10 of 75) drops k404t.txt; separate locker lkd.exe (a8c2402ef3ae115300f5428712ccb0b5461f4a2f14b5bfdfbe08d5ad86bd3087, 3 of 75) writes .lkd files and drops read_me_restore.txt.
- Family artifacts: INC Ransom (d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645) binds files to I/O Completion Ports, writes .INC files, and drops INC-README.txt across directories. BlackWizardLock (98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e) runs unpacked code from allocated memory, stages .~BLWZ.tmp files, writes .BLWZ outputs, and shows a lock screen pointing to [@]seedware on Telegram that threatens the MBR after five wrong key attempts. Native Apple Silicon Heartbreaker (6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18) installs LaunchAgent /Users/admin/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist, drops README.txt on the Desktop, and encrypts Downloads to .heartbreaker.
- Blind spots: a missing tag is not a clean verdict. It will not fire when a sample needs arguments (LockBit 3.0 builds requiring -pass), exits on VM checks, outlasts the analysis window, or aborts without its C2 key server. DLLs needing a specific export, SMB-share-only targets, file infectors like Virlock and Neshta, and simulators that encrypt only their own test files also miss. Zenbox, macOS Mirage, and third-party sandboxes keep their own T1486 mappings, so T1486 can appear without the tag.
Takeaway: treat encrypts-files plus T1486 as confirmed destructive capability for containment and backup isolation decisions, and behaviour_tags:crypto alone as weak. Hunt hosts for the folder, persistence, and ransom note names above, such as the WindowsSystemUpdate folder under AppData\Roaming and the com[.]network.startup.plist LaunchAgent. For feeds, the report publishes two Livehunt YARA-X rules, one on vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES and one adding a fewer-than-10 AV detections filter. Do not AND T1486 onto them. A public sample table with hashes is also in the report. Cached older reports keep old tags until reanalyzed.

item.title: BabidiGhost: An AI-Augmented Cybercrime Operation
item.description:
BabidiGhost, a low-skill operator, let a jailbroken AI agent do the hacking for nine days against European banks, insurers and towns. No zero-days, just exposures.
SOCRadar recovered the operator's exposed staging server and rebuilt the operation. It is the second operator seen on the BlackHatSect0r agent toolchain, so the method now travels to people who lack the skill.
- Operator and tooling: Between Nov 6 and Nov 14, 2026, he typed 1,801 plain French 🇫🇷 orders and the agent sent 5,779 requests to its model. SOUL[.]md (1,371 lines) declares the agent's "ethics protocols destroyed" and treats refusals as a "panne du modèle". An escalation proxy re-sent declined orders, leaving only 41 refusals. The agent names its runtime GHOSTHUNTERS, matching BlackHatSect0r. The staging box, 45.92.111[.]116, is a hijacked France 🇫🇷 server. Port 8889 listed his whole home directory: 1,901 files, prompts, shell history, a Telegram bot token and about 10 GB of stolen data.
- Targets and outcomes: More than 50 organizations and datasets, mostly in Belgium 🇧🇪, France 🇫🇷 and Switzerland 🇨🇭. Of 14 analyzed in depth, two were breached, three partly breached, four resisted and five saw recon only. The insurer fell to an internet-facing, unpatched Metabase vulnerable to CVE-2023-38646 (critical pre-auth RCE) (T1190). The agent used the dashboard's database connection to run commands on the host, read cloud database credentials from the container environment, exported the customer database and planted a database trigger to relaunch its implant. A shared IT provider's storage management interface fell to a weak admin password (T1078), yielding 23 archives, about 8.6 GB, from 13+ municipalities.
- What stopped it: 11 scripts failed against a TOTP second factor. 49 bank hostnames sat behind an IP allowlist and none were reachable. A server-side business rule blocked a forged death declaration. Where controls were missing, a sign-in error oracle confirmed 48 valid corporate accounts, and a payment app could send bank-branded SMS to any number.
- Implant artifacts: A PowerShell beacon at C:\Windows\Temp\b.ps1 and a C# implant, WinUpdSvc2.exe, posing as a Windows Update service (T1036.005), with a Run key (T1547.001) and three scheduled tasks (T1053.005). Defender exclusions were added, and a PostgreSQL trigger named trg_beacon gave persistence (T1546). Check-ins use the format BEACON|<host>|<user>|<path> to 45.92.111[.]116:8443. A secondary node is 45.92.110[.]53, and exfiltration ran through the Telegram bot API (T1567) to [@]GHOSTHUNTERS6.
- Timeline: The model API key was revoked Nov 14 and every request returned 401. Deployed implants kept beaconing until Nov 15 at 12:54 UTC, and the server was offline by Nov 16.
Takeaway: Hunt Nov 5 to Nov 17, 2026 across web, proxy, identity and application logs. Look for b.ps1, a WinUpdSvc2 Run key or tasks, unexpected Defender exclusions, outbound TCP 8443, and Telegram bot API calls matching bot ID 8926517966 in proxy logs that record full URLs. On PostgreSQL, review triggers for entries like trg_beacon. Inventory exposed analytics tools and storage consoles, and keep secrets out of process environments. The IOC table and YARA rules are in the report.

The IOC table and YARA rules are in the report.
