item.title: ARMORY CASTLE Chains Second Zero-Day Vulnerability to Seize VMware vCenter
item.description:
Suspected China-nexus ARMORY CASTLE (ex UNC5221) used a second zero-day, vCenter CVE-2026-123890, after breaching BeyondTrust Remote Support. Exploited in early September, before the November 19 disclosure.
- The flaw: CVE-2026-123890 lets an unauthenticated attacker get an SRP-6a session key over DCE/RPC on port 2012 by abusing predictable UUIDv1 timestamps. The result is an authenticated session as administrator[@]vsphere.local, with command execution and file pulls such as the .mdb database via vmdirdbcp. It affects vCenter 7.x and 8.x. It resembles CVE-2026-59309 (vmdir LDAP bypass, disclosed July 29, 2026), but the tool's July 13 Go build timestamp ran against a server already patched for that CVE. Go build metadata can be altered.
- Entry and pivot: after the CVE-2026-102764 Remote Support breach (patched in BT26-05, per the October 15 report), the group ran Nmap for VMware ports 9080, 5480, and 2012, then moved to internal Linux appliances without EDR. It dropped the SLIMSAVAGE webshell (ActiveSer.jsp, password 123), then about four hours later the CAGEMATCH webshell (u.jsp) for uploads to /tmp. Root came from using gdb to set SUID on /bin/env.
- Tooling on disk: BONESAW (/tmp/123, Go, named vcenter-db-teamcheck-go) exploits the flaw, steals the LMDB database, extracts the SAML signing key, and creates an SSO admin account. SAWSNAKE (/tmp/sss) is a Go port of vcenter_saml_login.py that forges SAML tokens for Golden SAML, bypassing MFA. BEARBONES (/tmp/dbr) is a backdoored Dropbear with banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, listening on TCP 33992 after an attempt on port 53. LAZYBONES (/usr/bin/vmtoolscs), a Slack-based backdoor, gave persistence on another appliance.
- Inside vCenter and ESXi: as Administrator, the group created a local account, briefly enabled SSH through the VAMI API, and took vCenter's master crypto key and PostgreSQL password file. It then reached ESXi as vpxuser and root and used vmfs_browser.py to pull NTDS data plus the SYSTEM and SECURITY hives straight from guest VM disks, staging the archive out through the Remote Support appliance. Reading VMDKs from the hypervisor means guest EDR and guest logs never see it.
- Why it matters: GTIG ties this to ARMORY CASTLE through overlapping tools, including LAZYBONES, used in early 2025 after CVE-2025-22457. The group has hit edge appliances since 2023, but burning a zero-day after initial access is an expansion. BONESAW's build date, over a month before this intrusion, suggests it was built for broader use. Defenders also get little help from the default VCSA firewall: no port-level control, can be disabled through VAMI, no logging of denied connections, and no outbound filtering.
Takeaway: patch vCenter per Broadcom's fix, but assume prior compromise if exposed since early September. Triage appliances for /tmp/123, /tmp/sss, /tmp/dbr, /usr/bin/vmtoolscs, ActiveSer.jsp, u.jsp, an unexpected SUID bit on /bin/env, and listeners on 33992. In vCenter, review new local and SSO admin accounts, VAMI SSH enablement, and SAML logins that lack a matching password auth. If any hit, treat the SAML signing key and vCenter master key as stolen and rotate them. Add default-deny egress and forward logs off the appliance. The 11 suspected obfuscation-network IPs and YARA rules are in the GTI Collection referenced in the report.

item.title: NGINX2Root: Five RCE bugs in NGINX, a Linux kernel path to root, and how to detect exploitation
item.description:
Five unauthenticated NGINX memory-corruption bugs (CVSS 4.0 9.2) are patched, but an unpatched Linux SCTP kernel bug turns worker RCE into host root, even from inside a Docker container.
Sysdig's report covers "NGINX2Root," disclosed Nov 18, 2026. No public PoC and no in-the-wild exploitation yet, but Xint and Wiz say they have working ASLR-bypass exploits.
- NGINX side: CVE-2026-123007 is the one to prioritize. It needs only HTTP/2, reaches the flaw by serving static files, dates to NGINX 1.9.5, and was found independently by four teams. Researchers confirmed RCE on official 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The others are narrower: CVE-2026-123633 (HTTP/2 plus upstream proxying), CVE-2026-123634 (proxy_pass built from request variables, resolver, subrequest via mirror or SSI), CVE-2026-121810 (HTTP/3), CVE-2026-113425 (mail proxy with auth_http). All score 8.1 on CVSS 3.1. Fixed in 1.31.9 and 1.30.7.
- Kernel side: a use-after-free and double-free in Linux SCTP, introduced in 4.15, leaks kernel memory and allows an arbitrary kernel function call. It has no CVE and no patch. The sctp module loads on demand, so an unprivileged NGINX worker opening one SCTP socket loads sctp.ko, which stays until reboot. Containers share the kernel, so the chain gave root on the host from the official nginx:1.31.8 image.
- Patch gap: distro packages keep their version string after backports, so nginx -v can mislead. Debian and Ubuntu listed every supported release as vulnerable to CVE-2026-123007 with no fixed package yet. Container images stay vulnerable until rebuilt and redeployed. Kubernetes ingress-nginx was archived Mar 24, 2026 and will not get these fixes.
- Evidence to look for: Falco sees syscalls, not the HTTP request, so watch what the worker does afterward: a shell or reverse shell spawned by an NGINX worker, a binary dropped and executed (for example from /tmp). Also check error.log and coredumpctl for worker crashes and segfaults, commands run as the worker's user, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections receiving a lot of data and sending little back. The report calls these general warning signs, not confirmed indicators.
- Patch-day noise: Sysdig's lab saw setuid and run-as-root alerts from an in-place live binary upgrade, but not from a config reload. Scope tuning to the maintenance window.
Takeaway: restart NGINX after upgrading, because a reload leaves old workers serving existing connections. Confirm every old worker exited. Until patched, disable HTTP/2 (blocks both HTTP/2 bugs), use a fixed proxy_pass upstream, and turn off HTTP/3, mirror, and SSI where unused. On hosts and nodes that don't need SCTP, add install sctp /bin/false under /etc/modprobe.d/ and run lsmod | grep sctp. That block does not unload a module already loaded, and a loaded module needs a reboot. If sctp.ko is already present on an NGINX host, treat it as a lead and review worker child processes. The report has no IOC list.

item.title: The Rise and Rise of DarkSword attacks
item.description:
DarkSword and Coruna iOS exploits were served through an abused Optimizely service across 178 major brands, exposing an estimated 16 to 45 million iPhone users on vulnerable iOS.
- Background: iVerify disclosed DarkSword infecting iPhones in March, and the source code later leaked to GitHub. Since then the exploit kit has spread among criminal groups, and many have extended it to steal more crypto wallets. Operators are copying desktop malvertising playbooks: on October 21, iVerify and Report URI disclosed DarkSword delivery through ad networks, which lets criminals target users on vulnerable iOS versions who are interested in crypto.
- The Optimizely abuse: Report URI found a new DarkSword and Coruna attack that abused Optimizely, the A/B content service many large brands use on their sites. 178 brands were impacted, across banking, SaaS, retail, media, airlines, healthcare, telecoms, crypto and more. About 15% had technology deployed that mitigated the attack, so their visitors were not affected. The payloads were identical to earlier variants, which 11% of iPhones are still vulnerable to by Apple's latest reported figures. The 16 to 45 million estimate comes from monthly unique visitors, the mobile share, and the vulnerable-iOS share. The low end uses global iPhone share of roughly 1 in 4, the high end North American share of about 60%. Report URI notified Optimizely, which posted a security update on November 17.
- The forensic problem: to iVerify's knowledge, no device it detected under DarkSword or Coruna attack received an Apple Threat Notification. Those notifications appear focused on nation-state tools like Pegasus and Paragon. Operators are also cleaning up better, and the traces that remain age off the device faster, so evidence effectively goes dark after a few days. Detection needs near real-time monitoring, and by the time any notification arrives, high-confidence data would likely be gone.
- Outlook: new campaigns are caught monthly. Newer variants include scaffolding for newer iOS versions, but iVerify has seen no successful attempt on devices past iOS 18.7. The report says LLMs are helping improve code and find vulnerabilities, though chaining them into a working exploit still takes skilled people. It also cites researchers demonstrating bypasses of lockdown mode and Memory Integrity Enforcement with frontier AI, and warns forward-compatible variants may exist unseen.
- Indicators: the report lists attacker domains, including 1688360[.]cc, 3601688[.]cc, linkforge[.]cc, webshell[.]lol and a set of random-label .icu domains such as 1y69gy2mdzaltz1[.]icu and 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu. It also lists attacker wallet addresses across several chains.
Takeaway: retro-hunt DNS and web proxy logs for the report's IOC domains now, since device-side evidence ages off within days and network telemetry may be all you have. Pull iOS version inventory and flag anything below 26.3, or below 18.7.7 for devices that cannot take the latest release. Add the IOCs to DNS or web filtering. The full IOC list, attacker wallets and the affected-brand appendix are in the report, so check which of those brands your users visit from mobile.

item.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
item.description:
Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 9.8) was exploited against a Russian 🇷🇺 organization soon after a public PoC appeared. Unauthenticated root command execution, but only on clustered Expressway Core and Edge.
- The flaw: Cisco disclosed it on October 21. It sits in the Expressway database service and stems from persistent cookies. An attacker holding them can reach the database service and issue certain RPC commands, which run root-level commands on the underlying OS. It affects virtual and appliance builds of Expressway Core and Edge when clustered. X15.5.20 fixes it, there are no workarounds, and X14 or earlier must move to a fixed release.
- Exploitation status: Cisco's advisory has not been revised and still says it knows of no public announcements or malicious use. But a PoC is on GitHub, and F6 says the attack it investigated came shortly after. F6 did not name the victim or attribute the activity to a known actor.
- Attack chain: the attackers first breached two internet-exposed Expressway X15.5.3 devices. From one of them they pivoted to two other cluster nodes on the internal network. Because the exploited service is a cluster feature, internal nodes are part of the blast radius, not just the edge box.
- Post-exploitation tooling: with root, the attackers staged custom Python scripts to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories, aiming to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive data. F6 found the scripts were modified on the fly during the intrusion, and the source contained characteristic comments and fix descriptions pointing to an AI assistant. Expect fast iteration, not a fixed toolkit.
- Detection angle: F6 points to the Erlang system log on Expressway devices as the place to look for exploitation. It also published IP addresses and file paths tied to the attack in a Russian-language press release.
Takeaway: if you run clustered Expressway, pull and preserve the Erlang system log from every node, internal ones included, before patching or rebuilding. Then check for unexpected Python scripts on the devices and for scanning, SMB, SQL Server, WinRM, or GitLab access originating from Expressway hosts. Compare cluster node IPs, file paths, and connections against the indicators in F6's press release.
If you cannot patch right away, F6 recommends blocking TCP ports 4371-4372 at the firewall except from trusted cluster node IPs. Then move to X15.5.20.

item.title: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
item.description:
nginx2root: five unauthenticated memory corruption bugs in nginx, plus a Linux kernel SCTP flaw that turns a worker foothold into root. CVE-2026-123007 (HTTP/2, present since 1.9.5 in 2015) is the worst. Not in CISA KEV as of Nov 19.
- The five CVEs: CVE-2026-123007 is an integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/write, needing only HTTP/2. CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free (HTTP/2, proxy_pass, worker low on worker_connections). CVE-2026-121810 is a use-after-free in HTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass. CVE-2026-123634 is a use-after-free in the resolver with variable proxy_pass plus a mirror or SSI subrequest. CVE-2026-113425 is a use-after-free in the mail proxy with auth_http. F5 rates each High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2). Code execution needs ASLR disabled or bypassed, and Xint's write-up shows CVE-2026-123007 leaking addresses to do that.
- How CVE-2026-123007 works: the WINDOW_UPDATE handler caps the connection send window at 2^31 - 1. But ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() refunds credit for queued DATA frames on a canceled stream with no cap. If the client enlarges the window between queueing and cancel, the window exceeds the max, the unsigned check wraps, and every later WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. Past 2^63 the signed comparison in ngx_http_v2_send_chain() produces a huge frame size and a buffer with last before pos, reaching memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain(). Xint, Rapid7 and Wiz report code execution. The fix adds h2c->send_queued so queued bytes count against the window.
- The kernel half: Xint found a use-after-free in the Linux SCTP send path, present since 4.15 (2018). An attacker already running as the nginx worker can get root, demonstrated from inside a Docker container. Many distributions auto-load the SCTP module on first SCTP socket open, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of Nov 18 no kernel fix existed and Xint is withholding details.
- Exploitation status: no reports of in-the-wild exploitation as of Nov 19. Rapid7 published a PoC meant only for a freshly started local container. Xint and Wiz have not released exploits, and fake exploits are circulating on GitHub. Censys's tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled, though backported fixes mean version strings alone don't prove exposure.
- What the evidence looks like: Rapid7 estimates reaching 2^63 takes roughly 2^32 WINDOW_UPDATE frames (about 52 GiB), and its route totals about 128 GB of HTTP/2 data. That means one long-lived connection delivering tens of GB to nginx while little comes back, far more than the logged requests explain. Other signals from the report: worker process <pid> exited on signal 11 (alert) alongside worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections (warn) on HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 proxy servers. The line could not cancel <name> resolving (alert) appears on unpatched versions for CVE-2026-123634, but its absence proves nothing. Mail proxy workers crashing with client resets during login point at CVE-2026-113425. The strongest sign of success is unexpected programs launched by an nginx worker, for example an auditd rule on execve for the worker's user.
Takeaway: patch to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (Plus 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distro's fixed build) and restart, because a config reload does not replace the running binary. If you can't patch yet, set http2 off; (1.25.1+), remove QUIC listeners and set http3 off;, bind mail listeners to trusted networks, and add install sctp /bin/false under /etc/modprobe.d/ (this does not unload an already-loaded module). A front-end proxy like Cloudflare's, which terminates HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and runs its own flow control, blocks the frame-level attacks, but only if the origin can't be hit directly, so enforce that with an IP firewall, not nginx config. It does not cover the mail proxy or fully cover the resolver bug. Note that the warn message above sits below the default error level, so raise error_log verbosity and preserve logs now. nginx2root: five unauthenticated memory corruption bugs in nginx, plus a Linux kernel SCTP flaw that turns a worker foothold into root. CVE-2026-123007 (HTTP/2, present since 1.9.5 in 2015) is the worst. Not in CISA KEV as of Nov 19.

- The five CVEs: CVE-2026-123007 is an integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/write, needing only HTTP/2. CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free (HTTP/2, proxy_pass, worker low on worker_connections). CVE-2026-121810 is a use-after-free in HTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass. CVE-2026-123634 is a use-after-free in the resolver with variable proxy_pass plus a mirror or SSI subrequest. CVE-2026-113425 is a use-after-free in the mail proxy with auth_http. F5 rates each High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2). Code execution needs ASLR disabled or bypassed, and Xint's write-up shows CVE-2026-123007 leaking addresses to do that.

- How CVE-2026-123007 works: the WINDOW_UPDATE handler caps the connection send window at 2^31 - 1. But ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() refunds credit for queued DATA frames on a canceled stream with no cap. If the client enlarges the window between queueing and cancel, the window exceeds the max, the unsigned check wraps, and every later WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. Past 2^63 the signed comparison in ngx_http_v2_send_chain() produces a huge frame size and a buffer with last before pos, reaching memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain(). - The kernel half: Xint found a use-after-free in the Linux SCTP send path, present since 4.15 (2018). An attacker already running as the nginx worker can get root, demonstrated from inside a Docker container. Many distributions auto-load the SCTP module on first SCTP socket open, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of Nov 18 no kernel fix existed and Xint is withholding details.

- Exploitation status: no reports of in-the-wild exploitation as of Nov 19. Rapid7 published a PoC meant only for a freshly started local container. Xint and Wiz have not released exploits, and fake exploits are circulating on GitHub. Censys's tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled, though backported fixes mean version strings alone don't prove exposure.

item.title: InfoSec News Nuggets: 11/19/2026
item.description:
A hijacked Optimizely script field reached visitors of 178 organizations, and trojanized PyPI agent-framework releases stole Azure and CI tokens through .pth files. CISA also added four exploited CVEs to KEV.
- Optimizely: on November 16 an attacker abused a flaw in the account signup flow of Web Experimentation to plant code in the optional Project JavaScript field. Optimizely's own CDN served it to visitors of BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC and others. The payload was a clipper that swapped Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron addresses in page text and on copy, plus an iOS-only loader. Later variants reportedly added a card skimmer. None of the sites were breached directly. Optimizely says it patched, removed the code and revoked tokens.
- agent-framework on PyPI: versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were published 33 minutes apart on November 17. Each drops a .pth file into site-packages, so the stealer runs on every Python start, including pip, even if the framework is never imported. It harvests environment variables, other processes and credential files. It mints Azure managed identity tokens for 12 resources, grabs Azure DevOps OIDC tokens and, in the second release, GitHub Actions OIDC tokens. Everything goes to a webhook[.]site URL. The second release moved the payload into a new module, so a diff against clean 1.26.0 would miss it.
- CISA KEV, November 18: four actively exploited CVEs, three of them CVSS 9.8 RCEs. CVE-2024-10441 hits Synology DiskStation Manager and BeeStation OS and is tied to C3RB3R ransomware on NAS devices. CVE-2026-90436 is unsafe reflection in unsupported Apache Axis 1.x, exploited via Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central. CVE-2026-90817 is unauthenticated code injection in REDCap. CVE-2026-40217 allows code execution through LiteLLM proxy's guardrail testing feature. Federal deadline is November 21 for the first three and December 2 for LiteLLM. CISA advises preserving evidence before patching exposed systems.
- Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938: a memory corruption bug in the assembly fast path of Java's Base64 decoder writes 62 bytes past a buffer. It affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. Oracle scores it 8.1 and Calif 9.2. Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against default Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. No in-the-wild attacks are confirmed yet. Fixes shipped November 17.
- Cold Relic (ColdRiver): Mandiant ties this FSB-linked Russian 🇷🇺 group to a chain of reuse. In late 2025 it hijacked an admin account at a U.S. 🇺🇸 organization, copied the cloud drive and employee directories, and kept reading mail through third-party apps, even after password and session resets. This year it used that material to impersonate an employee to a contact at a second U.S. 🇺🇸 organization over an encrypted messaging app. It then sent links to relevant documents that harvested Microsoft credentials and tokens and led to bulk cloud file theft. Compromised websites screen and redirect targets, and new operations were seen this month.
Takeaway: for agent-framework, check lockfiles, install and build logs (without running pip) for 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 since November 17. Look for unexpected .pth files in site-packages, and avoid running Python in affected environments until rebuilt from 1.26.0. Treat every reachable credential, including Azure, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions tokens, as exposed and rotate it. For Optimizely, review your Project JavaScript field for code you did not write. For Cold Relic, a password and session reset is not enough: audit third-party app access to mailboxes and cloud drives. On exposed Synology, Axis, REDCap or LiteLLM hosts, preserve evidence first, then patch.

item.title: NGINX2Root: What NGINX Admins Should Know
item.description:
NGINX2Root: five NGINX flaws led by CVE-2026-123007 can give an unauthenticated attacker code execution via HTTP/2, HTTP/3, the DNS resolver or the mail proxy. Public PoC exists, no in-the-wild exploitation reported yet.
- Scope: Xint (Theori) reported all five on October 16, 2026, and F5 shipped fixes on November 18, 2026, the day of disclosure. F5 scores each 9.2 Critical under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 High under CVSS v3.1. Affected: NGINX Open Source before 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and NGINX Plus before 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1. Plus R33 through R36 have no patch, so those customers must move to a 37.x build.
- Config decides exposure: CVE-2026-123007 is the broadest, a send-window miscount in HTTP/2 flow control that corrupts memory and needs only HTTP/2 on a reachable listener. CVE-2026-123633 (HTTP/2) and CVE-2026-121810 (HTTP/3) are use-after-free bugs in connection draining with proxying to a backend. CVE-2026-123634 is a resolver use-after-free needing a request-derived proxy_pass target plus SSI or mirror subrequests. CVE-2026-113425 hits the mail proxy when proxy and auth_http are combined.
- Root chain: code execution lands as the NGINX worker, then a separate Linux kernel SCTP use-after-free or double free (code introduced in Linux 4.15) escalates to root. The researchers say the chain also crossed a Docker container boundary. That kernel bug has no CVE and no fix yet. ATT&CK per the report: T1190, T1068, T1611.
- Exploit reality: the public PoC for CVE-2026-123007 (GitHub, November 18) gets code execution against NGINX 1.31.8 with HTTP/2 over TLS in a Docker lab. It needs x86-64 with AVX-512 and a particular glibc memory-copy routine, has to defeat ASLR, and pushes roughly 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic down a single connection. A proxy terminating HTTP/2 in front of NGINX will most likely stop it. The discoverers and another team hold working exploits but withheld the final steps. Fake exploit repos are circulating, so vet anything you pull.
- Evidence to look for: worker crashes and core dumps (grep 'exited on signal' /var/log/nginx/error.log), an HTTP/2 connection open for minutes ingesting large volumes while the access log shows few requests, a worker spawning a shell or other program, and outbound connections or DNS lookups the host does not normally make. The warning signs come from CIRCL's advisory; the grep is from the report's checks.
Takeaway: scope first, then fix. Run nginx -v and match against your distro advisory, since backports keep old version numbers (Ubuntu shipped fixes November 19). Run nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -nE 'http2|http3|quic|resolver|proxy_pass|mirror|ssi on|auth_http' to see which flaws apply. Check bundled NGINX in container images, appliances and load balancers. Community ingress-nginx is retired with no fix planned. After upgrading, do a full restart, because a reload keeps the old binary running.
If patching waits, disable the feature behind each flaw. Turning off HTTP/2 covers only CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, and disabling mirror alone leaves CVE-2026-123634 open. On hosts that do not need SCTP, add install sctp /bin/false under /etc/modprobe.d/ and confirm with lsmod, since an already-loaded module stays active until reboot or removal. Check sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space (2 is full) and look for services launched with setarch -R. Preserve error logs and worker core dumps before restarting.

item.title: CVE-2026-124749: pam-mysql: inverted PAM_DISALLOW_NULL_AUTHTOK gives a pre-auth authentication bypass
item.description:
CVE-2026-124749 (CVSS 9.8): pam-mysql inverts PAM_DISALLOW_NULL_AUTHTOK at both authenticate call sites. On a stock sshd, an unauthenticated client can log in as any account whose stored password is SQL NULL, using any password.
- The defect, against v0.8.2: pam_mysql.c passes !(flags & PAM_DISALLOW_NULL_AUTHTOK) at :4708 and :4799, which is 0 exactly when the application set the flag. On the null branch (:3874 sets vresult = null_inhibited, :3877 returns success when vresult is 0), the password comparison is nested inside if (row[0] != NULL) at :3689 and never runs. The two pam_sm_chauthtok call sites pass a literal 0 and are correct. The report does not address in-the-wild exploitation; it describes an end-to-end reproduction over a real sshd on Debian trixie.
- Why a default sshd is the vector: OpenSSH sets the flag precisely when PermitEmptyPasswords is no, which is the default. The safe config reaches the permissive path. Setting PermitEmptyPasswords yes suppresses the bug but disables OpenSSH's own guard at auth-passwd.c:93-94, which opens the empty-stored-password case. It trades one bypass for another.
- Scope: every released version, including the newest upstream commit from 2024-03-14. The 0.8.x line covers Debian 11/12/13/14/sid, Ubuntu 18.04/20.04/22.04, Devuan, Kali, FreeBSD, Gentoo and others. The 1.0 betas cover Fedora 39-44 and rawhide, Nix, Mageia 10, Rosa and ALT. On 0.8.x the exploitable schema is a nullable password column. On the 1.0 line an empty stored password is also exploitable (src/authenticate.c:104 and :127), so NOT NULL DEFAULT '' schemas flip from protective to exploitable. The report cites PostfixAdmin (mailbox.password, admin.password) and Froxlor (ftp_users.password) as shipped schemas.
- Did it happen to you? OpenSSH cannot tell a bypass from a real login. "Accepted password for nullpw" and "Accepted password for normalpw" look identical. The discriminator is the database: any accepted password login for an account whose stored password was NULL or empty is necessarily a bypass. Run SELECT username FROM users WHERE password IS NULL OR password=''; and correlate those names against "Accepted password for" lines in the auth log. Current table state proves nothing about the past, so use the binary log or a backup from the period.
- pam_mysql's own audit table is a trap. log.enabled defaults to 0 (pam_mysql.c:2897, gated at :4331), so default deployments recorded nothing. When enabled, the failure string is misspelled AUTHENTICATION FALURE, so grepping FAILURE returns nothing. A weak secondary signal: the bypass leaves one SUCCESS (FIRST_PASS) row with no preceding failure.
- Fix status: upstream master has commits 6e2c52eb (the !! polarity correction) and 46175520 (a nullok option, default off, giving vresult = !ctx->nullok || null_inhibited). Debian trixie's security upload went to security-master on 2026-11-17. Bookworm goes through LTS and is not uploaded yet, so it is still exposed. The upstream v0.8.x branch is not updated, and the 1.0 line has no fixed tag (newest is 1.0.0-beta3). The reporter did not check the other distributions.
Takeaway: apply the shipping fix, but the real remediation is the rows, not the flag. Purge credential-less rows from every table used for authentication, then add NOT NULL with no empty-string default. Then run the credential-less-rows query against historical data and your sshd auth logs to look for past bypass logins. Preserve binary logs and backups from before any cleanup.

Debian trixie's security upload went to security-master on 2026-11-17. Bookworm goes through LTS and is not uploaded yet, so it is still exposed. The upstream v0.8.x branch is not updated, and the 1.0 line has no fixed tag (newest is 1.0.0-beta3). The reporter did not check the other distributions.

Takeaway: apply the shipping fix, but the real remediation is the rows, not the flag. Purge credential-less rows from every table used for authentication, then add NOT NULL with no empty-string default. Then run the credential-less-rows query against historical data and your sshd auth logs to look for past bypass logins. Preserve binary logs and backups from before any cleanup.

item.title: BYOD Ransomware: An Identity-First Extortion Campaign Moving Into Hospitals and Universities
item.description:
BYOD, a new ransomware and extortion group, claimed at least nine victims in five weeks, including UNM Health Sciences Center and Vanderbilt. No CVE is tied to any attack. Every account points to identity infrastructure.
- UNM Health Sciences Center (Oct 26): the state's only Level 1 trauma center diverted ambulances from 12:30 to 2:30 p.m., and more than 30 clinics cancelled appointments and surgeries. Staff were told to unplug desktops, and audio messages played on computers. BYOD claimed 36,000 systems, including Active Directory forests, Group Policy and the Entra tenant, plus two Oracle databases. UNM says only some end-user devices were hit, not core systems or servers. BYOD later offered free decryption keys to healthcare, which implies encryption did happen.
- Vanderbilt (Nov 9): the university told everyone to shut down devices and leave campus Wi-Fi. It warned about unexpected login approval requests and unusual permission changes in OneDrive and Box. Campus computers played "You have been compromised by BYOD." The ransom note was README_BYOD_31.txt, with negotiation through the Session messenger. BYOD claims domain controller control and over one million Social Security numbers. Vanderbilt has not confirmed any of that.
- Initial access is thin but consistent. Michigan State linked BYOD's Nov 1 claim of 1.3 million student records to a credential compromise it detected in early October, which suggests data theft first and extortion about a month later. For Trump Mobile (3,615 customer records published), a BYOD member claimed a remote access trojan on a third-party carrier employee's computer. Both routes use a legitimate identity or endpoint, not an exploit.
- ATT&CK mapping from the report, with status: T1078 Valid Accounts (confirmed at Michigan State), T1078.002 Domain Accounts, T1484.001 Group Policy Modification and T1078.004 Cloud Accounts (all claimed by BYOD), T1621 MFA Request Generation (possible, from Vanderbilt's warnings), T1213 and T1486 for collection and encryption, and T1491.001 as the closest match for the audio messages.
- Hunt starting points the report gives: privileged group changes (Windows Security events 4728, 4732, 4756) and unexpected account creation (4720). Group Policy changes (event 5136 and SYSVOL), especially new scheduled tasks or startup scripts. Cloud identity events such as new Global Administrator assignments, MFA prompt bursts and newly registered authentication methods. Processes playing audio or text-to-speech on many machines at once. Shadow copy and backup deletion.
Takeaway: separate what victims confirmed from what BYOD claims, since the gap is the central question in every case. If you already handled a credential incident, review what those accounts touched in the weeks before the reset. There is no CVE or patch to wait on, so hunt the identity-layer behaviors above across directory, cloud, endpoint and network together. Rehearse restoring identity infrastructure from offline backups, and keep downtime procedures that do not depend on the network.

item.title: Credential stealer slipped into Microsoft’s official Python agent framework
item.description:
Microsoft's official agent-framework package on PyPI shipped a credential stealer in versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, published November 17, 2026. The payload runs at Python startup through a .pth hook, so the framework never has to be imported for it to execute.
- Scope and timeline: StepSecurity, OX Security and Socket caught the releases. PyPI quarantined both, but the attacker uploaded 1.26.2 after 1.26.1 was already quarantined, which shows publishing access persisted. OX counts 192,534 monthly downloads for the package. 1.26.0 is the last clean release. None of the reports explain how the attacker got publishing rights.
- Stealth: Both malicious versions kept their dependency on the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0, so the framework worked normally while the stealer ran. In 1.26.2 the attacker restored Microsoft's original package initializer and moved the hook into a new file named af_runtime_diag.pth. Diffing only the package initializer would miss it.
- What it takes: The stealer collects environment variables with names containing strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, AZURE, AWS and GITHUB. It reads the environments of up to 300 other processes. It copies .env files and credential files for Azure CLI, pip, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face.
- Fresh tokens: Socket notes it actively requests new Azure managed-identity and CI federation tokens, and 1.26.2 added GitHub Actions OIDC tokens. StepSecurity cautions the code only attempts these requests, and there is no confirmation that any tokens were issued.
- Exfiltration: Everything is compressed, encoded and sent in a single request to a webhook[.]site endpoint, so egress logs are a strong evidence source.
Why it matters: as Coder's Eric Paulsen puts it, a build system that can ask a cloud provider for tokens is itself a credential. StepSecurity warns that rotating stored secrets will not cancel identity tokens that were already issued. OX recommends treating every secret reachable from an affected host as compromised.
Practitioner takeaway:
1. Find every host, runner and image that installed agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. Check lock files, build logs and package inventories. 2. Search those environments for af_runtime_diag.pth, and review installed .pth files generally. 3. Hunt proxy and DNS logs for connections to webhook[.]site from build systems and developer machines. 4. Isolate affected hosts and runners before running Python or pip again. Rebuild from a clean base and pin agent-framework to 1.26.0. 5. Beyond rotating secrets, review OIDC permissions, federated credentials and managed-identity role assignments. Look for token requests from those identities after the install time.
Preserve the affected environments before rebuilding if you need to prove what ran.

item.title: Major African Stock Exchange Targeted in AI-Assisted Attack
item.description:
A likely AI-written toolkit ran 41 PowerShell modules under an IIS web shell at an African stock exchange in about three minutes, hunting credentials and exfiltrating via hex-encoded DNS to oast[.]pro.
- Symantec's Threat Hunter Team saw the modules run between 08:44 and 08:47 UTC (3m12s) on September 20, 2026, a new one every few seconds, from a web shell under the IIS worker process. They harvested secrets and tested them against the exchange's investment API and a securities depository gateway. Earliest malicious activity on the server dates to April 2026, possibly longer.
- Module coverage: GPP cpassword theft, AWS keys and database connection strings in SYSVOL, web roots and C:\Deployer, cloud and DevOps tool hunting, IIS site and app pool mapping, SharePoint keyword search, TFS and SCCM queries, and an AWS RDS PostgreSQL probe on port 5432. Four modules hit the investment API with a guessed login and a reused bearer token, and tested several API keys, including a blank one, against the depository gateway, connecting by IP with a manual Host header and certificate validation disabled. The report does not say whether any credential worked.
- Exfil is the standout. Each module hex-encoded its output, split it into 50-character chunks and resolved one DNS name per chunk under a single token on the public out-of-band testing service oast[.]pro (token danoam334iqjo0ap2scg6ofosjxfgqhsa). Pattern: index.hexchunk.modulelabel.token. Module labels include spid1, awslocal1, wmi1. Empty output sends the hex sentinel 454d505459. The collector is invisible to Symantec, so data loss is unconfirmed.
- Why AI is suspected: every module shared the same scaffold, error handling, hex routine and sentinel, and the DNS loop was copied byte for byte into all 41 scripts instead of written once. Generic variable names, one script with a unique progress variable and a deliberate invalid-credential test also fit iterative prompting. Symantec says none of this is conclusive alone, and it could not identify a model.
- Attribution is split. Six persistence implants (one first seen in 2020) are tied to China-linked Witchetty (aka LookingFrog) with high confidence. The toolkit is not attributed to any group. It could be Witchetty with new tooling, a more capable second operator, or an unrelated actor on the same compromise. Symantec found no evidence of privilege escalation or data theft. Motive is unclear: financial targeting, but a specific investor's number was checked, so espionage is not ruled out.
Takeaway: hunt DNS resolver logs for queries to oast[.]pro, especially labels with a numeric first label, a hex chunk up to 50 characters, then a short module label. Look for bursts of PowerShell launched under the IIS worker process, and treat any IIS web shell as a lead to initial access, which Symantec suggests may have been an exploited vulnerability. Treat every secret reachable from that server (GPP passwords, SYSVOL, config files, API keys, bearer tokens) as exposed and rotate it. File hashes and the network IOC are in the report.

item.title: Spying on Governments with Zero Lines of Malware: A Custom SoftEther Bridge in Webworm’s Toolkit
item.description:
Rapid7 found a custom SoftEther VPN Bridge build that Webworm, a China-aligned APT, likely uses against governments. It is rebuilt from source with the detection fingerprint stripped, and has no added backdoor. Rapid7 attributes it with moderate confidence.
The actor's earlier use of stock SoftEther was publicly documented, so it appears to have gone back and removed the easy detection points. Only one AV vendor flagged the sample on VirusTotal, even though it has been public since January.
- Build and identity: the sample is a Windows x64 PE, a modified SoftEther VPN Bridge 4.44 build 9807. The PDB path still reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\...\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb. PE metadata is changed to OriginalFileName netcapa.exe, "Network Monitor Software", published by "Network Systems Solutions Inc." (T1036.005). The Version field is unchanged at 4, 44, 0, 9807. Rapid7 found no additional malware functionality beyond the changes below.
- Sloppy rebranding: "SoftEther VPN" becomes "NtMonitor VPN" in debug banners, service names, registry keys, the HTTP 401 page, and firewall rule names. It is inconsistent. The entry-point service name is still SEVPNBRIDGE, and many registry paths still reference "SoftEther Project". That gives you pivots on a host. The firewall rules come from stock SoftEther behavior (T1686.003).
- Network stealth: the stock endpoints /vpnsvc/vpn.cgi and /vpnsvc/connect.cgi become /update/alive.cgi and /update/picture.cgi. The upstream GIF handshake watermark is replaced with a truncated PNG of the Windows logo, so stock clients and servers can't handshake with this build, and its peers can't be matched on the well-known GIF pattern. C2 rides HTTP(S) and SoftEther's protocol (T1071), and the host acts as an internal proxy and network bridge (T1090.001, T1599).
- Disk artifacts removed: hamcore.se2 normally sits beside the executable and is an easy installation tell. Here it is trimmed to a minimum and embedded as a PE resource with a custom resource directory walk, adding about 1.5 MB to the binary. The config moves from vpn_bridge.config to setting.conf, encrypted with a custom RC4-like cipher. Encrypted files start with the ASCII magic bytes RCEN and contain the key (T1027.013, T1140, T1027.005).
- Attribution and scope: this fits ESET's reporting on Webworm shifting from custom malware to dual-use tools. In the decrypted configs Rapid7 Intelligence has, the VPN cascades a remote network into the local one. In cases that don't look like tests, the remote IP sits in AS 20473 (The Constant Company, LLC, including Vultr), which has been tied to Webworm before. Webworm focuses on governments, especially in Europe. Rapid7 calls this a hybrid: stock SoftEther rebuilt from source, not trojanized, with its fingerprint erased.
Takeaway: with TLS inspection, hunt for POST requests to /update/picture.cgi with Content-Type image/jpeg and a body starting with 89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a 00 00 00 0d 49 48 44 52, the custom PNG watermark. On hosts, look for a SEVPNBRIDGE service, a setting.conf starting with RCEN, registry keys under "SoftEther Project", and internal "NtMonitor VPN" strings, which all samples seen share (PE metadata such as netcapa.exe differs across samples). The report links IoCs and a YARA ruleset on Rapid7's public GitHub, and a Python script on the Rapid7 Intelligence GitHub decrypts the RCEN configs to recover the remote peer. The endpoints, watermark, and branding are trivial for the actor to change next, so government defenders should learn baseline SoftEther behavior rather than rely on these strings alone.

item.title: Detecting Timeroasting the Hard Way
item.description:
Timeroasting's extended MS-SNTP authenticator has no public cracking support and no accurate detection rule. A Huntress researcher reversed netlogon.dll to fix both gaps, producing a verified hashcat module and engine-validated Suricata rules.
Key findings:
- MS-SNTP sends authenticated NTP in two wire formats. The 68-byte legacy form uses MD5 and hashcat mode 31300 cracks it. The 120-byte extended form uses an SP800-108 counter-mode KDF (PRF: HMAC-SHA512, label: the 8-byte "sntp-ms\0" with the null included, context: the RID as a little-endian 32-bit value) followed by HMAC-SHA512 over the 48-byte NTP response. That extended form has been the Windows default since at least 2016, it is live and answering on fully patched Windows Server 2025 DCs today, and hashcat has no released module for it. The researcher reversed w32time.dll and netlogon.dll on a live DC (build 26100.33438) in radare2, confirmed the KDF chain against a live DC's output, and published a verified hashcat module (placeholder mode 31350) alongside a pure-Python reference implementation and the hash format $sntp-ms-sha512$RID$checksum$salt. The known-answer test vector in the report lets any reimplementation check its work. Benchmarks: 17.6 MH/s on an Apple M3 Pro GPU, ~339 kH/s on a Kali CPU box.
- Timeroasting leaves no authentication events: no 4768, 4769, 4624, or 4776 events, because the targeted accounts never log on. The DC answers any RID that resolves to a computer or trust account, with zero authentication required. User account RIDs return no reply, so the gaps in a sweep's output are your user population, not filtered results. The accounts that matter are the ones that break rotation: pre-created (pre-Windows 2000) machines whose password is literally the lowercase account name, the Seamless SSO account AZUREADSSOACC (which does not auto-rotate and whose key forges Entra SSO tickets), and any machine whose pwdLastSet is far past the 30-day rotation window. Microsoft Defender for Identity's "Suspicious SAM Account Name Change" alert names timeroasting in its description but fires on a directory modification (event 5136, a sAMAccountName change): it covers only the privileged, account-rename targeted variant, not the unauthenticated sweep.
- The durable detection signal is not packet size. Modern Windows members already send 120-byte extended requests as normal time sync, so alerting on 120 bytes fires across the whole fleet. The 68-byte legacy form is now the odd one out on a modern fleet, because both public sweep tools (SecuraBV's timeroast[.]py and timeroast-ng) emit only 68-byte legacy requests. The signal that holds regardless of size: a legitimate member asks the DC to sign only for its own machine account's RID, so a request where the RID at packet offset 48 (little-endian, 4 bytes) does not match the source host's own RID is anomalous on a single packet and catches a slow, paced sweep that no volume threshold would. The volumetric fallback, 25 authenticated NTP requests (dsize >56, client mode 3 on the low 3 bits of byte 0) from one source to a DC in 60 seconds, is the easy first rule but a patient attacker can pace under it.
- The Suricata rules in the report are engine-validated against a real capture (41 legacy and 41 extended packets): a size-agnostic volumetric sweep rule (SID 5200010) and an extended old-key flag rule keyed on the 0x01 bit at offset 53 (SID 5200002). The researcher learned the hard way that C-style block comments inside Suricata rule bodies cause silent load failures, so zero rules loaded until they were stripped. Do not build a rule that simply alerts on 120-byte authenticated NTP: on a modern fleet that fires on every Windows member doing routine time sync. The report also covers DigestRoast (the same MD5 MAC construction callable directly over MS-NRPC opnum 24 on \PIPE\netlogon, requiring Builtin\Administrators on the DC, so it is a footnote not a threat) and Trustroasting (trust account RIDs answer the same unauthenticated MS-SNTP sweep and crack with hashcat mode 31300, but only matter when the trust secret is weak or non-rotating).
Practitioner takeaway: the durable hunt is an IP-to-RID enrichment check, not a Suricata rule. For every authenticated MS-SNTP packet to a DC (payload length 68 or 120, byte 0 low 3 bits equal 3 for client mode), extract the RID from payload bytes 48-51 as a little-endian 32-bit integer, resolve the source IP to a computer account via DHCP or DNS then an LDAP lookup of objectSid, and alert when the requested RID does not match the source's own. The Suricata rules, the hashcat module (module_31350.c, the OpenCL kernel m31350-pure[.]cl, and the m31350[.]py self-test oracle), the Python reference cracker, and the known-answer test vector are all in the report. Enable Windows Filtering Platform auditing (event 5156) on your DCs so w32time's UDP/123 accepts are logged, and baseline your fleet's 68-versus-120 split before writing any size-based rule.

Key findings:

- MS-SNTP sends authenticated NTP in two wire formats. The 68-byte legacy form uses MD5 and hashcat mode 31300 cracks it. The 120-byte extended form uses an SP800-108 counter-mode KDF (PRF: HMAC-SHA512, label: the 8-byte "sntp-ms\0" with the null included, context: the RID as a little-endian 32-bit value) followed by HMAC-SHA512 over the 48-byte NTP response. That extended form has been the Windows default since at least 2016, it is live and answering on fully patched Windows Server 2025 DCs today, and hashcat has no released module for it. The researcher reversed w32time.dll and netlogon.dll on a live DC (build 26100.33438) in radare2, confirmed the KDF chain against a live DC's output, and published a verified hashcat module (placeholder mode 31350) alongside a pure-Python reference implementation and the hash format $sntp-ms-sha512$RID$checksum$salt. The known-answer test vector in the report lets any reimplementation check its work. Benchmarks: 17.6 MH/s on an Apple M3 Pro GPU, ~339 kH/s on a Kali CPU box.

- Timeroasting leaves no authentication events: no 4768, 4769, 4624, or 4776 events, because the targeted accounts never log on. The DC answers any RID that resolves to a computer or trust account, with zero authentication required. User account RIDs return no reply, so the gaps in a sweep's output are your user population, not filtered results. The accounts that matter are the ones that break rotation: pre-created (pre-Windows 2000) machines whose password is literally the lowercase account name, the Seamless SSO account AZUREADSSOACC (which does not auto-rotate and whose key forges Entra SSO tickets), and any machine whose pwdLastSet is far past the 30-day rotation window. Microsoft Defender for Identity's "Suspicious SAM Account Name Change" alert names timeroasting in its description but fires on a directory modification (event 5136, a sAMAccountName change): it covers only the privileged, account-rename targeted variant, not the unauthenticated sweep.

- The durable detection signal is not packet size. Modern Windows members already send 120-byte extended requests as normal time sync, so alerting on 120 bytes fires across the whole fleet. The 68-byte legacy form is now the odd one out on a modern fleet, because both public sweep tools (SecuraBV's timeroast[.]py and timeroast-ng) emit only 68-byte legacy requests. The signal that holds regardless of size: a legitimate member asks the DC to sign only for its own machine account's RID, so a request where the RID at packet offset 48 (little-endian, 4 bytes) does not match the source host's own RID is anomalous on a single packet and catches a slow, paced sweep that no volume threshold would. The volumetric fallback, 25 authenticated NTP requests (dsize >56, client mode 3 on the low 3 bits of byte 0) from one source to a DC in 60 seconds, is the easy first rule but a patient attacker can pace under it.

- The Suricata rules in the report are engine-validated against a real capture (41 legacy and 41 extended packets): a size-agnostic volumetric sweep rule (SID 5200010) and an extended old-key flag rule keyed on the 0x01 bit at offset 53 (SID 5200002). The researcher learned the hard way that C-style block comments inside Suricata rule bodies cause silent load failures, so zero rules loaded until they were stripped. Do not build a rule that simply alerts on 120-byte authenticated NTP: on a modern fleet that fires on every Windows member doing routine time sync. The report also covers DigestRoast (the same MD5 MAC construction callable directly over MS-NRPC opnum 24 on \PIPE\netlogon, requiring Builtin\Administrators on the DC, so it is a footnote not a threat) and Trustroasting (trust account RIDs answer the same unauthenticated MS-SNTP sweep and crack with hashcat mode 31300, but only matter when the trust secret is weak or non-rotating).

Practitioner takeaway: the durable hunt is an IP-to-RID enrichment check, not a Suricata rule. For every authenticated MS-SNTP packet to a DC (payload length 68 or 120, byte 0 low 3 bits equal 3 for client mode), extract the RID from payload bytes 48-51 as a little-endian 32-bit integer, resolve the source IP to a computer account via DHCP or DNS then an LDAP lookup of objectSid, and alert when the requested RID does not match the source's own. The Suricata rules, the hashcat module (module_31350.c, the OpenCL kernel m31350-pure[.]cl, and the m31350[.]py self-test oracle), the Python reference cracker, and the known-answer test vector are all in the report. Enable Windows Filtering Platform auditing (event 5156) on your DCs so w32time's UDP/123 accepts are logged, and baseline your fleet's 68-versus-120 split before writing any size-based rule.

item.title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
item.description:
Zero-day under active exploitation: suspected PRC-nexus actor ARMORY CASTLE used CVE-2026-123890, a vCenter SRP session key disclosure, to get administrator@vsphere[.]local. It was used in early September 2026, before VMware's Nov. 19, 2026 disclosure.
- Attack chain: ARMORY CASTLE came in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day and pivoted to internal Linux appliances without EDR. It ran nmap for ports 9080, 5480, 2012, 443 and 389, and visited /sdk and /ui. Port 2012 is the vCenter SSO control RPC that the exploit needs. On the appliance it dropped the SLIMSAVAGE webshell (ActiveSer.jsp, secret pwd=123, runs /bin/sh -c) and then CAGEMATCH (u.jsp), which accepts multipart uploads into /tmp. Root came from setting SUID on /bin/env with gdb, fed a base64 command via /tmp/gdb_file.
- The vCenter exploit: CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated SRP-6a session key disclosure over DCE/RPC in vmdir, caused by predictable UUIDv1 timestamps. It yields an authenticated administrator@vsphere[.]local session on vCenter 7.x and 8.x. The Go tool BONESAW (/tmp/123, internally vcenter-db-teamcheck-go) pulls data.mdb from /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/, extracts the STS SAML signing key, creates an SSO admin and grants Global Administrator on the root folder. Its csa subcommand leaves tenantcredential .pem, .der and .context.json files under a temp/extracted_tenant_signer_<host> directory. The build timestamp is 2026-07-13, before the related CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed, though Go build metadata can be altered.
- Golden SAML and persistence: SAWSNAKE (/tmp/sss) forges admin SAML assertions from the stolen keys, bypassing MFA, then gets deleted along with its idp_key.pem, trusted_cert_2.pem and domain.txt output. BEARBONES (/tmp/dbr) is a Dropbear SSH backdoor with a hardcoded password hash, plaintext credential logging and host keys in /tmp. It identifies itself as SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 and was run as a listener on TCP 53 and then 33992. Pivoting on that banner exposed a suspected obfuscation network of compromised firewalls and routers, such as 103.147.251[.]5, 118.174.128[.]34 and 81.45.89[.]43.
- vCenter and ESXi: the actor created a local admin sps-<REDACTED>[@]vsphere[.]local and turned SSH on with a PUT to /rest/appliance/access/ssh, then turned it off after taking the vCenter master key and PostgreSQL credentials. It then used the vpxuser account against the ESXi Host Client, logged in over SSH as root, and added its key to root authorized_keys. It staged a hidden .a directory on a VMFS volume, unpacked vmfs-pydist.tar.gz and ran vmfs_browser.py against flat VMDKs to extract NTDS, SYSTEM, SECURITY and DNS data from guest VMs. Everything was packed into o.tar.gz, pulled via scp and the .a directory removed. Staged archives were then pulled from the Linux appliance to the Remote Support appliance via HTTP GET.
- Another appliance got LAZYBONES (/usr/bin/vmtoolscs), a Go backdoor using Slack as C2 with AES-256-CTR messages, 150 to 450 second jitter and cmd, upload, download and sleep commands. Persistence is a systemd service set to restart every 50 minutes. It was previously seen in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion in early 2025 after CVE-2025-22457.
Takeaway: if you run vCenter, treat it as potentially compromised until you have checked. Look for unexpected SSO admin or machine accounts, and for SSH enable/disable calls to /rest/appliance/access/ssh in quick succession. Check for connections to TCP 2012 from non-admin hosts. On Remote Support and internal Linux appliances, check for SUID on /bin/env, executables in /tmp, and JSP files named ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp. On ESXi, look for a hidden .a directory on VMFS volumes, new root authorized_keys entries, and vmfs_browser.py. Hunt for the SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 banner on internal listeners (e.g. TCP 53/33992) and outbound, and for Slack API traffic from appliances. Rotate the STS signing key and vCenter secrets if you find evidence of access. Appliance .bash_history is deletable, so forward shell and firewall logs off-box. IOCs and YARA rules for the webshells, BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES and LAZYBONES are in the report. Patch with Broadcom's fix.

item.title: Inside Turla’s Cereal: 12 Exchange loaders, older traces and new ways to hunt
item.description:
Turla's Cereal toolset lives inside Exchange. ESET disclosed it on Nov 10, 2026. ReversingLabs then correlated file evidence, finding 12 related loader files, one sample in its corpus since 2022, and detection gaps from naming and sandboxing.
Russia-aligned Turla used Cereal against Exchange servers at two government organizations. ESET detected it in Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 on Nov 28, 2025. In Romania 🇷🇴, ESET found a compromise dating to Dec 23, 2025, with selective collection of email involving NATO and EU institutions. ESET attributed it to Turla with high confidence.
- How it hides: CerealLoader is the .NET component written to disk. It decrypts and runs other assemblies. CerealNeuron passively listens for encrypted requests to web paths resembling Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync, so there is no outbound beacon to hunt. CerealBox works inside the Exchange transport pipeline through injected code and wraps handlers of already registered transport agents. Mail keeps flowing and no new agent appears in configuration. ESET assesses CerealNeuron as a separate family that may have drawn on Neuron, and CerealBox avoids the agent registration that exposed LightNeuron.
- Loader count and naming: ReversingLabs found 12 related files. That is six of ESET's 11 listed CerealLoader samples, two extra WTSAPI32.dll candidates, and four byte-different copies of known builds. BlankPage, CerealMood and CerealLoader can label the same files. Microsoft Defender uses Backdoor:MSIL/BlankPage.C, .E and .F variants, and Malwarebytes uses Trojan.Turla. A hunt on "CerealLoader" alone misses samples.
- Proxy DLL construction: The Microsoft.Ceres.dll loader presents as SensApi.dll, "SENS Connectivity API DLL", version 10.0.20348.1. All three exports forward to the genuine C:\Windows\System32\SensApi.dll, a side-loading proxy. Other loaders borrow names like version.dll, WTSAPI32.dll and Microsoft[.]Search.Platform.dll. Two version.dll loaders share import hash 6585e33ab016ca2c68ba7eec691fbeb5. A pivot returned eight files: five malicious, three goodware, so it is a lead, not a verdict.
- Timeline caution: One ESET-listed loader reached the corpus on May 11, 2022, matching ESET's earliest sample, compiled Apr 27, 2022 and uploaded from Kazakhstan 🇰🇿. A second WTSAPI32.dll candidate (SHA-256 beginning 2751ae95) was first seen Nov 18, 2025, ten days before ESET's first detection. Both are file visibility, not proof of deployment or earlier victims. The report adds no new victims or initial access method.
- Detection blind spots: Loaders awaiting their Exchange or Windows host context scored low in sandboxes, despite sleeps and unusual process creation. In older Turla tooling, two NetBootstrapper DLLs extracted from NetInjector containers had zero scanner detections standalone, yet a sandbox flagged both with a Turla signature. Embedded-file analysis tied them back to the malicious parent.
- Hash-only gaps: The four byte-different copies share the original's .NET MVID, compile timestamp, import hash and structural hash but differ cryptographically. One copy appended two .dnmd sections of 23,552 bytes, which points to post-processing by analysis tooling. A hash list built from ESET's SHA-1 values would not cover them.
Takeaway: Run a targeted hunt on Exchange hosts, not an assumption of compromise. Look for unsigned .NET DLLs with a native entry point whose module names borrow Windows or Exchange components (version, wtsapi32, sensapi, Microsoft.Ceres, Microsoft[.]Search.Platform). Check for proxy DLLs forwarding exports to System32. Inspect web logs for requests to OWA, Autodiscover and ActiveSync paths, normalizing case. Map each hit to its parent process. Treat import hash matches as leads only: the first native-entry rule matched 60 legitimate signed Exchange assemblies until an unsigned-file condition was added. The report includes the SHA-256 values and two YARA rules in its appendix. ESET publishes only SHA-1.

item.title: BankWeaver Campaign Abuses Digital Banking Middleware to Deploy Web Shells
item.description:
BankWeaver: attackers traded an anonymous token for an admin token on an exposed Temenos Quantum Fabric auth service, then uploaded Java webshell FabricShell and recon tool FabricShadow to a financial institution.
- Entry: Forescout found it during a breach investigation at a financial services institution in early September. Opening the Spotlight app (usually /apps/spotlight/) returns an X-Kony-Authorization JWT for an anonymous user. One Fabric authentication service was set to anonymous app-user access instead of private, so it exchanged that token for a privileged Fabric token with no credentials (T1190, T1078). Temenos traced this to configuration, released updates and guidance, and advised restricting internet access to Spotlight and the Fabric admin and auth services.
- Persistence: with the admin token, the actor sent a POST to /workspace with zipimport?isAsync=true carrying a zip with Endpoints/java.xml, Operations/recon.xml and Operations/dbxdb_CustomQuery.xml under Apps/_Integration. That built a service that allowed OS command injection via {"cmd":"<command>"}. They tested with ls and pwd, spawned a netcat reverse shell, and pulled shell.sh-style scripts from sendit[.]sh, plainraw[.]com and temp[.]sh. Typos and repeated commands point to hands-on-keyboard activity.
- Payloads: FabricShell is a webshell registered through Kony's JavaService2. It checks each request for cmd, sql, user, pass and db. With cmd it runs /bin/sh -c and returns output plus exit code. Without it, it opens a JDBC connection and returns up to 50 rows (T1505.003, T1059.004). FabricShadow hooks DataPreProcessor2, which fires before every data request. It collects hostname, interface addresses, env var names, Java version, service account, id output and listings of /tmp and the working directory. It wraps output in RECON_PREPROCESSOR, RECON_DONE, RECON_ERR and RECON_FROM_FABRIC markers, POSTs it to C2 with header X-A: k1, and leaves a local copy in /tmp.
- Infrastructure: the actor used victims as staging points. FabricShell held fallback PostgreSQL credentials for another victim, and FabricShadow pointed to that victim's Red Hat Process Automation Manager, which acted as an exfil webshell. Over 30 IPs rotated as sources, mostly compromised UK 🇬🇧 NAS devices and home routers with exposed CWMP, plus a few VPS nodes. One residential proxy IP was seen downloading an ELF that fingerprints the host, persists via BitTorrent DHT and enrolls it in a botnet. Forescout has not tied that to BankWeaver. Payload hosting also includes 37.187.78[.]41.
- Scope: one confirmed compromise. Six more banks across Asia, the Middle East, Europe and the Americas appeared to share the configuration and exposure, but compromise there is unconfirmed.
Takeaway: the report has an IOC table (hosting, service and class names, host artifacts, content markers) and an ATT&CK mapping. On Fabric servers, hunt for ReconJavaService, recon_svc.jar, ReconPreProcessor, /tmp/.recon_out and the RECON_* markers. Alert on Java or Tomcat parents spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, nc or tar, and on outbound connections to ports 5005, 5006 and 25565. Treat ZIP imports, JAR registration and service publication as privileged changes and compare them to a signed inventory. Preserve disk, memory, logs, JARs and /tmp artifacts before cleanup. Then revoke Kony, JWT and JSESSIONID sessions and rotate credentials, including any found in WAF or app logs.

item.title: Device Code Phishing Resurges in November Through Fake SharePoint Payment Documents
item.description:
Device-code phishing against Microsoft 365 resurged in November. Payment-advice ZIPs with SVG redirectors lead to fake SharePoint pages that push recipients into the genuine Microsoft device login.
- Delivery: Hornetsecurity saw a sparse first email whose subject was a single period, with a recipient-personalized ZIP filename supplying the payment-advice pretext. The "HTML" inside was actually an SVG/XML document with a transparent full-canvas rectangle, so clicking the "security check" ran JavaScript. The script split an encoded string into fragments, reversed alternating ones, restored a substituted Base64 alphabet, decoded Base64, then applied a repeating-key XOR to recover the URL and assign it to window.location.href. A second campaign (SpwcinBillPaymentReports[.]zip) swapped the loader: 475 obfuscated string fragments, a checksum check, a derived XOR keystream, then document.write to inject the recovered page.
- Gate and lure: the first destination, 9l2v3vupv5.synerghylnksloads[.]cfd, ran a gate that scored browser-window properties and mouse or touch interaction. Its code includes a branch that redirects low-scoring visits to a benign site, which diverts some automated analysis. Passing visits reached a keyed page impersonating a SharePoint workspace of remittance reports with check images, showing a verification code and a copy control. Recipients were told to open a sign-in window, enter the code, authenticate and return to the document tab.
- The abuse: the sign-in lands on login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/deviceauth, a genuine Microsoft page. The attacker's client holds the device_code and polls for tokens, while the victim gets the short user_code. The victim completes real authentication, including any MFA, and the attacker's client receives the tokens. The question that matters is who initiated the request, not whether the page was real.
- Campaign plumbing: while the lure stays open, the browser calls /api/status/28475 and /api/heartbeat/28475 on the campaign host. In the second sample, the code sends an immediate heartbeat, then one every ten seconds, with session-status polling every three seconds. A captured-status handler hides the lure and shows an access-granted message or a configured exit page. That per-session polling of the status/heartbeat paths is a pattern you can hunt in proxy logs.
- Related infrastructure: tgg5rqrdcb.synerghylnksloads[.]cfd (joint-check variant, same parent domain as the first case), ngjedt0xrv.promtateusachorloadscorp[.]sbs (second sample), and 5txpm30dqe.krointechbillpaycheckingusalexingto[.]sbs (ElectronicFundsTransferRemittanceAdvice.html variant). One SVG variant routed through hxxps://base-hub-yw7q.p-xxorevv8.workers[.]dev/l/taaeR_gygko, adding a Cloudflare Workers hop. The first sample's HTML/SVG redirector SHA256 is bbf9f563371d6afc449c69546a4ec39e831ca18d3bf3764b7b4c27f525426140.
Takeaway: in Microsoft Entra sign-in logs, filter Authentication Protocol for Device code and review successful sign-ins with no business reason, checking application, account, source and timing. Correlate those with proxy hits to the hosts above and the status/heartbeat paths to rebuild the victim's workflow. Original transfer method helps trace sessions that began as device code even after a later renewal uses another flow. If a user completed such a flow, review the resulting authorizations and sessions promptly. Audit legitimate device-code use, then test the Conditional Access policy (Authentication flows, Device code flow, Block access) in report-only mode before enforcing. The full IOC table with hashes and domains is in the report.

item.title: CVE-2026-114938: OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Vulnerable To Pre-Authentication RCE (Java4Shell)
item.description:
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS v4.0 9.2 Critical) is a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's AVX-512 VBMI Base64 decoder. Calif[.]io demonstrated pre-auth RCE in default Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.
Disclosed November 17, 2026 alongside the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group advisories and Oracle's patch release. Zscaler published the breakdown below.
- The flaw: the HotSpot C2 JIT compiler emits a hand-rolled x86-64 Base64 decoding routine using AVX-512 VBMI. An arithmetic underflow in the store mask calculation for improperly padded Base64 tails lets malformed input trigger a 62-byte heap out-of-bounds write. It is only reachable on CPUs exposing avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids, and AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 (Graviton, Apple Silicon, Ampere Altra) and older x86-64 are not affected. The report says OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer is affected, plus Oracle Java SE, GraalVM, and downstream builds including Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine and Red Hat OpenJDK.
- Blast radius: Base64 sits under HTTP auth, cookies, tokens, TLS certificate parsing, REST payloads and uploads. Calif[.]io showed post-auth RCE in Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Netflix Spinnaker, plus a client-side TLS exploit against Java clients that connect to a malicious server.
- Exploit shape on the wire: the report lists JIT warm-up floods (rapid repetitive requests with valid Base64 fields to push the code into C2 compilation), then connection parking for heap grooming: several concurrent connections from one source IP send partial HTTP bodies, stall, then release the final bytes at the same time. The trigger is a Base64 string of 64 or 128 characters followed by an invalid tail (=, ==, X=, X==, XY=, ===). It also flags JavaBleed response anomalies: unusually large HTTP responses right after a spike in IllegalArgumentException errors.
- Host-side evidence: look for bursts of IllegalArgumentException with Illegal base64 character or invalid padding in application logs. Check for repeated HotSpot SIGSEGV crashes in hs_err_pid*.log, in G1 GC routines or StubRoutines::base64_decodeBlock. A Java process spawning unexpected OS shells or reconnaissance commands is the post-exploitation tell.
Takeaway: scope first. On Linux, grep /proc/cpuinfo for all four flags (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2) to find hosts that can actually run the vulnerable path. Then hunt those hosts for the exception spikes, hs_err_pid*.log crashes and JVM child shells above, and pull proxy logs for the 64 or 128 character padded-tail pattern and same-IP parked connections. Collect hs_err_pid logs and application logs before you restart JVMs, since patching requires a restart.
Fix: patched builds from November 17, 2026 onward (the report cites Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 8u513, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1), then restart all JVM processes and containers. If you cannot patch, start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics (recommended). -XX:UseAVX=2 also works on x86-64 only, and ARM64 JVMs will fail to start with it. Nginx proxy_request_buffering on disrupts the heap grooming timing but does not cover single-request chains like Elasticsearch or upgraded WebSocket tunnels. Network and host indicators are listed in the report.

item.title: CA-26-049: Qubole Cross-Account AWS Trust Abuse Campaign
item.description:
A threat actor used credentials tied to a Qubole-associated AWS account to assume trusted integration roles in dozens of customer environments in October. No CVE was involved. Valid External IDs did not stop it, and dormant roles were especially exposed.
- The access path: Qubole Data Service integrations rely on cross-account IAM roles whose trust policy lets a Qubole AWS account call STS AssumeRole, usually with an External ID. Every role assumption attributed to the actor carried a valid External ID and succeeded. The External ID is not a secret and does not protect you once the vendor identity itself is compromised. The report notes that public sources do not explain how the credentials were obtained, and no Qubole incident statement had been found at publication.
- Post-access behavior: broad List and Describe activity across S3, EC2, RDS, IAM, KMS, and data services. Then retrieval of Lambda environment variables, Secrets Manager values, and SSM Parameter Store entries. The actor validated discovered AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and Okta credentials with TruffleHog, and collected S3 data with ListBuckets, ListObjects, HeadObject, and GetObject. Mapped to T1078.004, T1580, T1555.006, and T1530. Stolen secrets can open doors well beyond the original role.
- Attacker fingerprints: session names often began with quiam-, including quiam-enum and quiam-scope-full. Traffic came from Mullvad VPN and OVH infrastructure, not the AWS ranges used for legitimate platform traffic. One principal ID appeared only in malicious activity. A second principal carried both malicious and legitimate Qubole traffic, so it needs network and behavioral context before you call it bad. The specific principal IDs are not in the public text; the report points to its Guardian Platform for detections and technical artifacts.
- Scope and caveats: dormant Qubole roles were especially significant because trust policies still allowed access with little or no legitimate vendor activity. The report also saw customer-owned access keys believed to support Qubole integrations abused in a separate cluster, not linked to this campaign, and worth its own investigation. Attribution is unestablished. A public claim by an actor calling themselves "n0n" is unverified. Researchers also found sso_agent.iso on attacker infrastructure but did not confirm deployment in victim environments.
DFIR angle: this is a CloudTrail story. Look for STS AssumeRole into Qubole integration roles where the source address is outside AWS, the role was dormant, or the session name starts with quiam-. Then correlate with rapid multi-service enumeration, GetFunctionConfiguration, GetSecretValue, GetParameter and GetParameters, and S3 ListObjects, HeadObject, and GetObject. TruffleHog user agents and bursts of GetCallerIdentity from newly discovered keys are useful corroboration, but they also show up in legitimate security testing, so do not alert on them alone.
Preserve logs first. Management events show the role assumption and many enumeration actions, but S3 object reads only appear if S3 data events or server access logs were enabled. Without those, you cannot confirm what was pulled.
Takeaway: inventory every current and legacy Qubole role and access key, then pull AssumeRole history for each. Treat any secret in Secrets Manager, SSM, or Lambda environment variables reachable by those roles as read, and rotate it, including downstream Entra ID and Okta credentials. Coordinate trust-policy changes with the vendor, and revoke dormant integrations rather than watching them. Even if you never used Qubole, review third-party roles and keys the same way.

item.title: Nginx2Shell: All You Need to Know About CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633
item.description:
Nginx2Shell: CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 allow unauthenticated RCE in NGINX itself, each rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. Fixed in 1.31.9 and 1.30.7. Rapid7 has published a public PoC for CVE-2026-123007.
Both bugs sit in how NGINX tracks HTTP/2 connections, and they are old. CVE-2026-123007 has been present for more than a decade and CVE-2026-123633 for nearly six years. Several teams found them independently: Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7 and Xint, many with AI-assisted code analysis. JFrog's report says there are no confirmed indicators of compromise yet, so in-the-wild exploitation is not confirmed.
- CVE-2026-123007: an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow control. When a stream is cancelled, NGINX adds the unsent data back to the counter without checking the protocol maximum. Once it passes the maximum, the WINDOW_UPDATE check wraps around and the attacker can keep raising it. The oversized counter becomes a negative length, and the TLS layer copies memory out of bounds, leaking memory and corrupting the heap. It was confirmed on 64-bit servers over HTTPS, even when serving only static files. Affects NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8.
- CVE-2026-123633: a use-after-free. A client sends a partial HTTP/2 HEADERS frame, and its connection lands on the idle list. When the request starts, the connection is never removed from that list. Later, while NGINX opens an upstream connection under low free-connection pressure, it can pick the busy connection to close, and the request keeps using the freed memory. It needs a backend, for example via proxy_pass. Affects NGINX Open Source 1.19.7 through 1.31.8.
- Exposure: HTTP/2 must be enabled, and NGINX Plus R33 and later is also affected. Directly internet-facing NGINX is most at risk: self-hosted web servers, Kubernetes ingress controllers, load balancers and appliances. A CDN or WAF that terminates HTTP/2 may block parts of the attack. The official Docker images were not yet updated at the time of the report. OpenResty and other bundled builds stay vulnerable until they ship fixes, and kubernetes/ingress-nginx is archived and will not be patched.
- Scoping check on each host or container: run nginx -v, then nginx -T and grep for http2 on or a listen directive with the http2 parameter. For 123633, also grep for proxy_pass, fastcgi_pass, uwsgi_pass, scgi_pass, grpc_pass, memcached_pass or tunnel_pass.
- Detection opportunities from the report: worker crashes in the error log such as "worker process 1234 exited on signal 11", unexpected commands or processes spawned by NGINX workers, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections moving unusually large amounts of data, a possible sign of a CVE-2026-123007 attempt.
Takeaway: patch to NGINX 1.31.9 or 1.30.7, or NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. If you cannot, set http2 off in affected server blocks (NGINX 1.25.1 and later), remove the http2 parameter from listen directives, reload, and confirm the old worker processes have exited. Preserve the error log before you reload. Then hunt back through it: grep "exited on signal" /var/log/nginx/error.log, or docker logs on the container with 2>&1 piped to the same grep, since containers log to stderr. Pair any crash clusters with process ancestry for children of NGINX workers. The report publishes no IOCs, so treat repeated signal 11 crashes on HTTP/2 hosts as a lead, not noise.

If you cannot, set http2 off in affected server blocks (NGINX 1.25.1 and later), remove the http2 parameter from listen directives, reload, and confirm the old worker processes have exited. Preserve the error log before you reload. Then hunt back through it: grep "exited on signal" /var/log/nginx/error.log, or docker logs on the container with 2>&1 piped to the same grep, since containers log to stderr. Pair any crash clusters with process ancestry for children of NGINX workers. The report publishes no IOCs, so treat repeated signal 11 crashes on HTTP/2 hosts as a lead, not noise.
