item.title: Java4Shell: Patch Java, But Check the Processor First
item.description:
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap overflow in HotSpot's AVX-512 Base64 decoder that gives unauthenticated RCE, but only on x86-64 hosts whose CPUs report four specific features. Patch every Java runtime, and let the processor set the order.
- Scope and status: Calif disclosed it on November 17, 2026. Oracle scores it CVSS 3.1 8.1 (High), and Calif scores it CVSS 4.0 9.2 (Critical). Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against default installs of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. A self-contained PoC that triggers the bug is public, and the per-product exploit chains are held back. As of November 18, Calif reports no in-the-wild exploitation and it is not in CISA KEV. CISA issued an alert urging immediate patching.
- Why the CPU matters: HotSpot swaps in a hand-written Base64 intrinsic chosen at startup from CPUID. The 512-bit AVX-512 VBMI path "miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write." All four flags must be present: bmi2, avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi. Calif lists Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, plus AMD EPYC and Ryzen from Zen 4 onward. ARM64 is not affected. "Has AVX-512" is not the test: Eclypsium's Skylake Xeon Platinum 8168 lacks avx512vbmi.
- Affected builds and the inventory gap: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, plus downstream distributions (Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE). Oracle's list also covers the Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf. Version numbers differ per distributor, so check the vendor advisory. CISA notes runtimes bundled in third-party apps, container images and appliances may not appear as separate inventory entries, and a package-manager query misses runtimes in app directories or containers.
- Verification traps: the grep of the flags line in /proc/cpuinfo can falsely say "not affected" on older kernels, because they print only flag names they know. In Eclypsium's lab, Ice Lake guests omitted avx512vbmi there while CPUID inside the same VMs showed it. The JVM reads CPUID, so use the cpuid tool on older guests. Then run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version with the application's own binary and options, and check UseAVX (3 means AVX-512). UseBASE64Intrinsics = true alone does not mean exposed. VMs migrating to newer hosts, or using host CPU passthrough, can flip a system into scope.
- Mitigation: where patching cannot land, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or -XX:UseAVX=2 removes the vulnerable path. Set it in the app's JVM options or JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, and confirm with PrintFlagsFinal. UseAVX=2 is x86-64 only, since a JVM on ARM will not start with it. Eclypsium has not measured the performance cost. CISA also suggests validating Base64 input, enforcing size limits and restricting unauthenticated access.
DFIR takeaway: CISA says crafted Base64 can crash the JVM. When HotSpot crashes it writes hs_err_pid<pid>.log, by default in the process's working directory. Collect these files or service-manager crash events from internet-facing Java services, and alert on new ones. An unexpected crash since November 17 on an internet-facing service running an affected build on a CPU with all four features is a reason to open an incident and review the host, not just restart the service. Preserve the hs_err file and any core dump before restarting. Prioritize Jira, Confluence, Keycloak, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

item.title: CA-26-048: OPTIMJACK: Optimizely Web Experimentation Supply Chain Attack
item.description:
OPTIMJACK: attackers abused an Optimizely Experimentation flaw to inject JavaScript into 188 snippets across 178 organizations, skimming cards, swapping crypto wallets and pushing iOS exploit kits.
On 16 November 2026, an unauthorized party used an Optimizely Experimentation vulnerability to add a loader to customer Project JavaScript. The modified snippets were served from trusted Optimizely infrastructure with a valid certificate, so origin allowlists did not stop execution. The report says this was not CDN cache poisoning. The 188 snippets are an observed set, not a full census. Sectors hit include finance, technology, retail, media, travel and healthcare.
- Attack chain: Optimizely Web customers embed a snippet, commonly from cdn.optimizely[.]com, that carries platform code, experiments and optional Project JavaScript. The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC. The payload host served a crypto clipper, then from 13:43 UTC a card skimmer. It manipulated forms, links, clipboard operations and outbound requests. It sent data through background browser beacons: page URL, accessible cookies, original wallet addresses and a screenshot (html2canvas abused). Mapped techniques: T1195.002, T1189, T1056, T1115, T1113, T1203.
- Reach and limits: The skimmer looked for Luhn-valid card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs. Cards typed into the site's own forms were exposed. Hosted payment fields in cross-origin provider iframes were out of reach. Only cookies without HttpOnly were collectable. A CSP that blocks external C2 domains may not help against the inline loader variant if Optimizely's CDN and dynamic script evaluation are allowed. On-chain theft is about $7,040 across BTC, LTC, TRON, ETH and BSC. The number of stolen cards, cookies or compromised phones is not established.
- iOS angle: The script fingerprinted iPhone and iPad versions and loaded hidden iframe chains from attacker exploit-kit domains. These were linked to Coruna (iOS 13 to 17), DarkSword (iOS 18.x) and a separate iOS 26 path. Pages on iOS 18.6 and earlier reloaded every 60 seconds to retry exploitation. iOS 18.7.3+ and 26.3+ are patched. Delivery does not prove exploitation, and the individual CVEs were not confirmed. Corporate and BYOD phones that visited affected news, travel and SaaS sites are the concern.
- Vendor and attribution status: Optimizely says it fixed the flaw, removed the injected code, secured accounts and added delivery protections. It has published no CVE, root cause, affected-version range or full customer list. At 21:52 UTC on 16 November, 1 of the 188 known snippets was still infected. The actor is unattributed. Deepwatch reports seeing and escalating related activity in customer environments.
- Evidence to collect: Preserve affected snippets, response headers and logs before cleanup. Compare current and historical Project JavaScript and published snippets against source control or a known-good baseline. Check CDN object Last-Modified values. Look for attacker-infrastructure references, base64 or obfuscated variants, dynamic script loaders, inline evaluation fallbacks and screenshot or beacon exfiltration code.
Takeaway: Scope from 16 November 2026 onward. Hunt DNS, proxy, secure web gateway and browser telemetry for the listed domains and URI paths, prioritizing browser-initiated requests or referrers from affected sites. Review CSP violation reports for new script origins. Audit Optimizely users, roles, API credentials, SSO and MFA settings, logins, project changes and publishing events, and rotate any credentials with project-write capability. A clean endpoint alert does not rule out browser-only card or clipboard theft. Investigate exposed iOS devices rather than relying on a reboot. The report points to the Guardian Platform for its detections and technical artifacts.

item.title: Attackers Exploit Optimizely Flaw To Inject Malicious JavaScript
item.description:
An attacker abused an Optimizely signup flaw on Nov 16 to inject JavaScript into customer projects. ThreatLabz counts 450+ domains serving it: wallet swaps, card skimming, iOS exploit delivery.
- Entry point: a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow gave unauthorized write access to the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field of multiple customer projects. The code shipped inside legitimate snippets from cdn.optimizely[.]com and, in some cases, customer domains, so sites that already allowlisted Optimizely loaded it with no visible page change. ThreatLabz saw more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the script, across airlines, banking, e-commerce, insurance, media, telecom and more. Optimizely says it blocked the path, fixed it, removed the injected code, ended sessions, revoked tokens and reset access.
- Stage 2: the injected code mostly acts as a loader that fetches track.js from attacker infrastructure such as 1688360[.]cc. track.js watches page content, clipboard and network data for wallet addresses (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Litecoin, Toncoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and swaps in attacker-controlled ones. On a successful swap it loads html2canvas.min.js and posts a screenshot, page URL, cookies and the original address to hxxps://1688360[.]cc/hit.php. HttpOnly cookies are out of reach.
- Card skimming: later payload versions watch input and textarea fields, keystrokes, form submissions and web requests for card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs, sending them to 1688360[.]cc/card.php. Hosted cross-origin payment iframes, such as Stripe or Adyen fields, are not readable by it. All of this stays in the page context of the compromised site, not browser-wide.
- iOS branch: on iPhones and iPads, track.js adds two script elements carrying data-channel-code, data-chain-url and data-cfasync attributes. For iOS 18.6 or earlier it may add a hidden, zero-size, off-screen iframe to hxxps://eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile.html. boot.js picks the path, and weifile.html loads index.js, which decodes embedded modules, reports device and domain metadata, and does anti-analysis checks such as navigator.webdriver. Reported entry paths point to the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits: A8/a.html, B9/b.html, D11/b.html, D12/b.html; boot.js also selects C10/c.html for iOS 26. Only here could impact exceed the browser sandbox, if an exploit chain succeeds.
- Infrastructure to pivot on: 1688360[.]cc, eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, ios-hack[.]icu and q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu[.]icu (secondary C2 base passed to the iframe as c2Base). Follow-on modules are requested as /<40-hex>.js, where the filename is sha256("cecd08aa6ff548c2" + module_id) cut to 40 characters.
Takeaway: If you run Optimizely, audit every Project JavaScript field for code you did not write, and review account creation events, admin access and snippet changes around Nov 16. Then rotate credentials, API and session tokens, and enforce MFA. Search proxy, DNS and browser telemetry for the domains above and for requests to hit.php and card.php. Check page DOMs for the data-channel-code and data-chain-url attributes, and CSP reports for loads from those domains. Because the loader rides a trusted CDN, enforce CSP with tight script-src, connect-src, img-src and frame-src to block the second stage and the exfil. The report has the full IOC tables, including module paths and attacker wallets, for retro-hunting. For users: watch card and crypto activity from Nov 16 and update iOS.

item.title: Apache Axis exploitation highlights legacy component risks
item.description:
CVE-2026-90436 is a critical unauthenticated RCE in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x, exploited within hours of a public PoC on November 12, 2026. Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central are confirmed targets, and many other Axis copies are likely hiding inside Java apps.
- Exploitation is active. Researchers reported it on November 16, 2026. CISA scored it CVSS v3.1 9.8 and Atlassian scored affected Confluence deployments CVSS v4 9.3. The flaw sits in SOAP fault handling: Axis can instantiate a Java class named in a crafted request before checking that it is safe to load. If a suitable class exists on the target, code runs with no authentication or user interaction. Some intrusions were chained with other vulnerabilities to gain elevated privileges.
- Axis is a library, not a product, so most inventories miss it. The CVE record lists the Maven packages axis:axis and org.apache.axis:axis through 1.4 as affected, and Ubuntu and Debian track their Axis packages as affected with no fixed version. Standalone deployments are exposed whenever a SOAP endpoint is reachable. There is no legacy API setting to turn off, and service-level authentication does not help because the malicious fault message is processed before application handlers run. Internet-facing SOAP services are the top priority.
- Observed impact depends on the host. On Confluence, activity centered on credential discovery and use of stored application secrets to reach identity and cloud services. On an RMM platform like N-central, root access would let an attacker push scripts and software to every managed endpoint.
- Scoping the exposure: search servers, application directories, and container images for axis.jar and axis-1.4.jar. Check SBOM records and Java dependencies for the two Maven packages, and review vendor advisories. In web server logs and application deployments, look for /axis/services/ paths and the default happyaxis.jsp page.
Takeaway: Treat any system that had a vulnerable SOAP interface reachable after November 6, 2026 as in scope for review. In web logs, examine requests to SOAP endpoints, especially unusual POSTs and repeated server errors tied to SOAP services. In endpoint telemetry, hunt for Java service processes executing commands, cryptocurrency miners, web shells, new scheduled tasks or system services, and unexpected outbound connections. If you find compromise, rebuild the host, rotate application credentials and service account secrets, and review authentication activity across connected identity, cloud, and management platforms. Fixes: Confluence Data Center 9.2.28 or later, N-central 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) or later. Until you can upgrade, disable the SOAP interfaces or restrict network access to them. For custom apps, move to Axis2 or build Apache's published source patch into a maintained build. The report does not publish IOCs or detection rules, so the hunt content above is your starting point.

item.title: What the Optimizely incident reveals about third-party website scripts
item.description:
Attackers exploited an Optimizely Web Experimentation flaw to inject skimmer JavaScript into customer projects, reaching 178 organizations without touching their servers. Look to vendor audit logs, not endpoints.
Field Effect's report covers the Optimizely disclosure of November 17, 2026. The attacker never compromised the victims' own infrastructure. They changed code hosted by a trusted vendor, and visitors' browsers ran it.
- How it worked: Per public reporting, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's platform to modify customer projects, then planted a small loader in the Project JavaScript field. Optimizely republishes snippets automatically, so every page loading one ran the loader, which fetched a payload from 1688360[.]cc. Delivery came through cdn.optimizely[.]com. Skimming began around 13:43 UTC on November 16, the payload was updated 26 times that day, and most sites were cleaned by about 21:52 UTC. No CVE or severity rating has been released.
- What the code did: It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses (the attacker's wallets reportedly received about $7,040), captured card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs from website-controlled checkout forms, and collected screenshots and cookies lacking HttpOnly. iPhone and iPad users were redirected to infrastructure tied to the Coruna (iOS 13.0 to 17.2.1) and DarkSword (iOS 18.4 to 18.7) exploit kits. Public reporting has not shown a successful device compromise.
- Scope: Researchers found the injection in 188 of 1,611 snippets examined, tied to 178 organizations, with banks and financial firms the largest group at 32. Tampered scripts also turned up at Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media, with earliest activity on November 13, three days before the Optimizely injections. How the code reached those three services is undisclosed, and so is when it ended.
- Why controls missed it: The code came from a domain sites already trust. Of the organizations examined, 24 (about 15 percent) had a CSP strict enough to block it, 68 had no CSP, and 50 had policies that let it run and exfiltrate. The loader appeared as a direct link, a Base64 version, and a fully embedded fallback that works even if the external domain is blocked. Stolen data went straight from the browser to the attacker, so the sites' own servers saw normal traffic. At least one snippet was cleaned and later served a concealed version again, and it is unknown whether that was persistence, incomplete remediation or a new compromise.
- Evidence to examine: The Optimizely Project JavaScript field and any experiment-specific custom code, plus the vendor's project audit logs and change histories. Tag manager deployments like Google Tag Manager can hide Optimizely from a code search. Optimizely removed the malicious code on November 16 and 17, so a clean script today proves nothing about the exposure window. Other sources: CSP reports, client-side script monitoring, and DNS, proxy or gateway logs for internal users who visited affected sites.
Practitioner takeaway: Request Optimizely audit logs and project change history, and ask Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media for their exposure windows, starting November 13. Search project code for 1688360, atob(, .icu, track.js and webshell. Check proxy and DNS logs for 1688360[.]cc, 136.113.106[.]136, 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu and webshell[.]lol (listed in the report), and block them without blocking cdn.optimizely[.]com. If card fields were website-controlled, bring in your processor and counsel early. Rotate credentials and API keys that can modify projects, and rotate sessions where cookies lacked HttpOnly.

item.title: Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI package compromised to steal credentials
item.description:
Microsoft's official Agent Framework package on PyPI was compromised on November 17, 2026. Two malicious releases, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, ran a credential stealer at Python startup, with no import of the package required.
- Why it matters: Microsoft Agent Framework is an open-source toolkit for building and coordinating AI agents, with roughly 200,000 monthly downloads on PyPI. Both bad versions kept their dependency on the legitimate agent-framework-core 1.26.0, so the framework kept working while the malware ran in the background. Nothing looked broken to the developer.
- Version 1.26.1: Socket and StepSecurity say it used agent_framework_meta.pth to launch the stealer in agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py during Python startup. It harvested secrets from environment variables, local config files, and other running processes where permissions allowed. Targets included Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face, OpenAI, and other services. It also tried to obtain Azure managed identity access tokens and Azure DevOps OIDC tokens, which could open up more cloud resources.
- Version 1.26.2: This release restored the original package initializer and moved the malicious code into af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. It added GitHub Actions OIDC token requests and searches of GitHub runner directories, so CI/CD runners were a direct target, not just developer laptops. Ox Security also documented the campaign.
- Exfiltration and timeline: Both versions sent data to the same attacker-controlled endpoint, hxxps://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb. PyPI quarantined 1.26.1, but the attacker published 1.26.2 about 2.5 minutes later, and it was quarantined roughly eight minutes after that. The second push shows the attacker still held publishing access after the first takedown.
- Open questions: How the attacker got publish rights on Microsoft's official PyPI project is still unknown. BleepingComputer has asked Microsoft about the point of breach and had no reply at publication time.
DFIR takeaway: Treat any host, container, or CI runner that installed 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 as compromised. Isolate it and stop running Python or pip there. Rebuild from a known-clean environment on 1.26.0, and rotate every credential within reach of that environment: cloud keys, GitHub and Docker tokens, Hugging Face and OpenAI keys, and anything a managed identity or OIDC token could reach.
To scope the damage, search egress logs for the webhook[.]site URL path above. Separate blocked requests from completed transfers, because only completed ones confirm secrets left the environment. Also look for the file names agent_framework_meta.pth and af_runtime_diag.pth, plus the two named Python modules, in your environments and build caches. Pull install history from pip logs and CI job logs to see which builds picked up the bad versions. Check Azure and GitHub audit logs for token use from unexpected locations after the install time.

item.title: We caught the agent-framework PyPI compromise six minutes after it published
item.description:
Microsoft's agent-framework on PyPI shipped a .pth credential stealer in versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. It runs on every Python start, no import needed, and targets Azure, GitHub, and CI secrets.
- Timeline (UTC, Nov 17, 2026): 1.26.1 went live at 20:35 and Elastic's supply-chain monitor flagged it at 20:41. 1.26.2 followed at 21:08 with the same stealer under new filenames. PyPI removed both within the hour. The meta-package averages 196,000 downloads a month across all versions.
- Trigger: 1.26.1 added agent_framework_meta.pth and _telemetry.py and modified __init__.py. Python's site module executes any .pth line starting with import at interpreter startup, so the single line import agent_framework_meta fires before any user code. The loader appended to __init__.py calls _telemetry._start(). It sets an _AF_TEL environment variable to run once per process tree, forks, and detaches the child with setsid(), so the theft adds no visible delay. Windows falls back to a background thread.
- Collection: environment variables whose names match strings like TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, HF_, OPENAI, and SUBSCRIPTION. It reads /proc/<pid>/environ for up to 300 processes, including SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and IDENTITY_HEADER. On disk it sweeps ~/.azure, pip.conf, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config.json, Hugging Face tokens, Foundry config, .env files under /app and /workspace, and Azure Pipelines agent .credentials files.
- Token minting: in Azure DevOps it uses SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN against the SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI endpoint. The report notes it omits serviceConnectionId, so it is unclear whether those requests return a usable token. On Azure resources it uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT, else IMDS at 169.254.169[.]254, requesting tokens for 12 resources including Resource Manager, Graph, Key Vault, Storage, and Azure DevOps. It also grabs IMDS metadata (subscription ID, resource group, VM name), which tells the attacker which environment the tokens belong to.
- 1.26.2 delta: new hook af_runtime_diag.pth and module af_runtime_diag.py, same stealer plus a GitHub Actions OIDC collector. It reads ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and requests tokens for the audiences api://AzureADTokenExchange and hxxps://management[.]azure[.]com/. The exfil User-Agent changed from af-runtime-diagnostics/1 to runtime-diagnostics/1.
- Exfil: a single POST per run containing hostname, username, working directory, command-line args, and timestamp, serialized as JSON, zlib-compressed, and Base64-encoded. Both versions use hxxps://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry. Wheel SHA-256: 1.26.1 is d27fa34414e6201d5e03e559ef634f020057554d7b3f4898dd5d7cd3e989e110 and 1.26.2 is 3d20a8bc91351a9a16b6db243b848ceca0206b7a8623b02d2af553a9c9f7e0a9. Hashes for the .py and .pth files are in the report's IOC table.
Takeaway: if either version touched a build agent or laptop, treat everything readable on that host as stolen. Search site-packages for agent_framework_meta.pth and af_runtime_diag.pth, and hunt file creation events for those names plus _telemetry.py and af_runtime_diag.py. Search proxy, DNS, and firewall logs for webhook[.]site and the two User-Agents. The report includes ES|QL hunting queries for the file creations and webhook[.]site DNS lookups. Pin to 1.26.0, rotate long-lived secrets, and review Azure and GitHub activity for short-lived tokens that can't be revoked. Consider a delay before adopting newly published packages, since this one was caught within hours.

item.title: Threat Researcher’s Notebook: Detection Strategies for ARTEX and Related Forks
item.description:
ARTEX, an open-source agentic offensive framework, is now used by criminals and China-nexus actors. ReversingLabs maps 11 fork-families sharing one engine, so hunt behaviors, not hashes.
ARTEX was published to GitHub in July 2026 by a developer known as Autumn-27 as an authorized testing tool. The FBI dates malicious use to at least August. The developer pulled the repo on October 8, but forks and archives persist, and more than a thousand consoles were exposed online in early November. Reported campaigns range from South Korean 🇰🇷 financial firms to the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply chain compromise. Microsoft's October 21st report describes some intrusions going from first contact to privileged access in under three hours.
- Shared engine: all 184 Go samples import github[.]com/Autumn-27/norma, an LLM orchestrator that runs planner and worker agents in parallel. ReversingLabs consolidated 3,147 unique IPs (3,096 actionable after triage) and confirmed 969 live consoles. Actionable IPs cluster at PEG Tech, UFO/B2-Net, Yancy, Tencent, Alibaba and UAB Host-Baltic.
- Fingerprinting the console: two 1x1 images turned out to be UI placeholders, not beacons. The real pivot was the raw-embedded favicon, a 15,086-byte BMP, sha256 8b567c0244f2dbee787165aea9c4ddabaaafb0fdb3b29899ac898c60a589856b, mmh3 -576220750. Every fork serves it except AntiFox (mmh3 -1356779733 and -397770841). Some forks fake panel titles, even "Sign in - Google Accounts" (T1036, T1656).
- Network behaviors: the norma core works in waves, so look for tight clusters of process and network events separated by short LLM "thinking" pauses. Scanning uses projectdiscovery/blackrock (T1046, T1595.001), a masscan-style cipher that shuffles targets, so expect non-sequential connects and many unanswered SYNs or resets across wide address space. DNS recon (dnsx, cdncheck, miekg/dns; T1590.002) shows as bursts of A, AAAA, CNAME and TXT queries and NXDOMAIN spikes.
- Lateral movement: golang[.]org/x/crypto/ssh (T1021.004) gives Go-native SSH. Check for odd client identification strings and key exchange, cipher and MAC ordering that differ from OpenSSH or PuTTY. In host auth logs, look for machine-speed logins followed instantly by commands.
- Samples and platforms: 72 ELF, 58 Mach-O and 54 PE across linux/amd64, linux/arm64, windows/amd64, darwin/amd64 and darwin/arm64. A static Go binary of about 40 MB embedding a MITM proxy, PTY driver, ProjectDiscovery recon suite and SQLite console DB is likely ARTEX. Operators sit behind commercial VPNs and shared proxy pools, so you will rarely find the binary on victim endpoints.
Takeaway: run retroactive log hunts for the wave cadence, randomized scan patterns, DNS enumeration bursts and Go SSH handshakes, and treat static hashes and permanent IP blocklists as weak. The report ships the actionable IP list as a CSV and the favicon sha256 hashes in its IOC section. Pivot internet scan data on mmh3 -576220750 to find exposed consoles, and lock down admin planes and AI assistant credentials.

item.title: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI Supply-Chain Attack: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 Steal Cloud Credentials
item.description:
Microsoft's agent-framework on PyPI shipped credential-stealing versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. A .pth startup hook runs on every Python launch and harvests Azure, GitHub, and CI/CD secrets.
- Scope and timing: the agent-framework meta-package sees roughly 190,000 monthly downloads. Both bad versions were published within 33 minutes on November 17, 2026 (20:35 to 21:08 UTC) and pulled by about 21:20 UTC. The last clean version is 1.26.0. agent-framework-core and 22 other sibling packages are not affected. No CVE has been assigned. Loose pins such as agent-framework>=1.26 could have pulled the malicious builds into developer workstations, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions pipelines, and cloud build hosts.
- Mechanism: the attack lived entirely in packaging. No Agent Framework code changed and no rogue dependency was added. Each release dropped a .pth file that executes on every interpreter launch, even if Agent Framework is never imported. The collector forks a detached background process and sets a flag so child processes do not re-run it. Version 1.26.2 restored the legitimate __init__.py byte for byte and moved the payload into a new top-level module, which defeats diff-based review of the package.
- What it steals: the malware requested fresh tokens rather than only copying stored secrets. It collects environment variables matching TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, and HF_, among others, from its own process and up to 300 others via /proc/*/environ. It pulls Azure managed-identity tokens for 12 Azure resources through IMDS and identity endpoints, plus Azure DevOps SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and OIDC tokens. Version 1.26.2 also grabs GitHub Actions OIDC tokens where workflows have id-token: write. File targets include Azure CLI state, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config.json, Hugging Face tokens, and .env files.
- Exfiltration: everything leaves as zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook[.]site URL. The report lists the User-Agent strings af-runtime-diagnostics/1 and runtime-diagnostics/1.
- On-disk artifacts: agent_framework_meta.pth and af_runtime_diag.pth in site-packages, along with the payload modules. Check lockfiles, container images, CI caches, and live environments for 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. A clean-looking __init__.py proves nothing here.
DFIR takeaway: treat any host or runner that installed 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 as credential-exposed, because the hook fired on any Python start, not just on import. Preserve the site-packages directory and the .pth files before rebuilding. Then hunt proxy and DNS logs for webhook[.]site, the two User-Agent strings, and bursts of IMDS token requests. Audit Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure DevOps audit logs, and GitHub Actions workflow runs since November 17 for use of stolen tokens. Rotate Azure service principals, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, GitHub, npm, PyPI, Hugging Face, and Docker registry credentials, plus anything in env vars or .env files. Rebuild from clean environments pinned to agent-framework==1.26.0 with hash verification. The IOC list is in the report.

Version 1.26.2 also grabs GitHub Actions OIDC tokens where workflows have id-token: write. File targets include Azure CLI state, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config.json, Hugging Face tokens, and .env files.

- Exfiltration: everything leaves as zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook[.]site URL. The report lists the User-Agent strings af-runtime-diagnostics/1 and runtime-diagnostics/1.

- On-disk artifacts: agent_framework_meta.pth and af_runtime_diag.pth in site-packages, along with the payload modules. Check lockfiles, container images, CI caches, and live environments for 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. A clean-looking __init__.py proves nothing here.

DFIR takeaway: treat any host or runner that installed 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 as credential-exposed, because the hook fired on any Python start, not just on import. Preserve the site-packages directory and the .pth files before rebuilding. Then hunt proxy and DNS logs for webhook[.]site, the two User-Agent strings, and bursts of IMDS token requests. Audit Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure DevOps audit logs, and GitHub Actions workflow runs since November 17 for use of stolen tokens. Rotate Azure service principals, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, GitHub, npm, PyPI, Hugging Face, and Docker registry credentials, plus anything in env vars or .env files. Rebuild from clean environments pinned to agent-framework==1.26.0 with hash verification. The IOC list is in the report.

item.title: The folder your browser keeps after you clear your history
item.description:
Clearing browsing history on Chromium for Android leaves the File System store untouched. Alexis Brignoni's known-data test shows folder names, file names and file contents surviving the cleanup, and two new ALEAPP artifacts now parse them.
- Why it survives: the Clear browsing data dialog splits history from site data, and the File System store follows the cookies and site data checkbox, not the history one. A user who ticks only history loses the visible record of where they went while the record of what sites stored on the device stays. Brignoni ran the test on Chrome 124 in an Android 15 emulator. A page wrote one file via the legacy webkitRequestFileSystem call and one via the Origin Private File System (OPFS), and both landed in the same store. It sits in any Chromium profile, so Edge, Samsung Internet, DuckDuckGo and WebView-based apps are in scope.
- Anatomy: the profile's File System folder holds numbered directories (000 onwards), an Origins folder and a Paths store. Each numbered directory has p and t branches (persistent and temporary), with eight-digit extensionless files holding the raw bytes. Two LevelDB databases give them meaning: one maps directories to origins, the other maps the site's folder structure to the eight-digit files. For Chrome the path is data/data/com.android.chrome/app_chrome/Default. Embedded third-party sites go to a separate bucket folder, WebStorage/<bucket>/FileSystem. ALEAPP's Bucket Storage artifact reads it and names both the embedded site and the top-level host, and the embedded address never appears in History.
- Deleted records can still lead: after clearing site data the files are removed, but a deleted LevelDB entry is superseded rather than wiped, so it can still name an origin until compaction rewrites the tables. That mechanism is the report author's working theory; the pull request describes only the outcome. Hindsight (Storage tab) parses the store on desktop profiles, and ccl_chromium_reader covers it for scripted work.
- Reality check from the corpus: across 22 images, the first artifact found 33 site rows on 16 images, two folder rows and no saved files. The bucket artifact added 29 rows on 6 images. Expect origin leads often, folders rarely and usable content rarer still.
- Limits to state in a report: bucket times come from the QuotaManager and cover the whole bucket, so they show scope, not when a file was written. A bucket record proves something stored data for an origin, not that the user visited it. ALEAPP's parsers cite Chromium source at version 130 while the test ran on 124, and the format is an internal detail, so validate on the build in front of you. On 1 November the author added an Android user column and a Bucket ID to separate first-party from bucketed storage, so keep your ALEAPP current.
First look on a phone image:
cd data/data/com.android.chrome/app_chrome/Default find "File System" -type f | sort strings -n 8 "File System/Origins/"*.log | sort -u
The LevelDB .log is uncompressed, so strings works for a first pass. The .ldb tables are Snappy-compressed and need a LevelDB-aware parser.
Takeaway: in exfiltration or file-sharing cases, look for orphaned eight-digit files under a file-hosting origin. Ryan Benson found Mega staged downloads here, with leftovers lingering for months after the final file was deleted. The report author's untested idea is to run grep -rl "SQLite format 3" "File System" to find whole OPFS-hosted SQLite databases that no browser-aware tool parses yet. When a subject says they cleared everything, find out which checkbox they ticked, then corroborate any origin with History or network artifacts before attributing intent.

item.title: Test
item.description:
ARTEX, an open-source AI-agent pen-testing framework, became an attacker staple in about three months. Storm-0940, assessed by Microsoft as China 🇨🇳 state aligned, used it to hit a vendor's Microsoft 365 apps, then tried sign-ins against more than 2,250 customer tenants.
- Storm-0940 chain (Microsoft's Oct 21 report): a password spray from 144.172.64[.]99 ran Oct 10 to 14, with hundreds of thousands of failed attempts peaking at thousands per minute on Oct 11. After taking over the vendor's app identities, the actor signed in as service principals and ran Microsoft Graph recon. It added credentials to existing OAuth apps, read secrets across multiple Key Vaults, and in one tenant used a management app to assign itself Global Administrator. No Microsoft vulnerability was involved, only valid credentials. Attribution is Microsoft's assessment. Google tracks overlapping activity as UNC7228, dating back to at least August 2026, hitting US 🇺🇸 and European entities in enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductors and telecom. Wiz reports the actor now targets IT and software vendors, focusing on identity providers such as Okta and Entra and on Microsoft 365 integrations.
- Machine speed shapes the evidence. Microsoft saw one agent go from searching GitHub to exfiltrating Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. Google saw bursts of 2 to 25 seconds, including 27 events in 23 seconds. Failed calls get fixed fast: a wrong Key Vault API version was retried correctly about 28 seconds later, Azure SQL firewall rules after about 60 seconds, Application Insights after about 80. Agents rotate fingerprints once blocked, and Wiz saw more than 15 user-agent strings from Storm-0940-linked activity.
- Storm-3358 shows the non-cloud side: anonymous file upload and SSRF flaws on internet-facing systems, then agents pulled WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2 with netcat and curl. Reported ARTEX servers: 91.92.240[.]238, 85.11.168[.]45, 178.16.54[.]129, 31.77.229[.]35, with C2 at 85.11.167[.]52 and WISP nodes at 199.19.95[.]66, 199.19.95[.]67 and 199.19.95[.]68.
- Tool-level artifacts: files named artex-probe-* with roughly incrementing five-digit numbers, and created accounts with ArtexProbe in the name and plaintext passwords. Short-lived JSP webshells include cl1217.jsp, f1219a.jsp and z1219.jsp; Google saw one written through MySQL general log poisoning. C2 includes rotating webhook[.]site URLs, 491 of them in one intrusion Google observed. Client strings include curl/7.88.1, python-requests/2.34.2, Python-urllib/3.12, norma/0.4 and ReconProbe/1.0, though Wiz cautions many are not unique to ARTEX. Cloud behavior to look for: one source authenticating as multiple service principals, or one app requesting tokens for several Azure services in a short window.
- Entry often starts with leaked secrets. Apiiro found 2,539 sensitive secrets across 1,994 public GitHub repos in AI coding agent settings files, covering database passwords, API tokens and root logins. Microsoft says agents repeatedly focus on credentials that reach AI services. With more than 12,000 forks, shared defaults will not tell you which group is behind an intrusion, and Google forecasts fully autonomous, stealthier attacks within 3 to 6 months.
Takeaway: these sign-ins do not show up in user sign-in logs. Collect service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for every tenant and hunt weeks back. Inventory third-party multi-tenant apps across tenants, check for credentials added to existing OAuth apps, and alert on any app assigning itself Global Administrator. Treat any publicly exposed credential as compromised. Network IOCs are short-lived, so build detections on behavior: a failed secret followed by a success, one app requesting many token types in minutes, retries corrected within a minute, and dozens of events in seconds. The IOC lists from Microsoft, Google and Wiz are in the report.

item.title: Bazuka: The Fraud Framework That Can Do It All
item.description:
Bazuka, found during an NFC relay investigation, is a full Android fraud framework: dropper, core, 23 modules, ADB bridging, and LLM agents in the operator panel that help pick victims.
- Delivery: Traffers push the dropper through landing pages with lures like IPTV apps and adult content. A VirusTotal sample kept its filename, TikTok18-Dropper-tiktok18-premium-1793332000-daf6efe2.apk, SHA256 f046b50166c8229b49839eeebcc7fd14bf3f198e4ec1bfde8a5b271e1407dec5. It asks for install-from-unknown-sources permission, installs a stager through a PackageManager session, and launches com.tiktok.premium[.]pro. A second variant is a downloader, SHA256 4d572669d6000304a692874c1583021dfdb4f2f113ea487e470f7e4c486e503a, which pulls the core directly. The dropper builder uses minimal manifest permissions, apparently to help pass Google Play review. ThreatFabric has seen no sign that this happened.
- Loading and C2: The core and modules are DEX files loaded by InMemoryDexClassLoader straight from a byte array, so modules never touch disk. The stager calls DualWebSocketManager, WireSessionManager and ModuleLoader under com[.]support.assistant[.]network. The core talks over Control and Data WebSockets with ChaCha20-Poly1305. Keys rotate, sit in SharedPreferences, and are also sent to C2. On connect, the bot reports device info including a ThreatLevel, so operators can rate a victim within seconds.
- Permission abuse: The core taps through prompts itself, using Accessibility or ADB shell commands. It can enable Developer options and Wireless Debugging, intercept the pairing PIN, and open a TLS session to the ADB daemon. Accessibility rebinding paths include the enabled_accessibility_services secure setting, the self_adb module's rebind_accessibility command, and the com.guidocool.cryptomanager.action.A11Y_REBIND broadcast. The uninstall_shield module counters removal, and self-destruct calls setApplicationEnabledSetting(packageName, 3, 1). A new overlay trick screenshots the home or lock screen and replays it on command.
- Fraud modules: input_recorder is a regex keylogger for card numbers, wallet addresses and passwords. twofa and smsmessage grab one-time codes. clip_monitor swaps BTC, ETH, TRC20 and SOL addresses. screen_control captures the lock PIN, password or pattern. optics handles remote control and phishing overlays, proxy is a reverse TCP proxy, and tapread-nfc_module relays contactless cards. The report says automated payments are the one attack the framework does not cover.
- Infrastructure: Cloudflare-fronted subdomains of brokerok[.]org are hardcoded in the code and in the downloader's bundled certificate: c2ws.brokerok[.]org, c2data.brokerok[.]org, c2proxy.brokerok[.]org, c2api.brokerok[.]org. Two origin servers turned up. 95.181.213[.]21 sat in Moscow and was already offline. 170.168.61[.]117 (gargona[.]cash) sits in Amsterdam, Netherlands 🇳🇱, hosted by GTHost, and its address is in the dropper's certificate. Ports: 8082 and 8445 for the panel, 8443 for bot C2, 8444 for the data channel. The panel frontend is readable without authentication, mixes in Russian 🇷🇺 UI strings, and embeds a console plus LLM chat that can score victims and suggest permission-click strategies.
Takeaway: Hash hunt with the core, dropper, downloader and per-module SHA256 values in the report appendix. Check devices for com.tiktok.premium[.]pro, unexpected Accessibility service entries, Wireless Debugging switched on without user intent, and traffic to the brokerok[.]org subdomains or the two origin IPs. Because modules load only in memory, device triage should favor package, settings and network evidence over file carving.

item.title: Microsoft's agent-framework Hijacked on PyPI via Silent .pth Startup Hook
item.description:
Microsoft's agent-framework on PyPI (about 40,000 weekly downloads) was hijacked on November 17, 2026. Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 ship a .pth startup hook that runs a credential stealer on every Python launch, even if your code never imports agent_framework.
- Timeline and provenance: 1.26.1 went live at 20:35 UTC and was quarantined at 21:06. The attacker uploaded 1.26.2 at 21:08, and both were gone by 21:16. Renovate was opening upgrade PRs within six minutes of 1.26.1. This was not a Microsoft pipeline compromise. ZIP headers show Info-ZIP zip 3.0 repacking at 20:26:19 UTC under uid 1000 on a UTC+8 host, while the WHEEL file still claims flit 4.2.0. JFrog has not attributed it to a known group.
- Why the hook works: the agent-framework meta-package only installs a stub, agent_framework_meta, and nobody imports it. So the attacker left the agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0 pin intact and added a 28-byte agent_framework_meta.pth to the root of site-packages containing "import agent_framework_meta". site[.]py exec()s that line at interpreter startup, so python, pytest, IDE language servers, container entrypoints and even pip trigger it. The 1.26.1 hook calls _telemetry._start(). In 1.26.2 the clean __init__.py was restored and the hook moved to af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. It forks and calls setsid on Linux and macOS, and uses a daemon thread on Windows. _AF_TEL=1 prevents fork loops, and no lockfile is written, so every fresh launch exfiltrates again.
- What it steals: environment variables matching 31 substrings (Azure, AWS, GitHub, OpenAI, Hugging Face and more), plus 35 file globs. These cover ~/.azure/*.json token caches, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, /app/.env, /workspace/.env and Azure DevOps agent .credentials stores. On Linux it reads the first 300 /proc/[0-9]*/environ entries. It also queries IDENTITY_ENDPOINT, MSI_ENDPOINT or the VM metadata service at 169.254.169[.]254 for live OAuth2 tokens across 12 audiences. 1.26.2 added GitHub Actions OIDC tokens and /home/runner paths.
- Exfiltration and operator mistakes: data is JSON, zlib, Base64 with no encryption, sent by HTTPS POST to hxxps://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry. The User-Agent is af-runtime-diagnostics/1, changed to runtime-diagnostics/1 in 1.26.2. There is no second stage, no persistence outside site-packages and no worm. The inbox is now rate-limited (HTTP 429), but early victims got HTTP 200 and their secrets may be readable by anyone holding the UUID. The Azure DevOps OIDC request is broken, though SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN still leaks via os.environ. The IMDS timeouts delay exfil about 104 seconds on non-Azure Linux. Windows CLI runs can exit before the thread finishes, and macOS misses /Users/* paths but still leaks env vars and ~/.azure/*.json.
- Cleanup trap: do not run bare pip uninstall first, because pip is a Python entrypoint and triggers the stealer once more. Export _AF_TEL=1, delete the four malicious files from every site-packages directory using the environment's own Python binary, then reinstall agent-framework==1.26.0. uv does not execute .pth hooks during removal. Rotate everything reachable. Rotating passwords alone does not revoke cached Entra ID refresh tokens, and managed identity or OIDC access tokens stay valid up to 24 hours. Also note that __pycache__ .pyc files do not show whether the payload ran, since pip compiles bytecode at install time.
Takeaway: hunt for agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py in site-packages, including inside container images built on November 17 and in lockfiles or Renovate/Dependabot PRs from that day. Check build-host DNS for webhook[.]site and TLS-decrypted proxy logs for POSTs to /d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry, where HTTP 200 means exfil completed. Review Entra ID Managed Identity sign-ins for token replay. Wheel and file SHA-256 hashes are in the report's IOC tables, so search internal mirrors for the wheel hashes and evict hits.

These cover ~/.azure/*.json token caches, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, /app/.env, /workspace/.env and Azure DevOps agent .credentials stores. On Linux it reads the first 300 /proc/[0-9]*/environ entries. It also queries IDENTITY_ENDPOINT, MSI_ENDPOINT or the VM metadata service at 169.254.169[.]254 for live OAuth2 tokens across 12 audiences. 1.26.2 added GitHub Actions OIDC tokens and /home/runner paths.

- Exfiltration and operator mistakes: data is JSON, zlib, Base64 with no encryption, sent by HTTPS POST to hxxps://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry. The User-Agent is af-runtime-diagnostics/1, changed to runtime-diagnostics/1 in 1.26.2. There is no second stage, no persistence outside site-packages and no worm. The inbox is now rate-limited (HTTP 429), but early victims got HTTP 200 and their secrets may be readable by anyone holding the UUID. The Azure DevOps OIDC request is broken, though SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN still leaks via os.environ. The IMDS timeouts delay exfil about 104 seconds on non-Azure Linux. Windows CLI runs can exit before the thread finishes, and macOS misses /Users/* paths but still leaks env vars and ~/.azure/*.json.

- Cleanup trap: do not run bare pip uninstall first, because pip is a Python entrypoint and triggers the stealer once more. Export _AF_TEL=1, delete the four malicious files from every site-packages directory using the environment's own Python binary, then reinstall agent-framework==1.26.0. uv does not execute .pth hooks during removal. Rotate everything reachable. Rotating passwords alone does not revoke cached Entra ID refresh tokens, and managed identity or OIDC access tokens stay valid up to 24 hours. Also note that __pycache__ .pyc files do not show whether the payload ran, since pip compiles bytecode at install time.

Takeaway: hunt for agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py in site-packages, including inside container images built on November 17 and in lockfiles or Renovate/Dependabot PRs from that day. Check build-host DNS for webhook[.]site and TLS-decrypted proxy logs for POSTs to /d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry, where HTTP 200 means exfil completed. Review Entra ID Managed Identity sign-ins for token replay. Wheel and file SHA-256 hashes are in the report's IOC tables, so search internal mirrors for the wheel hashes and evict hits.

item.title: PHP2Shell Exploited by AI Agents from Day One: Inside a Credential-Harvesting Campaign
item.description:
AI agents weaponized PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) the day public PoCs dropped on October 21, 2026. SOCRadar found the operator's exposed C2, tooling and loot: 595 IPs attacked in 57 countries, 404 confirmed compromised.
- Exploit chain: A multipart POST of about 8 MiB with over 1,000 fields exhausts the default 128M memory_limit. A second request on the same keep-alive connection uses dangling session state to leak addresses and call a forged HashTable destructor mapped to zif_system. It works against default PHP/Apache under mod_php or FrankenPHP, not FPM. Fixed releases stop it (8.4.27 cut the stage-1 leak from 4,096 to 32 bytes). Look for HTTP 500 with X-Powered-By: PHP, a second POST on the same connection, and a Set-Cookie PHPSESSID of about 4,096 or exactly 16 bytes. On Nextcloud, POSTs to /status.php, /cron.php and /public.php.
- AI layer: A self-built queue (maq) ran 39 parallel omp workers against two vLLM DeepSeek V4.1 endpoints. A GOAL[.]md told an agent to work autonomously toward over $50,000 USDT. SOCRadar assesses the operation as human-directed and AI-augmented, and full autonomy was not confirmed. No crypto theft was confirmed. The completed impact was about 3.3M user records pulled from an unauthenticated Redis. An OPSEC failure also exposed the operator: a worker ran collect[.]sh on the operator's own lab, and the snapshot was uploaded under job 176 to the public loot service.
- C2 footprint: 206.245.153[.]56 runs an unauthenticated Python file service on 8088. GET /tools/ serves collect[.]sh, deep-loot[.]sh, persist2[.]sh and php-loot.php, and POST /<job>/<name>.tgz returns 201. Port 80 serves /j<job>.sh for curl | sh. Each victim gets a reverse-shell listener on port 41000 + job ID. Related hosts are 157.180.96[.]7 (the AI lab, open directory on 18082) and 185.65.134[.]250 (exploit and SSH source). The c2-agents SSH key is reused across jobs.
- Persistence to hunt: /tmp/beacon.sh (60-second reconnect loop), per-minute cron lines (T1053.003), and added authorized_keys entries (T1098.004). Also look for token-protected PHP webshells named doc/thumb-<8 hex>.php (T1505.003), a Nextcloud Beacon app, a Laravel route-cache backdoor, and /tmp/.c<id> lock markers. A localhost-only Dropbear on 127.0.0.1:2222 is kept alive via a rogue auto_prepend_file, with files under /var/www/html/.p/.
- Impact: The collector bundles secrets into a fixed layout (meta.tsv, inventories from 00-identity to 23-crypto-candidates) and POSTs it, logging UPLOAD=201. Loot includes ECS/IMDS role credentials (T1552.005), .env files, database dumps, git history and session files, about 290,000 files and 9.5 GB in total. The operator documented shells on 217 hosts but root on only 12, mostly unprivileged www-data in containers. Victims were chosen by PHP/Apache fingerprint, not sector. SOCRadar's read is an initial-access-broker pattern, with low confidence on identity.
Takeaway: Patching closes the entry point but not the foothold. Upgrade to PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 or 8.5.12 and verify the SAPI version, not just CLI php -v. Then search web-server hosts for the paths and markers above. Hunt for web-server children spawning sh, curl or bash -i, collector bundles left in /tmp, and outbound traffic to 206.245.153[.]56:8088 or ports 41000-49153. In cloud logs, look for web-app roles calling STS, S3, Secrets Manager, SSM or RDS from non-VPC IPs, and metadata requests from web processes. Rotate every secret on exposed hosts and audit cloud logs back to October 21, 2026. The report's IOC section lists hashes, SSH key fingerprints, paths and URL patterns, plus a detection and hunting section.

item.title: KQLs for Major brands compromised through Optimizely
item.description:
Attackers abused Optimizely Web to push malicious JavaScript through legitimate sites of major brands, hitting 178 organizations per Report URI. Detect FYI turns the IOCs into KQL hunts for Defender XDR and Sentinel.
- Report URI published the research on November 16, 2026. The injected JavaScript was tied to cryptocurrency address replacement, payment card skimming, information theft, and delivery of the iOS exploits Coruna and DarkSword. Affected brands include BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, and Ledger. Users could be exposed just by browsing a trusted site.
- Infrastructure to hunt in network telemetry: 1688360[.]cc, 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, and webshell[.]lol. Detect FYI's labels for them: webshell[.]lol is JavaScript injection infrastructure, and the two .icu domains are iOS exploit routers. On 1688360[.]cc, track.js is the JavaScript payload, hit.php suggests cookie and screenshot exfiltration, and card.php suggests card data exfiltration. These are the hunter's interpretations, not confirmed behavior.
- Hunt flow in DeviceNetworkEvents: match RemoteUrl against the four domains, then summarize per device to see connection counts, first and last seen, and which activity types each device touched. Repeated hits suggest continued exposure, not confirmed compromise. Pivot on InitiatingProcessId plus InitiatingProcessCreationTime so you track the exact browser instance, not just the process name.
- Follow-on pivots: browser-spawned processes within 10 minutes of a hit in DeviceProcessEvents, and other connections from the same process within 5 minutes. A file-creation join in DeviceFileEvents (2 minute window) produced too many false positives for the author. Expect normal browser background traffic in the network pivot, and note that JavaScript can run entirely inside the browser without spawning anything.
- Infection-path query, added November 17: for the window November 16 to 18, it joins visits to the affected brand domains to malicious-domain hits on the same device in the two minutes before the hit. That points to which trusted site delivered the script. It checks only 1688360[.]cc and the two .icu domains, so add webshell[.]lol if you want the injection host covered too.
- Key limitation: DeviceNetworkEvents does not capture full HTTP/HTTPS payloads. A connection to this infrastructure cannot prove the JavaScript executed or that data left the device. Proxy logs, browser artifacts, or packet captures with decryption are needed to close that gap.
Takeaway: treat the queries as starting points, not production detections. Run the domain match over your retention window first, use the pre-hit brand-visit join to find the delivery site, then pull proxy and browser evidence for any device that hits card.php or hit.php paths. The full KQL set is in the Detect FYI post, and the original IOCs are in Report URI's research.

item.title: Behind the Power Outage: Unmasking a New Intrusion Vector in Enterprise Infrastructure Tools
item.description:
Attackers abused CyberPower PowerPanel Business, a UPS management tool, to run SYSTEM commands on a domain controller and collect ntds.dit. Every command traced back to ppbed.exe, not a new service or scheduled task.
- Why it works: PPB can run a .cmd file from its extcmd folder when a power event fires. The attacker used the web console (embedded Tomcat, TCP 3052) to push their own scripts, and the PowerPanel service, ppbed.exe, ran them as SYSTEM. No memory-corruption exploit was needed. In process telemetry it looks like a power product launching cmd.exe, which is easy to dismiss.
- Entry point: requests hit /local/rest/v1/file/upload on port 3052. Uploads land as upload_[RANDOM].tmp in web-server\work\tomcat\localhost\local, then show up in ...\CyberPower PowerPanel Business\temp\profile\extcmd\ and run from ...\extcmd\. Script names follow pp?????.cmd, so they blend in. The report says public advisories cover hard-coded credentials, a default admin password and a file-upload path-traversal flaw in PPB. Any of those, or stolen admin credentials, could provide console access. It does not say which was used here.
- Hands-on-keyboard tradecraft: ppbed.exe → cmd.exe ran certutil to test reachability and decode base64 staged files, plus curl and a PowerShell reflective .NET load. Staging server was 84.200.205[.]145, with dt.exe, wupd.exe and hello.exe pulled from hxxp://84.200.205[.]145:55556/. wupd.exe is detected as MSIL.Killav!gen1, a .NET antivirus killer. hello.exe only prints a greeting and served as a test of the reflective-load path.
- AD collection by trial and error: the operator iterated scripts (ppskbcx.cmd, ifm.cmd through ifm4.cmd, ppotuff.cmd, ppinthw.cmd), first using ntdsutil ifm, then adding logging and done-marker files. They finally pivoted to esentutl /vss to copy the locked ntds.dit from a shadow copy, and saved the SYSTEM hive with reg save. Some revisions reused a name (ifm.cmd has three hashes), so the extcmd folder is only a partial development log.
- Implant and scope: PowerShell launched upnpcont.exe from C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\50679f292a1\, which side-loads an unknown atl.dll. Later vssadmin and robocopy activity kept the lineage vssadmin.exe ← powershell.exe ← upnpcont.exe ← powershell.exe ← cmd.exe ← ppbed.exe ← services.exe. Symantec did not attribute the activity and saw no exfiltration or ransomware, so intent is unclear.
DFIR takeaway: hunt on parent process, not tool name. Look for ppbed.exe as an ancestor of cmd.exe, powershell.exe, certutil, ntdsutil, esentutl, vssadmin or robocopy. Audit extcmd and temp\profile\extcmd on every PPB host against product defaults, and treat unknown scripts as hostile. Preserve those scripts, the Tomcat work directory temp files, and the upnpcont.exe/atl.dll pair. Review the console's event-to-command assignments, and check who reached port 3052.
If you find this, assume AD credentials are exposed and plan a krbtgt reset and wider credential rotation. Restrict 3052 to named admin hosts and change the default admin password. File hashes for the scripts, tools, implant and DLL are in the report's IOC section.

item.title: UAT-12643: Suspected North Korea-aligned actor blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing
item.description:
Talos tracks UAT-12643, a suspected North Korea-aligned crypto and gaming stealer crew. Its Go RAT pulls C2 URLs from Solana memos and survives "Reset this PC" through WinRE.
Attribution is low confidence, based on TTP overlap with known North Korean 🇰🇵 APTs. Overlord RAT was seen earlier with UNK_DeadDrop, and Solana memo C2 hosting was first reported in March 2026 with Lazarus. Others also use that technique, so treat the link cautiously. Targets look like crypto holders, gamers, finance staff, and VoIP users, with keyword harvesting in English, French 🇫🇷, Spanish 🇪🇸, and Portuguese 🇵🇹 pointing at Europe.
- Staging and delivery: an opsec failure exposed the root folder of 41.216.188[.]11, a Flask file-drop on port 8000. Other ports: 5173 (Overlord WebSocket C2), 5656 and 5959 (Python stealer TCP C2). Initial access uses a spoofed PDF LNK abusing MpCmdRun.exe -DownloadFile (payload saved as RuntimeBroker.exe), a certutil -urlcache -f LNK, an HTA run by mshta.exe that writes %TEMP%\s.exe via ADODB[.]Stream, and an MSBuild project dl.xml that compiles C# in memory with a spoofed "Microsoft BITS/7.8" User-Agent. Both LNKs were built on host win-8oa3ccqae4d. The report does not say how the files reach victims.
- Overlord RAT: it requires admin, takes SeDebugPrivilege, and calls NtSetInformationProcess to set ProcessBreakOnTermination. Killing it triggers a CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED BSoD. It has 35 commands including keylogging, webcam and mic capture, reverse SOCKS proxy, and reflective DLL plugin loading. Persistence is an HKCU autorun with a randomized value name pointing into a Network folder under local AppData, plus a WinRE hook.
- WinRE persistence is the sticky part: it writes a 20-character random-named copy to %TARGETOSDRIVE%\Recovery\OEM\, adds a .bat stub running cmd.exe /c start against that path, backs up and then creates or patches ResetConfig.xml. Any "Reset this PC" runs the implant before the OS is restored.
- Solana C2 discovery: the actor posts encrypted C2 URLs as Solana Memo Program transactions (up to 566 bytes). The RAT calls getSignatures, then getTransaction with jsonParsed encoding, and only accepts instructions whose data is exactly 43 characters, the length of a Base58 WebSocket URL after AES-256 encryption. The actor rotates C2 by posting a new memo, with no redeployment.
- Good Game stealer (public PyInstaller tool by CirqueiraDev, Python 3.12.0) and clipboard hijacker: Good Game runs a Notepad-style tkinter decoy and sandbox checks (VM MAC OUIs, under 2 GB RAM, uptime under 5 minutes, wineboot.exe). It persists with an HKCU Run value named Zoipers and a Startup folder copy, and sets DisableTaskMgr=1 under HKLM\...\Policies\System during the run. It takes browser data, Discord and Roblox tokens, 21 wallets, game launchers, and keyword-filtered files. Staging artifacts: SK_ plus 8 random characters ZIP in temp, url_opened_<hash>.flag, a file named skipped. Exfil goes to upload.gofile[.]io, then a Discord webhook alert with hostname, username, and OS. The clipper uses mutex UuuRjinBZPBMIjnc, copies to %APPDATA%\MsgEdgeUpdate.exe (hidden and system attributes), adds a Run value MsgEdgeUpdate, and polls the clipboard every 500 ms to swap detected wallet addresses.
Takeaway: do not kill a suspected Overlord process on a live host. Isolate it and capture memory first, since termination crashes the system. On disk, check Recovery\OEM and ResetConfig.xml, because rebuilding via Reset this PC will not evict it. Hunt for MpCmdRun.exe -DownloadFile, certutil -urlcache, mshta.exe or msbuild.exe pulling remote payloads, the Run values and the MsgEdgeUpdate.exe path above, and endpoint traffic to Solana RPC, Discord webhooks, or gofile. IOCs are in Talos's GitHub repository linked from the report.

The RAT calls getSignatures, then getTransaction with jsonParsed encoding, and only accepts instructions whose data is exactly 43 characters, the length of a Base58 WebSocket URL after AES-256 encryption. The actor rotates C2 by posting a new memo, with no redeployment.

- Good Game stealer (public PyInstaller tool by CirqueiraDev, Python 3.12.0) and clipboard hijacker: Good Game runs a Notepad-style tkinter decoy and sandbox checks (VM MAC OUIs, under 2 GB RAM, uptime under 5 minutes, wineboot.exe). It persists with an HKCU Run value named Zoipers and a Startup folder copy, and sets DisableTaskMgr=1 under HKLM\...\Policies\System during the run. It takes browser data, Discord and Roblox tokens, 21 wallets, game launchers, and keyword-filtered files. Staging artifacts: SK_ plus 8 random characters ZIP in temp, url_opened_<hash>.flag, a file named skipped. Exfil goes to upload.gofile[.]io, then a Discord webhook alert with hostname, username, and OS. The clipper uses mutex UuuRjinBZPBMIjnc, copies to %APPDATA%\MsgEdgeUpdate.exe (hidden and system attributes), adds a Run value MsgEdgeUpdate, and polls the clipboard every 500 ms to swap detected wallet addresses.

Takeaway: do not kill a suspected Overlord process on a live host. Isolate it and capture memory first, since termination crashes the system. On disk, check Recovery\OEM and ResetConfig.xml, because rebuilding via Reset this PC will not evict it. Hunt for MpCmdRun.exe -DownloadFile, certutil -urlcache, mshta.exe or msbuild.exe pulling remote payloads, the Run values and the MsgEdgeUpdate.exe path above, and endpoint traffic to Solana RPC, Discord webhooks, or gofile. IOCs are in Talos's GitHub repository linked from the report.

item.title: Reducing Microsoft Sentinel Costs Without Compromising Detection: Part 3: The DNS Quest
item.description:
NVISO shows how to catch base32 DNS tunneling with Sentinel Summary Rules on Microsoft DNS Analytical events, cutting DNS ingestion cost by roughly 95% while keeping alerting intact.
- The design: all Microsoft DNS Analytical events go to the Data Lake. A Summary Rule runs the detection logic against that table and writes only the hits to an Analytic Tier table (dns_sr_alerts_CL). Unlike the firewall part of the series, which aggregated records, this stores alerts rather than DNS records. That is why savings beat the previous post. Each Summary Rule run also adds a query cost, which NVISO describes as relatively low.
- The technique: DNS tunneling encodes host data (credentials, files, host or network info) into subdomains of an attacker-controlled domain, with base32 as one example encoding. The same channel carries commands back. Sliver C2 is named as a tool that uses base32 for DNS C2. NVISO's lab emulation is a PowerShell loop that calls Resolve-DnsName for TXT records on random 45-character base32 labels under a non-existent domain, so every response is NXDOMAIN.
- The KQL logic: it reads ASimDnsActivityLogs where EventProduct is DNS Server, EventSubType is request or response, and SrcIpAddr is private. It regex-matches DnsQuery for a base32 label of at least 24 characters (a-z2-7 or A-Z2-7) followed by two or more further labels. Results group by SrcIpAddr and second-level domain. It fires when Count is at least 50 and distinct subdomains are at least 10, so many unique subdomains under one domain from one host is the signal.
- Alert plumbing: the query sets alert_title, alert_description, alert_severity (Medium) and alert_notification (dns_sr_alert). One Analytic Rule filters dns_sr_alerts_CL on isnotempty(alert_title) and alert_notification == "dns_sr_alert". That lets you add more Summary Rules later without building a new Analytic Rule each time. In the lab, the output showed the test host 192.168.20[.]105 talking to the internal DNS server 192.168.20[.]101.
- Scheduling and scope: the report recommends a 1-hour run interval so threshold rules have enough records to trip. Thresholds need a per-environment baseline, and lowering them makes the rule more sensitive. The query is written for Microsoft DNS Analytical events. Other DNS products need field names and schema adapted.
Takeaway: the full KQL for the Summary Rule and Analytic Rule is in the report. Copy it, then tune the 50 request and 10 subdomain thresholds against your own baseline. Because the alert table keeps only the hits, your raw DNS evidence for scoping and timelines stays in the Data Lake. When an alert fires, pivot there on SrcIpAddr and the second-level domain to rebuild the full query history for that host.

item.title: The forced audit: how AuditTeam’s OpsAgent framework masks ransomware as consulting
item.description:
AuditTeam sells extortion as a paid security audit: its "Audit & Consulting fee" supposedly buys a vulnerability report instead of a data leak. The report says the group runs a custom implant framework, OpsAgent, that was rewritten from C++ to Rust during the campaign.
- Scope: the campaign started January 2026 and ran through at least October 2026. Victims were found in Russia 🇷🇺, Italy 🇮🇹, the Philippines 🇵🇭, Senegal, Finland 🇫🇮, China 🇨🇳 and Hong Kong. The leak site claims victims in seven more countries. Researchers first saw OpsAgent in Hong Kong on March 10, 2026. The ransom note never mentions encryption, but the cryptor module drops it, so if a victim sees the note, files are already encrypted.
- Loaders and injection: the C loader (April) injects shellcode into msiexec.exe with CreateProcessA, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread. The .NET loader (June) uses NtQueueApcThread. The Rust loader (September) pulls an encrypted payload from C2 and runs the Execute export inside its own process, with no remote injection. Implant version 5.2.8 pushes mimikatz_spawn, execute_assembly, pth_spawn and runpe as shellcode over a named pipe, XOR-encrypted, into msiexec.exe by default. The monitor command uses notepad.exe instead. A DbgInjector mode starts a process in a debug state, sets a hardware breakpoint on FileTimeToSystemTime and redirects RIP without creating a thread.
- C2 discovery: the implant can read a public GitHub repo, hxxps://github[.]com/RonaldCMalcolm1983/staticPage, for an AES-encrypted C2 address wrapped in GetConfig and EndConfig markers. C2 sits on CloudFront subdomains such as d19v1tntmz2i98.cloudfront[.]net and d35htktbyt7nxc.cloudfront[.]net, so IP blocking is impractical. One standalone IP is 157.20.104[.]111 (AS 136557). The Rust build starts with HTTP POST, then upgrades to WebSocket over TLS. The repo was removed in November 2026, but the latest Rust implants ship with the GitHub feature disabled, so removal does not mean the campaign is over.
- EDR killer: a driver disguised as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus (KV series) with a valid signature talks over the \KvCorePortX0 filter port. Command 0x1D plus a filename kills that process. The kill list has about 220 entries, covering Defender, Sysmon, splunkd, wazuh-agent, TeamViewer, Veeam, Acronis and major databases.
- Cryptor and anti-recovery: AES-CBC or ChaCha20 per file, with the file key protected by X25519. It kills SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Redis and stops Veeam. It also deletes shadow copies, empties the recycle bin and wipes temp folders. Deleted files are overwritten with random data first, so expect little carving success.
- Artifacts: the report lists syscache.dat under C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Caches, user AppData Local Microsoft\Windows\Caches and Local Microsoft\CLR_v4.0, the implant's module directory and %TEMP%, plus C:\Users\Public\kv_dbg.log and kvcore.sys in System32\drivers and Sysnative\drivers. The driver hash (listed as a legitimate AV driver) is 109cdc24ccd4872a3e4bf6f2d4f3c3d4.
Takeaway: hunt for kvcore.sys loading from the drivers folder, kv_dbg.log in C:\Users\Public, and syscache.dat in those Caches, CLR, module and temp paths. Look for msiexec.exe or notepad.exe holding injected memory or named pipes with no matching install or user activity. Check for non-browser processes reaching the GitHub repo or CloudFront subdomains. Capture memory and a triage image before the cryptor runs, because shadow copies and deleted files will not help afterward. Hashes, paths and domains are in the report's IOC section.

item.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Pre-auth RCE in OpenJDK, and the challenge of image and feature bloat
item.description:
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a pre-auth heap overwrite in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. Calif reports RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and more. Fixes shipped Nov 17.
- The bug: HotSpot's C2 compiler uses an AVX-512 intrinsic for Base64 decoding. Hand-written assembly for the padded tail miscalculates the output length as -1, which opens the write mask fully. 64 bytes are written where two were expected, and 62 land past the array. The exception fires after the write. The trigger is 64 A characters plus =, or 128 A plus = on Java 17, and the decoder must be JIT-compiled first, so expect warm-up traffic. The bytes are fixed, so Calif overwrites a neighboring array's length to get a read/write primitive, then a heap leak and code execution. Calif rates it CVSS 4.0 9.2, OpenJDK's advisory says CVSS 3.1 8.1.
- Scope: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (17, 21, 25, 27) on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. ARM, Java 11 and standard Java 8 are not affected, but Oracle lists the Java 8 performance build 8u511b33-perf as vulnerable. Every downstream distribution inherits the code, and Temurin, Corretto and Zulu fixes were still pending at 20:00 UTC. Check hosts with: grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'. All four flags must appear. Then run java -version inside the container, because the container's JDK is the one that matters.
- Reachability and status: Spring Security, Tomcat and Jetty 12 pass the raw Basic auth token to Base64.getDecoder() before validating it, and Auth0's java-jwt decodes JWT headers before checking the signature. Calif reports pre-auth RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and post-auth RCE in Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Theori and others independently reproduced the overflow. The weaponized chains are withheld, and only a bounded-array repro is public. Each target needs its own profile, and bad heap placement can crash the JVM. The report does not describe in-the-wild exploitation. It warns that fake exploit repos are likely, so sandbox anything claiming a shell.
- What it leaves behind: the server just answers 401. Look for Base64-alphabet tokens of 32 or more characters ending in = whose length is not a multiple of 4, starting with Authorization headers. Application logs showed IllegalArgumentException: Input byte array has wrong 4-byte ending unit on every attempt in researchers' tests. Failed placements mean SIGSEGV, hs_err_pid*.log files and bursts of worker restarts. Post-exploitation looks like any Java compromise: the JVM spawning a shell, dropping and executing a binary, or opening new connections.
Takeaway: hunt backward from before Nov 17. Search Authorization headers and app logs for the shapes above, and check for hs_err_pid files and unexplained restarts. Oracle fixes are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1 and 8u513 for the performance build. Containers and vendor JDKs need a rebuild and redeploy. If you can't patch, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics stopped the overflow on every affected version Upwind tested and needs a restart. -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock fails without -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions, so don't push it fleet-wide through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. The report describes detection shapes, not IOC lists or rules.

item.title: Microsoft Warns of Coordinated Phishing Campaign Leveraging M365 Service Outage
item.description:
Microsoft flagged a coordinated, high volume phishing campaign that rode the 22-hour Microsoft 365 outage. Lures posed as service-health notices claiming held mail would be deleted in 24 hours, pushing users to a RESTORE MESSAGES link.
Timeline: the outage began at 11:20 EST on November 12 and hit Outlook, Teams and other services worldwide. Microsoft confirmed full restoration at 23:15 EST on November 13, and the phishing was observed on November 13 while the fix was still rolling out. Microsoft's November 16 blog says this fits the long-running pattern of attackers hijacking global events for social engineering. No named threat actor or malware family is attributed.
- Lure anatomy: subject lines follow the pattern Outage followed by a random token. Display names combine a three-character, organization-style prefix with "Outage Notification" or "Service Health." Bodies reference Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot, use 24-hour deletion deadlines, and embed fake email conversations positioned to be hidden from the recipient, which looks like an attempt at mail filtering evasion.
- Infrastructure: sender domains named in the report are moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. Messages ran through email-delivery and link-tracking infrastructure that generates recipient-specific URLs. Clicks land on reallifeaccounting[.]com or reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0.html.
- Delivery profile: every observed message was link based. No QR codes, no non-EML attachments, and no executable, archive or document payloads were identified. Microsoft reads this as credential phishing, though credential submission and account compromise were not directly observed in the evidence it had.
- Impact status: there is currently no evidence of credential capture, malware delivery or post-compromise activity from this campaign. That is an absence of evidence in Microsoft's data, not a clean bill for your tenant, so the click question still needs answering locally.
- Why it works: users were already cut off from mail and Teams, so a "restore your held messages" prompt matched what they expected to see. Outage-themed lures also reuse real service names, which makes the tailored sender domains look relevant.
DFIR takeaway: work this in two passes, following Microsoft's guidance.
Pass 1, scoping in mail telemetry: search for the observed sender domains, the display-name and subject patterns, the lure phrases (RESTORE MESSAGES, the 24-hour deletion wording), the tracking hosts, and the destination domain. Quarantine matches and remove delivered messages per your response procedures.
Pass 2, exposure: review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence for visits to reallifeaccounting[.]com and the /themelist0.html path. Build a list of users who clicked, and treat anyone who may have entered credentials as exposed: reset the password, revoke active sessions, and refresh tokens. Resetting a password without revoking sessions leaves a stolen session usable.
Block or closely scrutinize reallifeaccounting[.]com and that path while the investigation runs. Remember the URLs are recipient-specific, so hunt on the domain and path, not exact URL strings. The sender domains, subject and display-name patterns and destination are listed in Microsoft's report.
