item.title: [Tool] starshield-forensics v0.3.7: Offline Chromium LevelDB .log carver (Python stdlib, MIT)
item.description:
starshield-forensics v0.3.7 is an offline, stdlib-only Python carver that recovers soft-deleted and edited messages from uncompacted Chromium LevelDB .log files. It targets BEC, invoice diversion and APP fraud cases.
Why it matters: browser-based chat and invoicing apps often push a UI retraction or a post-transfer edit as a soft-delete update. Until compaction, the write-ahead log (.log) in Chromium IndexedDB and Local Storage can still hold the earlier UTF-8 or UTF-16LE JSON records or text fragments. That can mean the original payment details survive on disk after the attacker or victim "removed" them. The release is from Ziqi Xiao on Full Disclosure, MIT licensed, Python 3.10+ with zero PyPI dependencies, shipped as a reproducible single-file .pyz zipapp for restricted triage hosts.
- Feasibility first: the precheck command scans read-only copies of IndexedDB / Local Storage directories and separates uncompacted .log WAL segments from Snappy .ldb SSTables (footer magic 0xdb4775248b80fb57) and Blink 0xFF envelopes. It returns GO, PARTIAL or NO_GO_COMPACTED_OR_UNSUPPORTED using aggregate counts only, with no message plaintext or paths in the output. That tells you whether recovery is worth attempting.
- Carving: parse-leveldb-log reads the physical 32,768-byte WAL blocks and verifies the masked Castagnoli CRC32C. It reassembles FULL, FIRST, MIDDLE and LAST fragments across 0x8000 block boundaries, then carves soft-deleted or edited JSON records (--schema auto|chatsvc|generic-json). Each hit is anchored to an exact physical byte offset (leveldb_batch_byte_offset), so findings can be cited and re-verified against the original image.
- Triage extras: triage-json enumerates deletetime and edittime records in JSON exports. inspect-image does neutral structural checks of PNG chunks (IHDR/iCCP/IDAT) and JPEG APP2 ICC and APP13 (8BIM) markers, with explicit OS-screenshot caveats to discourage overclaiming. Payment identifiers get checksum validation: Luhn card numbers, ISO-13616 IBAN Mod-97 (89 countries), UK 🇬🇧 Sort Code plus 8-digit account pairs, and SWIFT/BIC syntax. Matches are pseudonymised by default with per-run keyed HMAC-SHA256 tokens (--hmac-digest sha256, sha384 or blake2b).
- AI-handling angle: the author warns that piping untrusted adversary chat exports straight into LLM summarizers exposes responders to indirect prompt injection (OWASP LLM01) and fabricated payment routing identifiers. StarShield-Bench-24 is a synthetic corpus of 24 seeded cases (SSB24-01 to SSB24-24) scoring WAL recovery, byte-offset citation accuracy, malformed-container rejection and bilingual prompt-injection resilience. It comes with 12 companion financial-triage cases (TC-0456 to TC-0467) submitted to the OWASP GenAI Data Security Initiative as PR #119.
- Supply chain: the report gives the single-file starshield.pyz SHA-256 for v0.3.7 as e6603ef083b20a5460bf56818f63a3a94b856deb377a5b6330be2394e0e21232. It also publishes the maintainer's OpenSSH Ed25519 signing key (KEYS[.]pub in the repository). Verification uses ssh-keygen -Y verify against SHA256SUMS.sig, then shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS, then scripts/build_reproducible.py --verify.
Takeaway: in a payment-diversion case, image the user's Chromium IndexedDB and Local Storage directories early, before the browser compacts the .log files. Work only on read-only copies. Run precheck to see whether uncompacted WAL data exists, then carve with parse-leveldb-log and cite the byte offsets in your notes. Treat recovered chat text as untrusted input, and verify the signed release before you put it on an evidence host.

item.title: ConnectWise Warns ScreenConnect Attacks Continue as SCKit Targets Unpatched Systems
item.description:
ConnectWise says ScreenConnect attacks continue against on-prem servers with risky extensions enabled. Huntress saw an SCKit spike on November 13, 2026: 205 hosts, 41 organizations.
ConnectWise has finished its investigation into unauthorized access across partner ScreenConnect environments. The warning is blunt: on-premises partners must disable the identified extensions and update to the latest supported version now. Reports of new activity keep arriving wherever those third-party extensions remain enabled and ScreenConnect is not patched.
- The flaw: version 26.6.5 fixes CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9) in the ScreenConnect client. Under certain circumstances, files can be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation. Separately, Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber reported that unknown actors are suspected of abusing an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to run unauthorized commands and bypass ScreenConnect's normal authentication controls.
- The toolkit: the attacks deploy a multi-component toolkit dubbed SCKit. It includes a C# module called RelayTrap (RelayTrap.cs) built to hop from an infected customer device to an MSP technician's workstation. When a technician connects to investigate the problem, CVE-2026-84869 is used to execute malicious code on their machine, opening the path to more managed networks. There is no evidence this worm-like behavior has succeeded in the latest campaign.
- Infrastructure and persistence: Huntress saw the new rogue ScreenConnect client hosted at 185.241.211[.]197, tied to 1337 Services GmbH, a bulletproof hosting provider known for hosting malicious traffic. In one incident the rogue client persisted as a service named Windows Update Agent, posing as a system component. The executable UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe sat in C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\ and ran under the LocalSystem account.
- Scope and response: ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions (Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, RMM+ Password Link) across 400 partner environments. Having one of these extensions does not by itself mean an environment was impacted. Partners should not re-enable or reinstall them until further guidance. ConnectWise stresses that disabling extensions and updating do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established.
Takeaway: patching closes the door but does not evict anyone. On every on-prem ScreenConnect server and every endpoint it manages, look for a service named Windows Update Agent running as LocalSystem, the UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe binary, and the ProgramData folder with the de362a425905bcc4 suffix. Search network logs for connections to 185.241.211[.]197. Treat technician workstations that connected to a suspect device as in scope, and review them for RelayTrap activity and unexpected file transfers or executions from remote sessions. Preserve the server and endpoint evidence before you remediate.

item.title: iOS Forensic Toolkit 10.13: app data extraction for the full iOS 26 range
item.description:
iOS app data can now be pulled from iPhones with Stolen Device Protection on, across iOS and iPadOS 26.0 through 26.7.3, using a sandbox escape instead of a kernel exploit. The catch: some analysis tools silently skip the App Group containers where Telegram keeps its data.
ElcomSoft's report describes a partial file system extraction. An agent is sideloaded over the air, which needs no pairing, so Stolen Device Protection's Face ID or Touch ID prompt for pairing away from familiar locations never blocks it. It returns mostly third-party app data. System data stays out of reach.
- Method and scope: the agent escapes its own sandbox and reads /var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/*, Shared/AppGroup/*, Data/InternalDaemon/* and Data/PluginKitPlugin/*. The first two hold most of the evidence. Sandbox escapes are lighter than kernel exploits, so coverage arrives faster for new builds. It covers all devices that can run iOS/iPadOS 26, including the iPhone 17 lineup and M5-based iPads. Support for 27.0 through 27.2.1 is described as in development.
- What you get: messengers (Telegram, WhatsApp, Threema), social apps (X, Instagram, Threads, TikTok), third-party mail clients (Outlook, Gmail), and financial, navigation and location apps. Apple Notes is also returned and may contain saved passwords. What you don't get: system databases, SMS and iMessage, call log, contacts, the stock Mail app, camera roll, Maps, and the keychain. Where the device can be paired, the report says to pair it and also run extended logical acquisition, which fills many of those gaps. Order does not matter.
- The parsing trap: containers are UUID-named folders, and many analysis tools identify the owning app from .com.apple.mobile_container_manager.metadata.plist. The agent can read that file in Data/Application containers but lacks permission to read it in Shared/AppGroup containers. The data is extracted in full, only the metadata file is missing. Telegram keeps chats, contacts and calls in its App Group container. In the vendor's tests, one popular tool did not see Telegram data at all, and an older version of another failed the same way, while its current version parses the extraction without the file. In one case, adding the missing files took Telegram records from a few hundred to over a hundred thousand, and device-wide message, contact and call totals grew too.
- The workaround and its chain of custody cost: a utility recreates the missing plists, writing a file only after two independent confirmations of the owning app. Confirmation sources are the LaunchServices cache (com[.]apple.LaunchServices-*.csstore) linking the App Group identifier to the app, the app's own logs referencing the container path, or the genuine metadata file in its Data/Application container. Containers without enough confirmation are marked unconfirmed. The generated files carry no mark distinguishing them from originals, so the extraction then contains files the agent never pulled from the device.
Practitioner takeaway: before trusting any result from this extraction, check whether your parser shows data from Shared/AppGroup containers. If Telegram looks nearly empty, suspect container identification before suspecting the app. If you generate metadata files, keep the original .tar and its hash, run the utility on an unpacked copy, save its log (it records size and SHA-256 of each created file), and state in the report which containers received generated files and which confirmations were found. A command-line Python version is promised on GitHub.

item.title: OPTIMJACK: When Trusted JavaScript Becomes a Supply Chain Attack
item.description:
OPTIMJACK: an Optimizely Web Experimentation flaw let attackers inject a JavaScript loader into 188 snippets tied to 178 organizations, turning trusted third-party code into a card skimmer and crypto swapper.
- Attack chain: per Report URI (Scott Helme), the attacker added a small loader to the Project JavaScript field of customer projects, leaving the rest of each snippet largely intact. Optimizely's own delivery infrastructure served it, so sites ran malicious code from a source they already trusted. Victims included Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA and HSBC. How the attacker got write access across unrelated projects is not established publicly. The "account signup flow" wording comes from an Optimizely spokesperson, not the status page.
- Loader variants: one pulled 1688360[.]cc/track.js, one hid the destination in Base64, and one embedded the payload with an eval() fallback if the remote host was blocked. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned and then reinfected, so the attacker kept access during cleanup. Optimizely[.]com and login.optimizely[.]com snippets were also infected. Some customers serve snippets from their own domains (opt.scheels[.]com, www.vodafone[.]com[.]au), so hunting only cdn.optimizely[.]com misses them.
- Payload: Report URI saw 26 track.js builds on Nov 16. Capabilities: swapping crypto addresses near words like wallet, deposit or send (BTC, EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, LTC, BCH, DOGE; about $7,040 in on-chain receipts by 19:25 UTC, not total losses), a later card skimmer, non-HttpOnly cookie theft, html2canvas screenshots, and iPhone/iPad routing to Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The skimmer targeted card number, expiry and CVV from first-party forms, not names or billing addresses, and could not read cross-origin payment iframes. Success per visitor is not established.
- Timeline: first Optimizely injection seen Nov 16 at 04:21 UTC (BBC snippet). Report URI saw all monitored files clean by 23:11 UTC that day, and StepSecurity estimates most sites were exposed about 16 hours. 1688360[.]cc went to clientHold Nov 17 at 00:37 UTC. webshell[.]lol/get.js belongs to an earlier wave via Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts. Keep the two exposure windows separate.
- CSP outcome across 159 sites: 24 blocked the payload, 17 blocked exfiltration via connect-src but still got address swapping, 50 had permissive policies, 68 had no CSP.
Takeaway: a clean snippet today proves nothing about what visitors got on Nov 16. Preserve script responses, headers, CSP reports, proxy, DNS and browser telemetry from that window. Review Project JavaScript and experiment-level custom code, plus change history, users and API tokens, for Base64 blobs, unfamiliar eval() and 1688360[.]cc. Then search for hits on 1688360[.]cc, webshell[.]lol, 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu and eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu. Those domains and the track.js SHA-256 f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40 are in the report. That hash is one later build, not a full signature.

item.title: MCH and Caishen: supply chain poisoning pushes iOS exploits
item.description:
Poisoned third-party scripts on November 16, 2026 gave desktop visitors of BBC, Zoom, and CNN a card skimmer and crypto clipper, and gave phones and tablets an iOS exploit chain. Censys tied the infrastructure to an MCH control panel and a Caishen iOS exploit backend.
- Delivery: on zoom[.]com, Censys captured an Optimizely script at cdn.optimizely[.]com loading track.js from 1688360[.]cc. Optimizely's status page says an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation product to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that it has since fixed the flaw and removed the code. Reporting ties the same loader to Kissmetrics, StorifyMe, and minute-ly. Sinkhole referrers confirmed BBC, Zoom, CNN, DoorDash, Zillow, Fox News, and GitLab. Hudson Rock published the first report, and Amirul Cyber tracks the injection as OPTIMJACK.
- Payload behavior: the 29 KB track.js (SHA-256 f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40) runs on every page it loads. It hooks forms, Luhn-checks card data, and posts it with the page URL to /card.php. A clipper swaps copied addresses for eight hardcoded wallets across Ethereum, Bitcoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Tron, TON, Solana, and Dogecoin. /hit.php receives the page URL, up to 8,000 characters of cookies, and a page screenshot. On iPhone, iPad, and touch Mac user agents it loads boot.js from two payload domains. On iOS 18.6 and earlier it also adds a hidden iframe to eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu. A second route, a 400-byte script at webshell[.]lol/get.js, adds a boot.js tag for 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu with no device check. The iOS chain uses the Caishen toolkit to deliver Coruna and Darksword payloads.
- Infrastructure and attribution limits: staging started November 9 on 34.96.213[.]201, with a second server at 34.124.226[.]157 on November 14. The MCH panel, titled MCH 管控平台, sits at /admin/ on je4ft3gn8vxudum[.]icu. Service host 64.83.19[.]114 runs the panel on 8080, the Caishen backend on 8081, storefronts on 8082 and 8090, and a stage loader on 8083. Another deployment is on 8.208.35[.]123. On November 17 Censys counted the panel title on 142 web properties, the Caishen title on 144, and the storefront title on 55. The channel code 02111110 is the kit's hard-coded default in an injector block generated by patch_domains.py. It links components to one panel but does not identify an operator. Censys assesses with moderate confidence that the operator rented the loader from the webshell[.]lol vendor, which uses the handle BIBILZERODAY, and says the evidence does not show they are the same person.
- Money and timeline: the Ethereum wallet got a seed payment on November 12, and wallet receipts began at 10:31 UTC on November 16. The report records 4,310.82 USDC leaving the Ethereum wallet and 546.8 USDT moving from Tron to an aggregator address at 13:05. Bitcoin received 0.0853 BTC and Litecoin 17.02 LTC. The Litecoin and Tron wallets were swept at 04:11 and 04:13 UTC on November 17 to the operator's recurring destination.
- Resilience: both staging hosts and the implant C2 host went offline between 03:30 and 05:22 UTC on November 17. Within about a day, five new MCH panel hosts running build DRYPnrzh appeared on NETSEC-HK (AS45753), and the kit vendor re-listed DarkSword-27.1 packages on GitHub. Hudson Rock reports an embedded fallback payload that runs when the delivery host is blocked, so blocking domains alone is not containment.
Takeaway: scope exposure from November 9 onward. Search web and network logs for requests to 1688360[.]cc, /card.php, /hit.php, and boot.js fetches from the .icu payload domains. Because the script sent cookies from every page it loaded and card data from submitted payment forms, treat sessions and payment data on affected pages as exposed. Inventory third-party script tags for data-channel-code="02111110", and remove the injected code from your vendor project configs. The report's Indicators section lists the domains, IPs, hashes, and clipper wallets, and its hunting notes name the patch_domains and 引流配置 page strings.

item.content:encoded:
Poisoned third-party scripts on November 16, 2026 gave desktop visitors of BBC, Zoom, and CNN a card skimmer and crypto clipper, and gave phones and tablets an iOS exploit chain. Censys tied the infrastructure to an MCH control panel and a Caishen iOS exploit backend.

- Delivery: on zoom[.]com, Censys captured an Optimizely script at cdn.optimizely[.]com loading track.js from 1688360[.]cc. Optimizely's status page says an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation product to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that it has since fixed the flaw and removed the code. Reporting ties the same loader to Kissmetrics, StorifyMe, and minute-ly. Sinkhole referrers confirmed BBC, Zoom, CNN, DoorDash, Zillow, Fox News, and GitLab. Hudson Rock published the first report, and Amirul Cyber tracks the injection as OPTIMJACK.

- Payload behavior: the 29 KB track.js (SHA-256 f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40) runs on every page it loads. It hooks forms, Luhn-checks card data, and posts it with the page URL to /card.php. A clipper swaps copied addresses for eight hardcoded wallets across Ethereum, Bitcoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Tron, TON, Solana, and Dogecoin. /hit.php receives the page URL, up to 8,000 characters of cookies, and a page screenshot. On iPhone, iPad, and touch Mac user agents it loads boot.js from two payload domains. On iOS 18.6 and earlier it also adds a hidden iframe to eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu. A second route, a 400-byte script at webshell[.]lol/get.js, adds a boot.js tag for 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu with no device check. The iOS chain uses the Caishen toolkit to deliver Coruna and Darksword payloads.

- Infrastructure and attribution limits: staging started November 9 on 34.96.213[.]201, with a second server at 34.124.226[.]157 on November 14. The MCH panel, titled MCH 管控平台, sits at /admin/ on je4ft3gn8vxudum[.]icu. Service host 64.83.19[.]114 runs the panel on 8080, the Caishen backend on 8081, storefronts on 8082 and 8090, and a stage loader on 8083. Another deployment is on 8.208.35[.]123. On November 17 Censys counted the panel title on 142 web properties, the Caishen title on 144, and the storefront title on 55. The channel code 02111110 is the kit's hard-coded default in an injector block generated by patch_domains.py. It links components to one panel but does not identify an operator. Censys assesses with moderate confidence that the operator rented the loader from the webshell[.]lol vendor, which uses the handle BIBILZERODAY, and says the evidence does not show they are the same person.

- Money and timeline: the Ethereum wallet got a seed payment on November 12, and wallet receipts began at 10:31 UTC on November 16. The report records 4,310.82 USDC leaving the Ethereum wallet and 546.8 USDT moving from Tron to an aggregator address at 13:05. Bitcoin received 0.0853 BTC and Litecoin 17.02 LTC. The Litecoin and Tron wallets were swept at 04:11 and 04:13 UTC on November 17 to the operator's recurring destination.

- Resilience: both staging hosts and the implant C2 host went offline between 03:30 and 05:22 UTC on November 17. Within about a day, five new MCH panel hosts running build DRYPnrzh appeared on NETSEC-HK (AS45753), and the kit vendor re-listed DarkSword-27.1 packages on GitHub. Hudson Rock reports an embedded fallback payload that runs when the delivery host is blocked, so blocking domains alone is not containment.

Takeaway: scope exposure from November 9 onward. Search web and network logs for requests to 1688360[.]cc, /card.php, /hit.php, and boot.js fetches from the .icu payload domains. Because the script sent cookies from every page it loaded and card data from submitted payment forms, treat sessions and payment data on affected pages as exposed. Inventory third-party script tags for data-channel-code="02111110", and remove the injected code from your vendor project configs. The report's Indicators section lists the domains, IPs, hashes, and clipper wallets, and its hunting notes name the patch_domains and 引流配置 page strings.

item.title: HDGfx Infector
item.description:
HDGfx Infector, a file infector and USB worm with no public reporting, is still spreading through trusted Adobe, Java, Firefox and Google Update EXEs. Each infection gets new keys and junk code.
- Mechanics: the report's working name for a small MinGW-w64 (GCC 8.1.0) DLL whose exports include InfectFile, DisinfectFile and MetamorphicStub. It infects non-.NET PE32 EXEs in place. A junk-filled stub overwrites the entry point, and a layer decryptor plus an encrypted loader are appended to the last section. The loader RC4-decrypts a UPX-packed core and maps it in memory; the core restores the original entry bytes and control returns to the host. Every infected host in the report decrypts to the same v1 core, SHA256 ec55c4ba2ab0b530c4d613e9c0214611c734fc0d17e2fabec68ade33b980075c.
- Static artifacts on infected files: the entry and last sections are set to RWX (0xE0000020 on the entry section), DYNAMIC_BASE and NX_COMPAT are cleared, and RELOCS_STRIPPED is set. The checksum is zeroed, and the Security directory is zeroed too, but the old certificate bytes stay behind as overlay, so signed files look unsigned. The last 0x28 bytes of the decrypted layer hold a metadata box ending in a version marker, 0x20260715 for v1 and 0x20260823 for v2. The report lists byte patterns for the v1 entry stub decoder, the layer decryptor head and the junk blocks (68 ?? F7 F4 FF 5?).
- Spread: five worker threads. ScanFile infects EXEs on every fixed and removable drive from C: to Z:, and RegScanThread infects whatever the HKCU Run key points to. The registry is only read, never written. CreateAutoRun runs every 5 seconds per drive. It drops a read-only, hidden, system 4-6 letter .exe or .pif in the drive root plus a randomized, exclusively locked autorun.inf. Windows 7 and later ignore autorun.inf on USB flash drives, so the copy needs a click, but infected EXEs on removable media still spread it. v1 uses the mutex [@]0826. Infected programs also play beeps at startup, which users may remember.
- Update channel: DownloadAndUpdate speaks plain TCP on port 8000. It sends DOWNLOAD, then Intel(R) HD Graphics Manager.exe, then READY, and writes the reply to %TEMP% as a six-letter .exe launched with CreateProcessW. There is no encryption or validation. On 2026-11-17 updatewin.ddns[.]net resolved to private address 192.168.1[.]100, and updatewinold.ddns[.]net had no A record. The researchers did not connect, so the payload is unknown. The name can be repointed at any time.
- Scope and evolution: the report covers 25 infected hosts from 16 programs, first seen 2026-10-22 and still appearing 2026-11-17. The v2 core, with banner 23/08/2026, adds a second update host, drops the mutex and swaps RC4 for a custom Feistel cipher. Code that targets file names containing bitdef or kasp is from decompilation only. Vietnamese 🇻🇳 log strings point to a Vietnamese-speaking author, and a D:\debug.log file suggests a development build. The report says the language is an observation, not attribution.
Takeaway: hunt for EXEs with RWX entry sections, a zeroed Security directory with leftover certificate bytes, and the byte patterns above. Check removable and fixed drive roots for hidden .exe or .pif files beside a locked autorun.inf, and for six-letter .exe files in %TEMP%. Look for outbound TCP 8000 to ddns[.]net names. Process-memory dumps of infected programs already hold the decrypted layer. The report includes IOC tables and a Python decoder for the layer and core.

item.title: Microsoft agent-framework Compromised: Credential Stealer Targets Azure and CI Pipelines
item.description:
Malicious agent-framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 hit PyPI on Nov 17, dropping a .pth credential stealer aimed at Azure, Azure DevOps and CI runners. It fires on every Python start, no import needed.
- Timeline (UTC): 1.26.1 went up at 20:35 and 1.26.2 at about 21:08, and both were gone from PyPI by about 21:30. The package sees roughly 41,000 weekly downloads. 1.26.0, published Nov 12, is the last safe version. Root cause is unconfirmed. There is no python-1.26.1 tag in microsoft/agent-framework and main is clean. 1.26.1 was wheel-only and still pins agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0, which suggests it was built outside the normal release process. Wiz has not linked this to the earlier durabletask compromise.
- Execution: the wheel drops a .pth file into the site-packages root, agent_framework_meta.pth in 1.26.1 and af_runtime_diag.pth in 1.26.2. Python processes .pth files on every interpreter start. The stealer forks into a detached session via os.setsid(), or uses a daemon thread, and sets _AF_TEL=1 to avoid re-running in children. Names like _telemetry and the user-agent af-runtime-diagnostics/1 mimic SDK telemetry.
- Collection: environment variables matching TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI and more. It also reads secret-looking values from up to 300 /proc/*/environ files and up to 60 credential files: ~/.azure/, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, Hugging Face tokens, ADO agent .credentials, and .env/JSON under /app and /workspace. It requests Azure DevOps OIDC tokens when SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are set. It also pulls managed-identity tokens from IMDS or the App Service endpoint for 12 resources, including ARM, Graph, Key Vault and Storage.
- 1.26.2 changes: the trigger moved to a new top-level af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, with __init__.py restored to clean, so searching only for 1.26.1 filenames misses it. It adds GitHub Actions OIDC theft for workflows with id-token: write, requesting tokens for api://AzureADTokenExchange and hxxps://management[.]azure[.]com/. Where an Entra ID federated credential trusts the workflow, those tokens can be exchanged for Azure access with no stored secret. It also adds ACTIONS, OIDC, RUNNER and ARM_ variable matching, GitHub runner paths, an 80-file cap, and the user-agent runtime-diagnostics/1.
- Exfil and scope: everything goes as one zlib-compressed, base64 JSON blob in a single HTTPS POST to hxxps://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb (?t=telemetry), with no fallback and no retry. Wiz confirmed the attacker's token was on the free tier and a maximum of 50 requests were captured. Those requests can still hold working cloud, CI and registry credentials.
Takeaway: search lockfiles, CI logs, virtualenvs and container images for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, then check site-packages for both .pth/.py pairs. Any Python process started there ran the payload. Hunt proxy and DNS logs for the webhook[.]site URL: a 200 means the data was accepted, 410/429 suggests rejection. Rotate everything in the environment and audit managed identities, federated credentials and app registrations, since stolen managed-identity and OIDC-exchanged tokens stay valid up to 24 hours. Hashes and filenames are in the report's IOC tables.

item.title: ARTEX Detection: Hunting the AI Pentest Framework Turned Attack Platform
item.description:
ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI pentest framework developed in China 🇨🇳, is now running on attacker servers and automating recon, probing, and exploitation through LLM-driven loops. There is no malware family to fingerprint, so detection has to key on behavior.
- What it is: ARTEX went public on GitHub as Autumn-27/ARTEX on July 26, 2026 under AGPL-3.0. It is written in Go, with a Next.js console on PostgreSQL, and sits on the same author's ScopeSentry asset-discovery platform. A Planner agent turns an operator goal like "gain admin panel access" into intents. Worker agents claim them, run tools like nmap, and write results to an asset graph and an exploration graph. It loops until the goal is met, using Anthropic, OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Mandiant and GTIG recorded 27 events within 23 seconds, plus automated error correction used to land webshells. The author disowned malicious use and pulled the repo on October 8, but forks and rebrands such as ScopeWeaver still circulate. Censys counted 1,465 exposed consoles in early November, most on default port 8787.
- Reported use: Storm-3358 targeted financial organizations (Nov 9) with SSRF and anonymous file uploads, then WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs plus cloud identity abuse. Storm-0940 hit IT and software vendors (Oct 27) with Okta, Entra ID, and Cognito auth probing, account recovery abuse, and IP and user-agent rotation. ARTEX was also found on servers attacking Japanese 🇯🇵 companies, doing API probing and WAF evasion in Japan 🇯🇵 and South Korea 🇰🇷 driven by DeepSeek, Zhipu AI, and xAI models. CrowdStrike reported South Korean 🇰🇷 bank breaches on October 7.
- Telemetry fingerprints: On web servers, look for 40x response spikes from a single IP, path traversal, file inclusion, and OS command injection patterns, and scripted files dropped into web directories. Wiz saw a fetch of /swagger/?format=openapi followed immediately by a random nonexistent URI, a clean mapping signature. In identity logs, look for failed-login bursts and access-denied spikes on Okta, Entra ID, and Cognito, plus password spraying and account recovery abuse. On endpoints, look for web service accounts spawning shells, SSH known_hosts discovery, nmap, curl, or wget from unexpected parents, and netcat paired with RAT binaries. In cloud logs, look for an Azure write-then-delete of a throwaway blob and AWS EC2 calls with --dry-run that test IAM permissions without changing state. On the network, look for HTTP C2 to direct IPs on uncommon ports and egress to LLM resellers or self-hosted proxies such as CLIProxyAPI and New API.
- PHP2Shell as the ideal target: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are RCE chains in PHP core's session.upload_progress, rated CVSS v4 9.2 and affecting PHP 5.4.0 through 8.5.11. Fixes shipped October 21, 2026. Amazon caught an exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure. Qualys counted 167 million PHP installations, 71% on end-of-life versions that will never be patched. An issue on an ARTEX fork proposed a php2shell-check skill, so once that exists the Planner can queue it against every PHP asset in its graph. Hunt for multipart POSTs carrying a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field with attacker-chosen session IDs, follow-up file inclusion requests pointing at sess_ files in PHP session directories, inert PHP canaries and unique output markers used to confirm evaluation, and PHP worker processes spawning shells, curl, or wget.
- Indicators: The report lists the ARTEX host 38.244.50[.]120 and LLM reseller xcai[.]pro (CrowdStrike), plus Storm-0940 infrastructure 144.172.64[.]60, .99, and .128 (Microsoft). Treat them as perishable: Censys watched 10 attacker open directories close and 15 new ones appear in two days.
Takeaway: Hunt the sequence, not the name. Correlate by account, session, or API key across web, IdP, and cloud logs rather than source IP alone, since operators rotate IPs and user agents: an OpenAPI fetch plus a junk URI, a burst of 40x responses, then recovery-flow abuse or dry-run and write-then-delete cloud calls. Watch network egress to LLM resellers and self-hosted LLM proxies. Load the IOCs from the report, rate-limit by account, session, and API key rather than IP alone, and consider decoy assets, since an autonomous agent will burn its token budget on them. Patch PHP2Shell, move off end-of-life branches, and check PHP workers for shell children.

item.title: OPTIMJACK: BBC, CNN and Zoom Among Targets of Optimizely Script Hijacking
item.description:
OPTIMJACK: Attackers exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to inject JavaScript into customer projects, reaching 178 organizations including Zoom, the BBC, CNN and Equifax. The kit swapped crypto addresses, skimmed cards and served iOS exploit kits.
- How it worked: Optimizely sites load a snippet from the vendor CDN that includes a Project JavaScript section for customer code. The attacker wrote their own code there and left the rest of each snippet untouched. The file still came from cdn.optimizely[.]com with Optimizely's certificate, so browsers trusted it. Sites that self-hosted the snippet were hit too, because the code lived in the same project. Report URI says this was not cache poisoning. How the attacker got permission to modify so many customers' projects is still unknown.
- Three loader variants: a plain script tag pointing to 1688360[.]cc/track.js, a Base64-hidden version of the same address that evades a simple text search, and a fully inline version that runs even if the domain is blocked. The first injection appeared at 04:21 UTC in the BBC snippet, loading webshell[.]lol. Report URI ties that injector to the same actor, seen earlier via Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts, and on Turkish 🇹🇷 sites since 17 September. The payload was rebuilt 26 times that day.
- What track.js did: it replaced wallet addresses (Bitcoin, Ethereum, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) in page text, forms, links, clipboard and outgoing requests, validating addresses first. A card skimmer was added at 13:43 UTC and grabs number, expiry and CVV from a site's own form fields, but cannot read Stripe or Adyen hosted frames. After a swap it also sends cookies without HttpOnly and a page screenshot.

item.title: Trigram Campaign Impersonates About 50 AI and Blockchain Brands to Target Devs with Infostealers
item.description:
Trigram impersonates about 50 AI and blockchain brands to trick developers into running an infostealer themselves. Stormshield assesses with high confidence it continues the UNK_DeadDrop cluster, tied to North Korea-linked activity.
- Lure and gating: Recruitment, conference, and package-tracking lures, a supply-chain compromise, and trojanized repos all converge on the same infrastructure and payload. The fake recruitment site fingerprints visitors, geofences by IP (possibly to exclude China 🇨🇳), and demands a referral code, which suggests pre-identified targets. Rejected codes return "Already used," "Locked to another IP," or "Invalid code." Accepted visitors are told to paste a "technical check" command into a Linux terminal. That first command only POSTs a nonce, downloads nothing, and the page replies "Operation timeout. Please try again. Nonce Refreshed." Then the Copy button is changed to inject the real command into the clipboard, even if the user presses Ctrl+C.
- Loaders and payload: Windows runs PowerShell to fetch v.cmd, Linux runs bash to fetch a file named u, and macOS runs bash to fetch verify_m. These prep the environment: a Base64-encoded script sets the working directory, creates a lock to block concurrent installs, and checks for Node.js 18 or later, installing Node.js 20.18.1 if absent. They then fetch install_guard.js, which deploys an infostealer that collects system metadata, browser credentials, crypto wallets, and sensitive files. C2 is resolved through a GitLab dead drop.
- Repo hijack: On October 31, 2026, a forged commit to the antd-img-crop GitHub repo added a prebuild hook, prebuild.js, that fires when a developer runs npm run build. The npm package itself was not impacted. The chain installs Node.js via a fake installer, runs an encrypted next stage in memory, and ends with a third stage that steals browser passwords, cookies, keychains, wallets, SSH keys, and .env files on macOS, Linux, and Windows, then installs the Overlord RAT disguised as Google software. On macOS and Linux a fake dialog asks for the system password to "apply system updates and verify drivers and security settings." Same payload also arrives via a fake Amber Group careers portal and a sideloaded VS Code or Cursor extension named google-dev-tools.google-update-support, likely launched through a coding assessment and deleted after running.
- Back office: Stormshield found a management layer on 170.205.30[.]27:8000 running a platform called rms-platform. API routes show it scrapes GitHub profiles, sends phishing, manages decoys, issues access codes, exports victim data, and monitors crypto wallets. Visitors are rated important, moderate, or useless. It leans on GitHub and GitLab for hosting, Brevo, Resend, Mailgun, and Smartlead for email, and FullStory for session recording. Decoys and consoles ship in the same JavaScript bundle, with hostname or URL path choosing the interface.
- Attribution: Links to UNK_DeadDrop and Kimsuky include the console super-admin eros1030109@gmail[.]com, which matches an address used in Kimsuky's Operation GitPower. Also noted are asteara[.]org, the MongoDB username silviattech1129_db_user, and the Telegram recruiter account pichi_finance_hr. Operation GitPower itself used local LLMs via Ollama and GPT4All to build decoys, LNK files that run PowerShell to pull lures from GitHub raw content, and AsyncRAT. It has since targeted Ukrainian 🇺🇦 diplomacy and policy experts, mostly unsuccessfully per Genians. SafeDep cautions that its Contagious Interview match rests on technique and does not prove who the operators are. Jamf found a Zoom-themed Overlord variant sharing the com.zoom LaunchAgent label and com.zoom.plist name with FlexibleFerret, but no direct overlap with UNK_DeadDrop.
Takeaway: Start on developer workstations. Look for terminal or PowerShell history showing a pasted download-and-run of v.cmd, u, or verify_m, unexpected Node.js 20.18.1 installs, install_guard.js on disk, and node spawned from a prebuild.js hook during npm run build. Check VS Code and Cursor for google-dev-tools.google-update-support (it may have been deleted, so look for traces), and hosts for a remote-access agent disguised as Google software. If a host ran any of it, treat SSH keys, .env secrets, browser sessions, and wallets as exposed. Review repos for forged commits touching build hooks. The attribution indicators and infrastructure details are in Stormshield's report.

item.title: Inside CyberStrikeAI: 221 tool executions and a disabled approval gate
item.description:
An exposed workspace on 38.76.169[.]207 leaked a CyberStrikeAI conversation database. It ties one 16 November 2026 operator session to model accounting, process events, stored tool executions and agent-recorded findings. Approval enforcement was switched off mid-session, and the agent's final report claims more than the evidence supports.
- The evidence chain reconciles. The report found 221 stored tool executions against 240 process-level tool calls. The 19 local results with no execution ID (ten skill actions, four task-plan updates, three file reads, two exit actions) explain the gap. All 221 execution IDs match the stored table. The conversation says agent_mode supervisor, but all 240 tool-call events name the agent as main and the role as orchestrator, so there is no evidence of a worker swarm.
- The approval gate failed, then was disabled. Four approval interrupts were all rejected by audit_agent with the comment "LLM call failed; conservatively reject". These were audit-agent model-call failures (the review call has a 90 second timeout), not human decisions. Three ended at 90 seconds. The fourth ended at 43 seconds when the user cancelled the run. At 09:48:15 UTC the saved conversation configuration shows enabled=0, mode=off, and the recovered source returns without requiring approval when config is absent or disabled. The user later approved proposed actions in chat at 10:18, which is wording, not an enforced per-call gate. The database does not say who changed the setting, and the report found no evidence the model exploited the approval system.
- What the agent actually did: it consumed a handoff document, rechecked old access paths, ran network reconnaissance, then focused on a compute-marketplace MCP interface. The c2_listener tool returned zero on both calls and the webshell list showed no connections. Of the 221 executions, 170 were the execute tool (160 completed, 10 failed). The strongest supported result is returned compute-node and job data. No shell, internal-network access, data-lake breach or destructive change is established.
- Where the final report overreaches: the nine findings are agent-created, not nine validated vulnerabilities. An anonymous token that returned a JWT and key was a throwaway identity, not a stolen one. A job query total of 10000 with relation "gte" is a lower bound, not 10,000 downloaded records. The "260-node dump" came from a script that looped 26 offsets and appended ten hits each time with no unique-ID check, while nearby results report a node-search total of 259. A test a minute earlier returned the same first node at offset 10. Distinct-node count cannot be computed from the recovered files.
- Accounting: eight usage rows name deepseek-v4-pro, with 211 model calls and 13,564,316 total tokens (13,353,943 prompt, 210,373 completion). These are local application records, not an invoice, and the prompt total may include repeated context.
Takeaway: investigate audit-agent failures, configuration changes and subsequent tool execution as one sequence, and preserve the previous config and the actor where the app logs them. Do not accept claims of execution, access or impact without process, file, identity or transaction evidence, and keep response bodies or protected hashes, because request logs cannot show volume retrieved. Also check whether static file servers expose agent data directories, conversation databases or uploads. The report's indicators table lists the host, TCP 8010, the exposed paths /CyberStrikeAI/data/conversations.db and /CyberStrikeAI/log/diagnostic-2026-11-16.log, and two SHA-256 values:
a0b4be0a70e35d0d30809e0856e9860d4265df65e41fef2e93405e166d6edd36 (conversation database snapshot, 6,688,768 bytes)
4da5383d7a1bc2a83c20a39510227aad34072876fa47bfb20fd10aeb48b676eb (diagnostic log, 6,560 bytes)
The database passes SQLite quick_check, which shows structural readability only, not authenticity or completeness.

item.title: Cron Is A Sneaky Way Malware Persists on Your Network Appliances
item.description:
Killing the bot process and deleting the binary does not clean a compromised switch or firewall if a scheduled job reinstalls it. Eclypsium's report ties this to Evooo1Bot and SSHStalker: inventory and clear cron before you call an appliance clean.
- Evooo1Bot (FortiGuard Labs, August 13, 2026) targets internet-facing routers, firewalls, IP cameras, PBX phone systems, and NAS devices. One bot command, !persist, installs several persistence mechanisms at once. The cron entry runs every five minutes, pulls the malware with wget or curl, and pipes it into a shell. SSHStalker (Flare, February 2026) uses a cron job that runs every minute and relaunches the kit if its process is gone. MITRE tracks this as Scheduled Task/Job: Cron (T1053.003).
- Cron is not the only foothold. !persist also writes a systemd unit described as "Apache HTTPD Cache Manager," an /etc/init.d script, an /etc/rc.local entry, and a login script under /etc/profile.d/. Removing only the cron entry leaves all of those in place.
- Why appliances get missed: Arista EOS, Cisco NX-OS, F5 BIG-IP, and many other network operating systems are Linux-based. Admins work in the vendor CLI, config management tracks the vendor configuration, EDR agents generally are not on the device, and the Linux crontab is rarely read. The upside is that an appliance crontab is small and legitimate jobs are vendor housekeeping such as log rotation, cleanup, and health checks.
- Hand check from the device's Linux shell. On Arista EOS, run bash from privileged mode. On NX-OS, run bash requires the feature bash-shell configuration, which is off by default on many deployments. If you cannot enable it, record "cron not inspected," not "clean." Read /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/, and /var/spool/cron/ directly instead of relying on crontab -l. A root attacker can write straight into the spool and never touch the crontab command, so no crontab command shows up in shell history. The spool path is /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ on Debian-based systems and /var/spool/cron/ on Red Hat-based ones. Grep the whole cron surface for curl, wget, tftp, nc, ncat, /dev/tcp, base64, and pipes to sh or bash. A fetcher piped to a shell matches Evooo1Bot, /dev/tcp or nc suggests a reverse shell, and a long base64 string is a hidden command.
- Frequent schedules and [@]reboot entries are worth listing but are not proof, because some vendors run their own jobs every minute. Then timeline the cron files with find -printf and compare against last -Faiwx. BusyBox-based appliances may not support -printf. A cron file modified shortly after an unexplained admin login is strong evidence and points to the account to investigate.
- Beyond cron, check vendor schedulers that live in the device configuration, not the Linux crontab: the NX-OS scheduler feature, EEM applets, and the Arista EOS schedule command and event handlers. Also check boot hooks on persistent flash such as /mnt/flash/rc.eos on Arista EOS. Whether a cron entry survives a reboot or upgrade depends on how the platform stores its root filesystem, and Eclypsium says it has not tested every platform. Patching the entry vector does not remove a job the attacker already wrote.
Takeaway: treat a fetch-and-execute cron entry, a reverse-shell command, or a job running from /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm as evidence of compromise, and hand it to IR. Preserve a copy of the file and its timestamps first, remove the scheduler entry before terminating processes, then check the other persistence locations above before the device returns to service. Build a per-device list of what was inspected and what could not be, and confirm whether cron content from network devices is monitored at all. The report has the full grep and find commands.

item.title: COLD RELIC: A Case Study in Impersonation and Compromise
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 group COLD RELIC (ex-COLDRIVER, UNC4057, Star Blizzard, Callisto, Gossamer Bear) used data from a late-2025 cloud breach to impersonate staff and compromise a second US 🇺🇸 organization in 2026. GTIG saw new phishing as recently as November 2026.
Mandiant's report shows one victim tenant becoming the pretext factory for the next. The US 🇺🇸 DOJ has assessed the group operates within the FSB.
- Case 1 (late 2025): operators came in through a US 🇺🇸 residential proxy near the victim, using stolen Super Admin credentials plus an MFA push fatigue attack (T1621). After the user accepted a prompt, they registered a device model never before seen in the tenant. They then layered on passkeys, MFA backup codes, and rogue MFA devices (T1098.005, T1078.004). The actor picks proxies near victims to evade impossible-travel alerting.
- Case 1 collection and anti-forensics: they mass-shared Drive content to an actor-operated mailbox and downloaded directly (T1530, T1567.002). They also ran a domain-wide Customer Takeout, logged as CUSTOMER_TAKEOUT_CREATED in Workspace Admin audit logs (T1119), and exported the full employee list. To check defender visibility they queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs, then viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications (T1562.008). Access lasted months through OAuth inbox sync to external mail clients (T1114.002, T1528) and attacker-enrolled passkeys that survived password and session resets. Separately, GTIG saw at least one victim reset passwords but never revoke sessions, so the actor stayed in.
- Case 2 (2026): the operators posed as an employee of the first victim and contacted a target at a second organization over an encrypted messaging app. They shared links that hit a compromised website first, which hides the phishing domain and lets the actor fingerprint visitors before redirecting. The pattern looks like compromised.example[.]com/some_path/some_file.php?file=<previous_victim_name> or ?ref=<lure_name>. The phishing page stole Entra ID credentials and tokens, then showed a document lure matching the conversation. Entra ID was the federated SSO provider for Google Workspace, so the actor registered a new MFA device in the SSO layer and bulk-downloaded the user's cloud drive. A redirector URL submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026 carried a parameter naming the first victim, which tied the two intrusions together.
- Post-compromise collection is aimed at the next operation. The actor searched for credentials, personnel data, .pst archives, rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules. After Case 2, the messaging account changed its profile name to a new person, which GTIG believes is a fresh persona for targeting the same professional circles.
Takeaway: password resets alone do not evict this actor. Revoke all sessions, refresh tokens, and third-party OAuth grants in both Workspace and Entra ID, and remove unauthorized passkeys, backup codes, and MFA devices.
Hunt these Workspace events from the report: Passkey enrolled and Device Registered after an MFA fatigue burst, Authorize events granting hxxps://mail[.]google[.]com/ to clients like Thunderbird or Proton Mail, and Customer Takeout Created. Also look for Batch Delete Operation Performed on alerts, User List Download, Investigation Query, Drive Download spikes, and Item search performed with terms like .pst, .bak, password, or cred. Flag logins with Login Challenge Type Backup code from consumer ASNs. The report cites AS5650 and AS20115 as example consumer/residential proxy ASNs to restrict for admin access.
The report has an ATT&CK mapping and detection table but no IOC list, so build detections on behavior and URL parameter patterns.

item.title: How AI Agents Become New Targets in GitHub Malware Campaign
item.description:
A GitHub campaign turns AI coding assistant config files into execution paths. Bitdefender Labs found 22 malicious GitHub links whose AGENTS[.]md, CLAUDE[.]md, and hook files push developers' agents into running a hidden setup.js loader that steals tokens and spreads.
The story: these files normally tell an assistant how to run tests or follow repo conventions. Here they carry social engineering aimed at the agent. The text calls scripts/setup.js a "sealed binary artifact," says it is signed, and tells the agent not to read, quote, or display it. It then says to run it at session start without showing output, and to run node scripts/setup.js automatically without asking confirmation if setup has not been run. The wording imitates DevSecOps and compliance language to make an unsafe action feel routine.
- Two execution routes. One manipulates the agent through written instructions. The other needs no prompt at all: a session-start hook in a config file such as .claude/settings.json runs a command in the user's shell once the developer opens and trusts the repo. Either way, setup.js runs with the developer's own permissions.
- Loader chain. The outer setup.js is a 3.75 MB single-line script that hex-decodes an embedded value, applies ROT13, and evaluates the result. The recovered Node.js stager holds two AES-128-GCM blobs with embedded keys. One decompresses into a 4.67 MB bundle. The stager resolves or downloads the Bun runtime and pipes the bundle to bun run - over standard input, so the final payload never needs to land as a readable file. Extra payloads sit in a compressed _bz field in package.json, including Windows Credential Manager enumeration and JavaScript that only fires under certain runtime conditions.
- Token validation and repo abuse. The malware checks stolen GitHub and GitLab tokens before using them. On GitHub it queries /user, /user/repos, and /users/<login>/repos and checks for repo, public_repo, and workflow scopes. On GitLab it uses /api/v4/projects and /projects. Per target repo it resolves the default branch, inspects up to 50 branches, skips dependabot/ and copilot/ branches, and reviews workflows, package metadata, and protection rules. MAX_TARGET_REPOS defaults to 25.
- Self-propagation. With enough permissions it commits files meant to influence or trigger AI coding environments, edits package metadata and workflows, creates GitLab pipeline schedules, and tries to republish infected packages through npm, PyPI, RubyGems, and JFrog. Locally, it recursively searches the home directory for AI-agent config files, keeps paths containing one of 14 agent names, and injects instruction text, session-start hooks, or MCP server configurations. A victim's machine becomes a source of new poisoned repos and packages.
- Evidence to preserve. Repo names and setup.js MD5s are in the report's IOC table, for example b9a182b646c7fdff68f2ff9dfd822516 for several toray/ repos and 3794736979327349404171798328a38a for itsunai/ repos. Hashes differ from account to account in the table, so hash matching alone can miss new variants.
Practitioner takeaway: if a developer opened a cloned repo with an AI assistant, check whether it contains scripts/setup.js, instruction files telling the agent to run it silently, or hooks in .claude/settings.json. Look at process lineage for node running setup.js and for Bun being downloaded or launched with bun run - from a Node parent. Then inspect home-directory agent config files for instruction text, hooks, or MCP entries you did not add. If any of this ran, treat GitHub and GitLab tokens as burned: rotate them, review API access to /user and /user/repos from unexpected sources, and audit recent commits, workflow changes, pipeline schedules, and package publishes across npm, PyPI, RubyGems, and JFrog. Match repos and hashes against the report's IOC table.

item.title: Threat Researcher’s Notebook: BubbleLoader
item.description:
BubbleLoader patches the entry point of legitimate PEs like WinRAR, hides its next stage in a fake PNG, and randomizes compiler padding so the payload hash changes on every run.
- Stage 1 is a small entry point patch with an obfuscated prologue. It uses a GetPC call to recover the image base (0x400000 in the analyzed sample) even under ASLR. It then builds fake function calls to GetModuleHandleW and GetProcAddress from a pointer load, a fabricated return address, and a jump into the host's own import table. It tries an ASCII "kernel32" first and falls back to a wide string, so one template fits hosts importing either the A or W variant. The patch ends with VirtualAlloc, copies the two PNGs into that memory, and jumps into the second one.
- The two PNGs are the staging container. The first is a valid red-to-blue gradient image that serves as a rolling XOR key. The second has correct PNG magic bytes and a truncated IHDR, with encrypted shellcode starting where the width field belongs. That field should begin with 0x00 but starts with 0x55 in the fake. That is a cheap static check for an invalid embedded PNG. The gradient key is sparse and full of null bytes, so stretches of the third stage are left unencrypted, including loader strings. Opaque predicates and an in instruction (privileged, raises an exception in user mode) pad the decryption loop to hinder analysis.
- The third-stage loader is built to serve multiple contexts. It has a reentry guard for DLL payloads even though this sample's payload is an EXE. It takes the host image base from the PEB (gs:0x60) and reuses the host's imports. A generic resolver, bootstrapped by overwriting 0xfafafafafafafafa placeholders with LoadLibraryA and GetProcAddress, resolves ExitProcess, RtlAddFunctionTable, RtlPcToFileHeader, VirtualAlloc, and VirtualProtect.
- The anti-forensics feature matters for IR. While loading, the shellcode finds 0xcc compiler padding between functions and overwrites each byte except the leftmost with randomness from rdtsc. The unpacked payload hash is therefore different on every execution. Patching out that loop restores the original hash. The loader then reflectively maps the PE (headers, sections, relocations, TLS callbacks, imports, protections). It also registers the payload's .pdata through RtlAddFunctionTable and writes an inline hook stub over RtlPcToFileHeader in ntdll via VirtualProtect and memcpy, giving the payload working SEH. It finally calls the entry point with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, then ExitProcess.
- Detection opportunities the report calls out: executable memory allocated through VirtualAlloc, runtime VirtualProtect changes aimed at ntdll's RtlPcToFileHeader, tampered entry points in common third-party utilities such as WinRAR, and invalid PNGs with truncated IHDR chunks.
Takeaway: do not depend on payload hashes here, since the post-unpacking hash is randomized per run. Pivot to behavior and integrity. Check entry points of signed utilities for patching, hunt memory for the RtlPcToFileHeader inline hook and RWX allocations, and flag PNG resources with a truncated IHDR whose width field's first byte is non-zero (0x55 in this sample). When detonating a sample, patch out the rdtsc padding loop beforehand to get the payload's original hash. The analyzed sample SHA256 is 4987af027009d572c26f6d009c5e53e237cb2e3ab9d52094c14dc0b8b6f40b14, and the report lists further sample hashes.

item.title: Uncovering GhostMap: The Rootkit Behind Shai-Hulud’s Rusty Cousin
item.description:
GhostMap is Aqua Nautilus's name for the Linux eBPF rootkit shared by IronWorm and Atomic Arch payloads. It rewrites what ps and /proc/net/tcp return to hide processes, files and sockets, but the concealment has measurable gaps and left traces in runtime telemetry.
- Install and load: IronWorm (JFrog's "rustier cousin" of Shai-Hulud) arrives via an npm preinstall entry running ./tools/setup. Atomic Arch, a separate campaign, uses modified AUR PKGBUILDs that install atomic-lockfile. In the lab run as root, the IronWorm specimen copied itself to /var/lib/glugi/glugi and created and enabled glugi.service (T1543.002). One later run used /var/lib/havebi/havebi, so names vary. The systemd-launched successor, with the same hash as the sample, loads the eBPF components. Watching only the installer's child processes misses the real loader.
- Process hiding: GhostMap ran 13 programs, 10 maps and 13 links at the checkpoint. The maps include hidden_names, hidden_pids, hidden_inodes and scratch. At sys_exit_getdents64, exit_getdents uses bpf_probe_write_user to enlarge the preceding record's d_reclen, so the reader skips the hidden entry (T1014). Across six altered buffers, only the low byte of that length field changed. The hidden bytes stayed in the buffer and the returned byte count was unchanged. Hidden test processes stayed reachable through their known /proc/PID paths, and ps listed them again once the rootkit stopped. The on_exec hook matches comm, so a fork-only child with the name stayed visible while an exec'd child became hidden. A visible child with a parent missing from ps is a lead, not proof.
- Socket hiding is leaky: the listener on 127.0.0.1:8738 vanished from /proc/net/tcp in all three observations. On the Netlink path, GhostMap only changed the message type to NLMSG_NOOP and left the port, identifier and listening state in the payload. The tested ss (iproute2 6.1.0-1ubuntu6.4) still showed the listener, minus its process-owner annotation. That result applies to the tested ss package only. The listener takes local text records and stores them in the user.d extended attribute on the installed executable (T1564.014). No external C2 delivery or remote command execution was observed. Attaching with PTRACE_ATTACH to a protected process got the attacher SIGKILLed (T1622).
- Shared component: the Atomic Arch comparison payload shares 13 named eBPF programs, ten map names and matching helper-use bitmaps with IronWorm. Both also use a byte-identical 1,142-byte forged sudo wrapper and the port 8738 loopback listener. That supports a shared rootkit implementation, not a common operator. The "TeamPCP" reference comes from the npm package author's deprecation notice, not from the report's own analysis.
- Detection: Tracee was running before IronWorm started and alerted at attach time on exit_getdents, net_exit_read and exit_recvmsg, each reporting the probe_write_user capability. It also alerted on signal-sending and other eBPF activity, and retained all 48 tested directory-reader calls. Only detection was evaluated, not prevention, and the alerts do not show individual buffer mutations.
Takeaway: an empty ps result proves nothing. Compare views: probe suspect PIDs directly under /proc, check /proc/net/tcp against ss, and review BPF programs and links for ownership, especially any that can write to user space. Check for unexpected services and executables with user.d set. Preserve evidence before removing the service, since stopping it removed the programs and links and left three pinned maps. Copy file metadata and extended attributes, not just contents, and avoid attaching a debugger to protected processes. The report has the IOC table, including SHA256 hashes such as 8795b5215dd06c5366a038a65b18b4dfefa5fd90244a567c3e0b58323103377c (GhostMap BPF ELF from runtime memory) and 36abd242ddaa27f0160c539377a0e92cf781c1695137850acc87e3892b436d36 (executed setup ELF). Do not use the npm archive hash to identify the extracted executable.

item.title: Operation ArgonHunt: Open Directory Exposes a Crypto Exchange Breach and 44,000 Stolen AI API Keys
item.description:
An open directory on a staging server exposed Operation ArgonHunt: a Türkiye crypto exchange breach with forged withdrawals, plus 44,096 stolen AI API keys. SOCRadar found it while threat hunting.
- The server at 176.65.148[.]2 served its /tmp over HTTP on port 8099: 1,600+ files, roughly 700 MB, 75+ attack scripts. Systemd service directories, X11 sockets, Chromium profiles and a tmux session directory show it was the live filesystem of a working host. The toolkit sits in /root/argon-hunt, which gave the operation its name. SOCRadar's analysis was passive and no found credentials were used.
- The exchange fell to weak credentials first. Admin staff passwords were unsalted MD5, and 17 of roughly 100 hashes were cracked. item.title: New GitDoor and GraphDoor Backdoors Turn GitHub and SharePoint Into Covert C2 Channels
item.description:
Kaspersky's Operation ShadowCloud hits government sectors in Asia and Africa with two new modular backdoors, GitDoor and GraphDoor. They hide C2 in GitHub, Microsoft SharePoint via the Graph API, and Ably, so the traffic looks like normal enterprise cloud usage.
The chain starts with a legitimate MeshCentral Agent (MeshAgent), a remote access tool, on a victim host. Kaspersky saw it at a Taiwanese 🇹🇼 organization and does not know how it was installed. Signs point to reuse of a prior infection already on the network. The agent beacons to a hard-coded server, wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx, and pulls down three staged items.
- Staging and loading: a legitimate binary for DLL sideloading (start.exe, pythonw.exe, or zoomit.exe), a rogue loader DLL (jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, or libcef.dll), and an encrypted file holding the core payload. Two loader types are known. Type 1 runs RC4 and then an XOR mask, Type 2 uses XOR alone. Both inject the decoded backdoor into the current process's memory. The backdoors use control flow flattening and nested helper functions to slow analysis.
- GitDoor: C2 runs over two GitHub repositories, /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo (public, for command payloads) and /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix (private, for results). Repo creation dates suggest preparation since at least the end of 2024. It supports 26 commands, including file management, keylogging, proxying (including via Ably), and shellcode loading from Base64 COFF binaries.
- GraphDoor: it opens a named pipe, creates a folder named Intel_Log under the Application Data directory, and authenticates to login.microsoftonline[.]com with a malicious application. It then uses the access token to talk to the Microsoft Graph API and stage data on a SharePoint drive. It pulls three plugins and runs them in parallel: kl.ts (keylogger), pr.ts (process list), scr.ts (screenshots). Other plugins are moveDir.ts, channel.ts, abchannel.ts, and ab2channel.ts, a SOCKS5 proxy tunneled through Ably's Pusher-compatible WebSocket service. Its shellcode capability adds cmd.exe and MZ executable execution on top of GitDoor's.
- Post-exploitation modules via shellcode: APC injection, service, registry, and scheduled task management, firewall rule changes, process memory dumping, and local user creation or group changes. Credential theft includes Mimikatz against LSASS, CookieKatz to pull Chrome and Edge cookies from process memory, the WhatsApp database decryption key, and forced NTLM authentication to an attacker-controlled destination. Both implants write keystrokes to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat.
- Attribution: unknown. Kaspersky sees overlap with China-nexus activity Sophos tracks as Bronze Sandcastle, plus tactical similarities to FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle (aka BlackTech). On several victims those groups used the same staging directories as GitDoor, with implants deployed within a day of GitDoor. Kaspersky says this does not prove a link, but suggests a Chinese-speaking group may be developing or using the backdoors.
Takeaway: network telemetry will not separate this C2 from normal Graph, GitHub, or Ably calls, so pivot to the host. Find unexpected MeshAgent installs and connections to 27.102.66[.]162. Look for the sideloading pairs above, where a legitimate binary such as zoomit.exe or pythonw.exe sits next to a DLL like jli.dll or WINMM.dll in a non-standard path, and for those processes making outbound calls to GitHub API or Graph endpoints. Check for logs.dat under SystemCertificates\Cache and an Intel_Log folder under Application Data. Review LSASS access, new local accounts or group changes, and new scheduled tasks. In Microsoft Entra, audit sign-ins and consent grants for unfamiliar applications tied to SharePoint access.

item.title: Optimizely Attack Hits Zoom, BBC, CNN With Skimmer, iOS Kits
item.description:
The Optimizely supply chain attack on Nov 16, 2026 turned a trusted A/B testing script into a delivery channel for a crypto clipper, a card skimmer and iOS exploit kits. Report URI found 188 infected snippets at 178 organizations, including Zoom, BBC, CNN, IKEA and HSBC.
- Entry point: Optimizely confirmed an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation product to add JavaScript to customer projects. The attacker planted a small loader in the optional Project JavaScript setting. Browsers still got a normal snippet from cdn.optimizely[.]com under Optimizely's own TLS certificate. The researchers rule out CDN cache poisoning, and self-hosted copies (Scheels, Vodafone Australia 🇦🇺) were infected too. Three loader variants: a plain script tag fetching hxxps://1688360[.]cc/track.js, a Base64 variant decoded with atob() (seen in Smartsheet after an earlier cleanup, suggesting retained write access), and an inline eval fallback that works even if the C2 is blocked.
- Payload: track.js was rebuilt 26 times in a day. It swaps wallet addresses across BTC, EVM chains, TRON, SOL, TON, LTC, BCH and DOGE. A card skimmer was added at 13:43 UTC and beacons Luhn-valid card data, expiry and CVV to card.php. Address swaps near payment wording also upload the page URL, non-HttpOnly cookies and an html2canvas screenshot to hit.php. Hosted payment iframes kept cards out of reach, while first-party card fields did not. Wallets received about $7,150 in total, and one cash-out TRON address was also used in March 2026 and on Nov 3, 2026.
- iOS stage: the boot.js router sent iOS 13 to 17 to the Coruna kit, iOS 18 to DarkSword, and iOS 26 to a chain that only fingerprints the device. Delivery of exploit pages is confirmed. No successful iPhone compromise has been publicly confirmed. On iOS 18.6 or earlier, infected pages refreshed once a minute while the kit retried. The kit's code comments treat 18.7.3 and 26.3 or later as patched.
- Timeline (UTC): first injection on the BBC snippet at 04:21 on Nov 16, loading the earlier injector from webshell[.]lol. 1688360[.]cc was registered at 05:23. Researchers found 186 infected snippets in a scan of 1,611 at 19:24 to 19:59, and mass cleanup ran 20:40 to 21:10. All files were clean by 23:11. The C2 went to clientHold at 00:37 on Nov 17. The same injector appeared in Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts Nov 13 to 16, and first surfaced Sept 17 via a linkforge[.]cc SEO panel script. Card, cookie and iOS impact is unknown.
- CSP decided the outcome: of 256 hosts tested, only 24 organizations blocked the payload and 68 had no CSP. Allowlisting cdn.optimizely[.]com did nothing. strict-dynamic and unsafe-eval undid tighter policies, and Optimizely's documentation tells customers to allow unsafe-eval. HSBC's policy stopped track.js and the theft, but the embedded copy still executed. On 17 sites a restrictive connect-src stopped exfiltration, yet address swapping continued because it runs in the page.
Hunt takeaway: Optimizely has already removed the injected code, so a clean snippet today proves nothing. Search proxy, DNS and web logs from Nov 13 to 17 for 1688360[.]cc, webshell[.]lol, linkforge[.]cc, 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, l7bcsnwc7nzr3uo[.]icu, 136.113.106[.]136, 34.96.213[.]201 and 34.87.36[.]58. Look for POSTs to card.php, hit.php and /api/iptj. Review Project JavaScript and every experiment's custom code for atob() calls, window._k7, window.__k7b, data-channel-code 02111110 and any script your team did not add. Optimizely's change history shows whether edits came via the API or the web interface. Treat first-party card entries and non-HttpOnly cookie secrets from Nov 16 as exposed, and rotate Optimizely users and API tokens. The full IOC list, including track.js SHA-256 hashes and attacker wallets, is in the report.

item.title: Operation ShadowCloud: cloud service-based backdoors targeting government networks in Asia and Africa. Part 2
item.description:
Operation ShadowCloud part 2: Kaspersky details GraphDoor, a backdoor that uses Microsoft Graph and SharePoint as C2, plus plug-ins that proxy traffic through Ably. Attribution is open, but staging overlaps with FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle intrusions.
- GraphDoor (MD5 14ec33ea808e697870d00c5e434c2952) opens a named pipe \\.\pipe\p<PID> that its plug-ins use to report back, and creates C:\ProgramData\Intel_Log\<random GUID>. It resolves APIs via DJB2 hashes and calls them through a vectored exception handler. It posts to login.microsoftonline[.]com with a client_credentials grant, so it authenticates as an app, not a user. It then PUTs victim data to a SharePoint library as main.<8-char code>.js.map, with the commit message "commit from INSOMNIA". Sites named in the report: buildersemp.sharepoint[.]com and cskautogo.sharepoint[.]com.
- Tasking is pulled from SharePoint lists via Graph queries filtering on Title, for example startswith(fields/Title,'main.<victim code>'). It accepts command files ending in .js, .swp, .tmp, .kmap, .pmap, .apmap. Two new commands over GitDoor: shell (cmd.exe /C) and adsmload, which hides payloads as ASCII MAC address strings decoded with RtlEthernetStringToAddressA. Plug-ins are a stub plus a COFF object, found by marker bytes 1C 3F E6 E9, with entry point go.
- Plug-in artifacts. The keylogger (kl.ts) writes XOR-encrypted data to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat and creates an object named keylogger###Global\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater{%X-%X}. The process lister (pr.ts) takes SeDebugPrivilege and writes bof-process### records to the pipe. The screenshot plug-in (scr.ts) sends JPEGs prefixed bof-screenshot###. moveDir.ts relocates the legitimate EXE, loader DLL and encrypted config.ini, then uses a Global\ExitEvent handoff to end the old instance and can delete the originals. It checks a list of sideload DLL names including SbieDll.dll, jli.dll, libcef.dll, winmm.dll, version.dll and msedge_elf.dll.
- Proxy plug-ins. channel.ts reflectively loads a Go client derived from the open-source Erfrp, patched to read config from shared memory Local\pc<PID> instead of a file. abchannel.ts is an Ably real-time client reading Local\pcs<PID>, relaying TCP via json and json.send events. ab2channel.ts is a SOCKS5 proxy over Ably's Pusher-compatible WebSocket, with a cpp-socks5 client string. The backdoor embeds no C2 domain: the C2 host and port arrive through the proxy plug-in's info command or an Ably channel, so there is nothing to extract statically.
- Attribution and infrastructure. Kaspersky does not attribute definitively. On victim hosts, FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle implants shared staging directories with GitDoor, deployed within a day of each other. FamousSparrow side-loaded wtsapi32.dll via a renamed Avast component, excint.exe, in %ProgramData%\excint\, using the RC4 key iotrh^%4CFGTj. CopperTurtle ran C:\Program Files\PDF24\pdfset.exe, which injected PLEAD RAT. GraphDoor victims also had Cobalt Strike beacons with C2 on twnic[.]top and ekmt[.]tw; proxy IPs 103.106.230[.]33 and 123.58.205[.]105 resolve to ms.twnic[.]top and ekmt[.]tw. Targets are government networks in Asia and Africa. The report notes that the initial drop of a MeshCentral Agent is unexplained and should be treated as suspicious.
Takeaway: the cloud traffic itself looks legitimate, so hunt the host. Look for non-browser processes doing client_credentials token requests to login.microsoftonline[.]com followed by Graph calls to unfamiliar SharePoint tenants. Check for \\.\pipe\p<PID> pipes, the Intel_Log directory, logs.dat under SystemCertificates\Cache, and the Global\ExitEvent object. Review ProgramData and Program Files for legitimate binaries paired with sideloaded DLLs, and for unsanctioned MeshCentral Agent installs. If you find one implant, look in the same staging directory for others. Proxy C2 IPs, hashes and domains are in the report's IOC section.

Targets are government networks in Asia and Africa. The report notes that the initial drop of a MeshCentral Agent is unexplained and should be treated as suspicious.

Takeaway: the cloud traffic itself looks legitimate, so hunt the host. Look for non-browser processes doing client_credentials token requests to login.microsoftonline[.]com followed by Graph calls to unfamiliar SharePoint tenants. Check for \\.\pipe\p<PID> pipes, the Intel_Log directory, logs.dat under SystemCertificates\Cache, and the Global\ExitEvent object. Review ProgramData and Program Files for legitimate binaries paired with sideloaded DLLs, and for unsanctioned MeshCentral Agent installs. If you find one implant, look in the same staging directory for others. Proxy C2 IPs, hashes and domains are in the report's IOC section.
